rigor.explanation: Sound economic core, but 'betrayal' leans on an emotional appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Free trade benefits Canadians by giving consumers choice of a wider range of products and fostering competition, which ultimately reduces prices. It also benefits Canadian businesses that produce products that New Zealanders want to buy. But free trade must go both ways.
rigor.explanation: Coherent reciprocity argument grounded in mainstream trade theory with clear premises.

rigor.statement: To Canadian farmers concerned about competition, I encourage you to look at New Zealand's experience. Today, you'd be hard-pressed to find a New Zealand farmer who wants to reverse the market liberalisation reforms of the 1980s.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning by analogy to NZ's experience; persuasive but partly an appeal to anecdote/analogy.

charisma.statement: Free trade benefits Canadians by giving consumers choice of a wider range of products and fostering competition, which ultimately reduces prices. It also benefits Canadian businesses that produce products that New Zealanders want to buy. But free trade must go both ways.
charisma.explanation: Frames the case in terms of mutual benefit to Canadians, appealing beyond her own side.

charisma.statement: To Canadian farmers concerned about competition, I encourage you to look at New Zealand's experience. Today, you'd be hard-pressed to find a New Zealand farmer who wants to reverse the market liberalisation reforms of the 1980s.
charisma.explanation: Directly addresses opponents' concerns and invites them in with a persuasive shared-experience appeal.

charisma.statement: Canada faces many of the same challenges as New Zealand. The ACT Party urges their Government to focus its time and resources on addressing those, rather than undermining our relationship for a cause that is actively making Canadians worse off.
charisma.explanation: Constructive framing that emphasises shared challenges, though ends with a pointed rebuke.

veracity.statement: Since then, the new Coalition Government – with ACT at its heart – has ended Labour and the Greens' war on farming.
veracity.explanation: 'War on farming' is partisan hyperbole; the claim overstates prior policy as an attack and its 'ending' as complete.

veracity.statement: New Zealand farmers feed 40 million people around the world.
veracity.explanation: A commonly cited round figure for NZ food exports; roughly in the right ballpark though imprecise.

veracity.statement: New Zealand farmers are the most emissions-efficient in the world, so punishing them, only for that production to be done offshore, makes absolutely no sense from an environmental perspective.
veracity.explanation: NZ pastoral dairy has low emissions intensity, but the flat superlative overstates a nuanced picture.

veracity.statement: The biggest challenge for many people in rural New Zealand right now is interest rates. They're higher than they need to be because of rampant inflation. Of course, inflation has been driven by massive government spending and excessive red tape which drives down productivity.
veracity.explanation: Partly accurate on spending and inflation, but oversimplified and the red-tape claim is unsupported.

veracity.statement: Stopping Significant Natural Areas was an early priority for me and the Government. Significant Natural Areas are parts of your land the council looks at and says "that looks pretty, you're going to lose your property rights over that". Under the indigenous biodiversity rules set up by James Shaw, councils were required to map out all the supposed Significant Natural Areas on private land in their districts.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the NPS-IB mapping requirement introduced under Shaw, though the 'looks pretty / lose property rights' gloss is a caricature.

veracity.statement: And the QE2 trust, where farmers voluntarily put covenants on special parts of their farms to protect them, If every QE2 covenant was stitched together it would be the land size of our fifth largest national park.
veracity.explanation: QE2 covenants do cover a large aggregate area; the specific 'fifth largest national park' comparison is plausible but not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: Despite that, farmer confidence has lifted because they see policies and actions from the Coalition Government that give them hope.
veracity.explanation: Farm confidence did recover from record lows over this period, but attributing it wholly to Coalition policy is a partial account.

specificity.statement: New Zealand farmers feed 40 million people around the world.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number but no basis or breakdown.

specificity.statement: We've removed that requirement and pushed the deadline out till 2030, while we do a proper review of the use of significant natural areas.
specificity.explanation: Names the action and a date (2030), though the review scope is left general.

specificity.statement: We're also removing stock exclusion rules. This would have forced farmers of some of the more extensive lightly grazed land, and most difficult terrain in the country, to fence off all waterways, for exceptionally low environmental benefits but at a massive cost to those farmers.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the rule and affected land type but no figures on cost or benefit.

specificity.statement: With ACT in Government, the starting point of the new RMA is going to be that it's your land, you can do with it what you like unless it's proven you are causing harm to your neighbours or the wider commons.
specificity.explanation: Articulates a concrete principle (presumption in favour of the landowner, harm-based test) for the RMA replacement.

specificity.statement: We wouldn't need to have fast-track legislation if we had the underlying policy right. Everyone should have a fast-track, whether they are building a wind farm, putting a culvert in, or building a deck.
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete examples (wind farm, culvert, deck) but no policy detail on how a universal fast-track would work.

specificity.statement: The recent budget was a step on the path to restoring fiscal discipline in Wellington. It didn't go as far as ACT would have liked, but it went further than it would have if ACT wasn't at the Cabinet table.
specificity.explanation: Directional claim about fiscal discipline with no figures or measures.

specificity.statement: And the QE2 trust, where farmers voluntarily put covenants on special parts of their farms to protect them, If every QE2 covenant was stitched together it would be the land size of our fifth largest national park.
specificity.explanation: Uses a concrete comparison to convey scale, though without a hectare figure.

civility.statement: All of those trends are well known. They all got worse under the latest Labour Government, but they all started before then. We’ve been drifting as a nation under successive governments.
civility.explanation: Comparatively measured — spreads blame across successive governments rather than a single-target attack.

civility.statement: We’re not even funding the Mongrel Mob to rehabilitate people from the drugs they sell anymore.
civility.explanation: A sensationalised, sneering characterisation rather than a fair account of the funding decision.

divination.statement: On trend the next left wing Government will be much worse than the Ardern regime.
divination.explanation: A prediction about a hypothetical future government extrapolated from a partisan 'trend' with no real evidentiary basis.

divination.statement: Make no mistake, our opponents and their damaging ideas could be back in power just over two years from now.
divination.explanation: A hedged prediction ('could') about the 2026 election — plausible given electoral cycles, and the timeframe is defined.

rigor.statement: Roger Douglas was better than Helen Clark. Helen Clark was better than Jacinda Ardern. Can you see where this is going?
rigor.explanation: Weak inductive extrapolation from a subjective, cherry-picked ranking to an implied inevitable decline — no evidence.

rigor.statement: My challenge to them is simple. If their ideas are so good, they should be able to persuade people to support them. If they’re not, then stop lowering the standards of political debate in our country.
rigor.explanation: Frames a reasonable point about persuasion but rests on a false-dichotomy structure (persuade or you're lowering standards).

rigor.statement: on average we find twenty-two per cent of New Zealanders rate their chances of voting ACT an eight or higher. That’s a much higher figure than New Zealand First, and even higher than the greens. ACT now has the third strongest brand in New Zealand politics
rigor.explanation: Builds a 'third strongest brand' conclusion on a self-commissioned, self-defined likelihood metric — selective evidence rather than actual vote share.

rigor.statement: All of those trends are well known. They all got worse under the latest Labour Government, but they all started before then. We’ve been drifting as a nation under successive governments.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges longer-run causes but asserts the 'trends' as established without citing the underlying data.

rigor.statement: Why did I as the MP for Epsom take on the unions, and let communities open better schools for mostly poor brown kids who never get a chance? Because nobody who sees the education statistics could stand idly by.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an emotional/anecdotal appeal ('nobody could stand idly by') and gestures at statistics without presenting them.

charisma.statement: Te Pāti Māori are bringing shame to the word Māori... it’s hard to believe the mighty totaras who built their party can approve of the outright hatred they are now spewing.
charisma.explanation: Purely divisive us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades or builds bridges.

charisma.statement: ACT has consistently, fearlessly and, most importantly, constructively, put the debate about our founding document on the agenda. We’ve forced the issue from dismissal to real debate. We want healthy debate so that we can find a way to be a united country.
charisma.explanation: Uses unity/'healthy debate' language, though on a highly contested topic it appeals mainly to its own side.

authenticity.statement: Many of you will know that I came to Parliament with a promise — to put the safety and wellbeing of the child at the centre of the state care system. Not the Treaty. Not whakapapa. Not politics. Just the best interests of the child.
authenticity.explanation: She did introduce a bill to repeal Section 7AA, so this stated commitment is backed by concrete action consistent with her record.

specificity.statement: Many of you will know that I came to Parliament with a promise — to put the safety and wellbeing of the child at the centre of the state care system. Not the Treaty. Not whakapapa. Not politics. Just the best interests of the child.
specificity.explanation: Names the goal and the system (state care) but frames it as a values statement rather than a mechanism.

specificity.statement: Race-based university admissions. Race-based procurement policies. Compulsory tikanga courses for real estate agents. A Waitangi Tribunal that thinks it has the power to summons a Minister that you elected into government.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete examples of policies she objects to, though without figures or precise references.

specificity.statement: And that’s why ACT is advancing a Treaty Principles Bill. To finally define the principles, through a democratic process, based on what was actually written and signed in 1840.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill and its aim (define principles democratically) but no detail on content or process.

strength.statement: Many of you will know that I came to Parliament with a promise — to put the safety and wellbeing of the child at the centre of the state care system. Not the Treaty. Not whakapapa. Not politics. Just the best interests of the child.
strength.explanation: Commitment tied to real legislative action (7AA repeal), but at this point only in progress, not delivered.

strength.statement: A few weeks ago, my legislation to repeal Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act passed its first reading in Parliament.
strength.explanation: Genuine progress she drove, but at this stage only a first reading, not enacted delivery.

strength.statement: And that’s why ACT is advancing a Treaty Principles Bill. To finally define the principles, through a democratic process, based on what was actually written and signed in 1840.
strength.explanation: An announced/aspirational bill; the Treaty Principles Bill was ultimately voted down, so follow-through did not materialise.

veracity.statement: No child should be taken out of a loving foster home because their carers are the “wrong” race, and no child should be placed back in an unsafe environment because that’s with the “right” race. But that’s what we’ve seen under Labour’s reforms of Oranga Tamariki, with Section 7AA being the justification for these decisions.
veracity.explanation: 7AA prioritises whakapapa/whanau connections, but the sweeping claim that it causes children to be pulled from loving homes or returned to unsafe ones is a contested characterisation stated as established fact.

veracity.statement: A few weeks ago, my legislation to repeal Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act passed its first reading in Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Factually accurate; the 7AA repeal bill did pass first reading in 2024.

veracity.statement: The so-called Treaty Principles are not written down or defined in any one place. They have emerged in the last few decades, one court decision at a time, from an unelected judiciary.
veracity.explanation: Partly true that principles are not codified in one place, but they originate in the 1975 Treaty of Waitangi Act (Parliament) as well as courts/Tribunal, so 'from an unelected judiciary' is misleading.

veracity.statement: Race-based university admissions. Race-based procurement policies. Compulsory tikanga courses for real estate agents. A Waitangi Tribunal that thinks it has the power to summons a Minister that you elected into government.
veracity.explanation: Each item references a real thing but is framed pejoratively ('race-based') in a way that omits context.

civility.statement: No child should be taken out of a loving foster home because their carers are the “wrong” race, and no child should be placed back in an unsafe environment because that’s with the “right” race. But that’s what we’ve seen under Labour’s reforms of Oranga Tamariki, with Section 7AA being the justification for these decisions.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of a Labour policy and its consequences rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: For Labour, the Greens, and Te Pati Māori to suggest that I'm not a real Māori or I can't think for myself because I don't follow their beliefs is a disgrace. It brings shame to our Parliament and makes a mockery of all New Zealanders who voted for change.
civility.explanation: Charged language ('disgrace', 'mockery') though it responds to genuinely demeaning attacks directed at her.

civility.statement: I find it offensive, and frankly racist, that anyone would put one aspect of their identity on a pedestal, above all the rest.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents' view as racist, an accusatory framing rather than substantive engagement.

rigor.statement: No child should be taken out of a loving foster home because their carers are the “wrong” race, and no child should be placed back in an unsafe environment because that’s with the “right” race. But that’s what we’ve seen under Labour’s reforms of Oranga Tamariki, with Section 7AA being the justification for these decisions.
rigor.explanation: Emotive framing ('wrong'/'right' race) generalised from asserted cases without evidence of prevalence.

rigor.statement: For Labour, the Greens, and Te Pati Māori to suggest that I'm not a real Māori or I can't think for myself because I don't follow their beliefs is a disgrace. It brings shame to our Parliament and makes a mockery of all New Zealanders who voted for change.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable grievance but leans on indignation rather than argument.

rigor.statement: I find it offensive, and frankly racist, that anyone would put one aspect of their identity on a pedestal, above all the rest.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to offence; asserts the charge of racism without a developed argument.

rigor.statement: The so-called Treaty Principles are not written down or defined in any one place. They have emerged in the last few decades, one court decision at a time, from an unelected judiciary.
rigor.explanation: A defensible point undercut by a selective account that omits the legislative origin.

specificity.statement: We’ve abolished Labour’s prisoner reduction target, because a self-imposed limit on our capacity to lock up people who would do you harm was madness. In fact at the latest Budget we prioritised funding for more than 800 additional prison beds.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific figure of 800+ prison beds and the policy reversed.

strength.statement: You’re no longer forced to pay lawyers, activists, and failed journalists to write sob stories for hardened offenders, because we scrapped funding for so-called cultural reports.
strength.explanation: A concrete delivered action she was responsible for as minister.

strength.statement: We’ve abolished Labour’s prisoner reduction target, because a self-imposed limit on our capacity to lock up people who would do you harm was madness. In fact at the latest Budget we prioritised funding for more than 800 additional prison beds.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered budget funding, not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: Within ACT’s first hundred days in government we ensured that if someone who victimises you is found to be a member of a gang, that membership will become an aggravating factor at their sentencing.
strength.explanation: A concrete legislative measure actually delivered early in the term, matching the stated commitment.

veracity.statement: You’re no longer forced to pay lawyers, activists, and failed journalists to write sob stories for hardened offenders, because we scrapped funding for so-called cultural reports.
veracity.explanation: The Government did scrap funding for section 27 cultural reports; the characterisation of authors and reports is loaded but the core action is accurate.

veracity.statement: We’ve abolished Labour’s prisoner reduction target, because a self-imposed limit on our capacity to lock up people who would do you harm was madness. In fact at the latest Budget we prioritised funding for more than 800 additional prison beds.
veracity.explanation: The coalition did drop the prison population reduction target and funded new prison capacity, broadly consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: In six years under Labour, gang membership on the National List increased by over 92%. The known gang members now number just under 10,000.
veracity.explanation: Gang List numbers did rise substantially over that period and neared ~10,000; figures are broadly in line with reported data though such tallies carry caveats.

veracity.statement: Within ACT’s first hundred days in government we ensured that if someone who victimises you is found to be a member of a gang, that membership will become an aggravating factor at their sentencing.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the gang-membership aggravating-factor legislation enacted.

veracity.statement: Labour’s rushed response to the Christchurch shootings punished every responsible licenced firearms owner in New Zealand for the evil actions of one Australian who never should have been given a firearms licence in the first place. And it didn’t work. Last year, New Zealand experienced half its yearly average gun deaths in a period of just 17 days.
veracity.explanation: The '17 days' statistic is presented without source and used to imply the reforms failed, a misleading juxtaposition; gun-death causes are not attributable to the buyback in this way.

veracity.statement: My colleague Todd Stephenson is the sponsor of a private member’s bill that would require any prisoner applying for parole to first undertake rehab or education courses. That bill has passed its first reading with support from those in Parliament. Shout out to Te Pati Māori, who forgot to cast their vote on that one.
veracity.explanation: Describes a real member's bill and its first reading; the jab about a missed vote is plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: The latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey shows that Māori - more than any other ethnicity – make up a large number - of the victims of crime. We make up 37 per cent of victims.
veracity.explanation: The NZCVS does show elevated Māori victimisation, but the precise '37 per cent of victims' framing is imprecise relative to how the survey reports rates.

civility.statement: You’re no longer forced to pay lawyers, activists, and failed journalists to write sob stories for hardened offenders, because we scrapped funding for so-called cultural reports.
civility.explanation: Denigrates report authors as 'activists and failed journalists' and offenders' accounts as 'sob stories' — personal disparagement.

civility.statement: Labour’s rushed response to the Christchurch shootings punished every responsible licenced firearms owner in New Zealand for the evil actions of one Australian who never should have been given a firearms licence in the first place. And it didn’t work. Last year, New Zealand experienced half its yearly average gun deaths in a period of just 17 days.
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism of policy, legitimate in target though framed emotively ('punished every... owner').

civility.statement: My colleague Todd Stephenson is the sponsor of a private member’s bill that would require any prisoner applying for parole to first undertake rehab or education courses. That bill has passed its first reading with support from those in Parliament. Shout out to Te Pati Māori, who forgot to cast their vote on that one.
civility.explanation: A light sarcastic dig at Te Pāti Māori rather than a serious personal attack.

civility.statement: Not once have I heard Te Pāti Māori stand up for Māori victims of crime – for any victims of crime. Not once.
civility.explanation: Sweeping dismissal of an opponent's concern for victims, us-vs-them framing.

civility.statement: Your protectors in Labour and the Greens have been turfed out of government. Now that ACT has its hands on the levers of justice we will not use a light touch... We threw out the wet bus tickets. The joyride is over. ACT’s road-spikes are permanently deployed.
civility.explanation: Metaphor-heavy attack on opponents ('protectors of criminals') rather than substantive engagement.

rigor.statement: Labour’s rushed response to the Christchurch shootings punished every responsible licenced firearms owner in New Zealand for the evil actions of one Australian who never should have been given a firearms licence in the first place. And it didn’t work. Last year, New Zealand experienced half its yearly average gun deaths in a period of just 17 days.
rigor.explanation: Cherry-picked statistic and post hoc reasoning ('it didn't work') plus loaded framing.

rigor.statement: The latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey shows that Māori - more than any other ethnicity – make up a large number - of the victims of crime. We make up 37 per cent of victims.
rigor.explanation: Cites survey evidence to support the point about Māori victims, a reasonable evidentiary basis.

rigor.statement: Not once have I heard Te Pāti Māori stand up for Māori victims of crime – for any victims of crime. Not once.
rigor.explanation: Absolute claim ('not once') from personal recall — hyperbolic and unfalsifiable as stated.

charisma.statement: Your protectors in Labour and the Greens have been turfed out of government. Now that ACT has its hands on the levers of justice we will not use a light touch... We threw out the wet bus tickets. The joyride is over. ACT’s road-spikes are permanently deployed.
charisma.explanation: Vivid rally rhetoric that energises supporters but is combative and us-vs-them, not consensus-building.

specificity.statement: From this weekend, no more forced 12am closures, no more confusion about what counts as a ‘substantial meal’, and no more telling customers they have to go home just as things are getting started.
specificity.explanation: Concrete named changes (12am closures, 'substantial meal' rule) with an immediate timeframe.

specificity.statement: This change brings some much-needed common sense back into the law. If a venue is licensed and operating responsibly, it should be able to decide its own hours.
specificity.explanation: States a principle (venues set own hours) but leans on the vague 'common sense' framing.

specificity.statement: More flexibility means more customers, more sales, and more vibrant communities. It’s good for business and good for the people who just want to enjoy a night out with friends and family.
specificity.explanation: General benefits asserted without figures or measures.

strength.statement: From this weekend, no more forced 12am closures, no more confusion about what counts as a ‘substantial meal’, and no more telling customers they have to go home just as things are getting started.
strength.explanation: Describes a law change actually passed via his amendment, taking effect immediately — delivered, not just promised.

divination.statement: More flexibility means more customers, more sales, and more vibrant communities. It’s good for business and good for the people who just want to enjoy a night out with friends and family.
divination.explanation: Prediction that deregulated hours will lift sales and vibrancy; plausible directionally but unquantified and uncertain.

authenticity.statement: Prior to the election, ACT campaigned on increasing defence spending to 1.5% of GDP, or $4.35 billion over four years, with a long-term target of reaching 2% by 2030.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a prior campaign position consistently; no visible contradiction, though delivery is not yet demonstrated.

specificity.statement: We have been taking the so-called benign strategic environment for granted, but the rule of history is that big fish eat the little fish. New Zealand needs to wake up, get together with its mates, and up our defensive capability – fast.
specificity.explanation: Calls for action but without concrete measures at this point in the statement.

specificity.statement: Prior to the election, ACT campaigned on increasing defence spending to 1.5% of GDP, or $4.35 billion over four years, with a long-term target of reaching 2% by 2030.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (1.5% of GDP, $4.35b over four years, 2% by 2030) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Does it make more sense for the government to own a television station, or a P8 Poseidon? Should we keep a 51% share in a power company, or get our hands on some more frigates?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete assets (TV station, P8 Poseidon, 51% power company share, frigates) illustrating the trade-off.

veracity.statement: Australia’s defence spending has already surged above 2%, heading to 2.4% by the end of the decade.
veracity.explanation: Australia's defence spending is around/above 2% of GDP with planned increases toward ~2.3–2.4%, broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: This morning, the New Zealand Initiative released a report valuing the government’s existing assets at $571 billion.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific attributed report figure; consistent with the kind of Crown asset valuations reported.

rigor.statement: We have been taking the so-called benign strategic environment for granted, but the rule of history is that big fish eat the little fish. New Zealand needs to wake up, get together with its mates, and up our defensive capability – fast.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to analogy/aphorism ('big fish eat little fish') rather than specific evidence.

rigor.statement: Does it make more sense for the government to own a television station, or a P8 Poseidon? Should we keep a 51% share in a power company, or get our hands on some more frigates?
rigor.explanation: Framed as a false dichotomy — the choices are posed as either/or when they need not be mutually exclusive.

authenticity.statement: ACT has the best track record of any party for telling it like it is and driving real change: getting inflation under control, backing people to earn and save, cutting red tape so businesses can invest, and making it easier to build the homes and infrastructure New Zealanders need.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit consistent with ACT's stated agenda, but 'best track record of any party' is self-assessment unverified from the text.

specificity.statement: The most glaring omission was the idea New Zealanders can least afford: Labour still has not explained how it will fund the roughly $13 billion hole created by its commitment to reverse the Government’s pay equity changes.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific figure ($13b) tied to a specific commitment (reversing pay equity changes).

specificity.statement: ACT has the best track record of any party for telling it like it is and driving real change: getting inflation under control, backing people to earn and save, cutting red tape so businesses can invest, and making it easier to build the homes and infrastructure New Zealanders need.
specificity.explanation: Names themes (inflation, red tape, housing) but no figures, mechanisms, or dates.

strength.statement: ACT has the best track record of any party for telling it like it is and driving real change: getting inflation under control, backing people to earn and save, cutting red tape so businesses can invest, and making it easier to build the homes and infrastructure New Zealanders need.
strength.explanation: Lists areas of claimed delivery, some in progress; mixes delivered items with broad claims without specifics.

veracity.statement: Hipkins’ examples of affordable policies included ‘free’ GP visits and a new Auckland harbour crossing without tolls on the existing bridge. But he can’t make the cost of those policies disappear. Someone has to pay, he just hopes Kiwis won’t ask who.
veracity.explanation: Accurately notes these policies have real fiscal costs; the motive attribution is opinion.

veracity.statement: The most glaring omission was the idea New Zealanders can least afford: Labour still has not explained how it will fund the roughly $13 billion hole created by its commitment to reverse the Government’s pay equity changes.
veracity.explanation: The ~$13b figure reflects the Government's savings estimate from its pay equity changes; presenting it as an unfunded 'hole' is contestable framing stated as fact.

veracity.statement: Hipkins didn’t even mention crime, and not a word on Labour’s view of the Treaty and how to keep the country united. This from the guy whose time as Police Minister led to a crime wave, and whose time as Prime Minister was met with record racial division.
veracity.explanation: Causal claims that Hipkins personally 'led to a crime wave' and 'record racial division' are simplistic and largely unsubstantiated.

civility.statement: That speech wasn’t lightweight, it was featherweight. Any politician could have read it out, because who doesn’t want good things?
civility.explanation: Mocking put-down of an opponent's speech rather than engagement with its content.

civility.statement: I listen to Chris Hipkins and I hear Jacinda Ardern ‘light’, a lilting voice that says all the right things, promises nirvana, but never says how we will pay for it. He reminds me of an anaesthetist before he gives you the injection that knocks you out and makes you forget the pain.
civility.explanation: Personalised ridicule (comparison to an anaesthetist, 'Ardern light') focused on character/style rather than substance.

civility.statement: Hipkins didn’t even mention crime, and not a word on Labour’s view of the Treaty and how to keep the country united. This from the guy whose time as Police Minister led to a crime wave, and whose time as Prime Minister was met with record racial division.
civility.explanation: Personal attack blaming Hipkins individually for a 'crime wave' and 'racial division'.

rigor.statement: I listen to Chris Hipkins and I hear Jacinda Ardern ‘light’, a lilting voice that says all the right things, promises nirvana, but never says how we will pay for it. He reminds me of an anaesthetist before he gives you the injection that knocks you out and makes you forget the pain.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical analogy and characterisation in place of argument, though embeds a real critique about unfunded promises.

veracity.explanation: Labour did restructure health (Te Whatu Ora); 'patients were ignored' is a contestable rhetorical characterisation.

civility.statement: It was a deck chair speech. All the changes he’s proposing involve politicians and bureaucrats being reorganised, and will have no effect on actual people.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'deck chair' metaphor, but aimed at the substance of the proposals (reorganisation) rather than the person.

civility.statement: But to give Hipkins credit, giving a speech in Auckland was probably a bold step for someone who struggles to think outside the Wellington bubble.
civility.explanation: Backhanded compliment that mocks the opponent personally ('Wellington bubble').

civility.statement: The amazing thing is Chris Hipkins’s changes could all be made without any real person in New Zealand noticing. It may not be long before some of Hipkins’s caucus decide to reorganise him.
civility.explanation: Jibe implying Hipkins may be rolled by his caucus — a cheap shot, though a common political jab.

rigor.statement: We’ve seen this before. Hipkins spent resources reorganising the health system, and what we got was a new org chart while patients were ignored.
rigor.explanation: Uses a past example to predict failure of new proposals — a reasonable analogy but asserted rather than evidenced.

specificity.statement: The citizens' arrest changes are huge for the retail sector. Victims who stand up for themselves and defend their property or workplace shouldn't have to fear being treated like criminals. Under the changes, a citizen's arrest can be carried out for any Crimes Act offence and at any time of day.
specificity.explanation: Precisely describes the legal change (any Crimes Act offence, any time of day).

specificity.statement: The other big win is instant punishment in the form of infringement fees for people caught shoplifting. A swift, certain penalty is the best deterrent. When would-be thieves know they can be stopped on the spot and penalised on the spot, the calculation changes.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (infringement fees, on-the-spot penalty) though without fee amounts.

specificity.statement: Importantly, these changes have come about by listening to the people on the frontline – dairy owners, bottle store operators, and retailers who deal with the consequences of lawlessness every day. I have even heard complaints of shoplifting from hospice shop workers.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete stakeholder groups consulted (dairy owners, bottle store operators, hospice shop workers).

specificity.statement: This new law adds yet another layer of accountability for criminals, on top of other initiatives ACT has already delivered – restoring Three Strikes, a new aggravating factor for offenders who target people working alone, and also for offences against people working at a business connected to the family home. We've also got the courts moving again and are putting the rights of victims back at the centre of our justice system.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete named initiatives, though without figures or dates.

strength.statement: This new law adds yet another layer of accountability for criminals, on top of other initiatives ACT has already delivered – restoring Three Strikes, a new aggravating factor for offenders who target people working alone, and also for offences against people working at a business connected to the family home. We've also got the courts moving again and are putting the rights of victims back at the centre of our justice system.
strength.explanation: Points to specific measures already enacted (Three Strikes restoration, sole-charge aggravating factor), demonstrating delivery rather than mere promises.

veracity.statement: The citizens' arrest changes are huge for the retail sector. Victims who stand up for themselves and defend their property or workplace shouldn't have to fear being treated like criminals. Under the changes, a citizen's arrest can be carried out for any Crimes Act offence and at any time of day.
veracity.explanation: Accurately summarises the announced expansion of citizen's arrest powers in the bill.

authenticity.statement: Since 2016, I've argued new migrants should understand a simple proposition: in New Zealand, regardless of your gender, sexuality, ethnicity, or religion, you have the same legal rights as everybody else.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistently held position over nearly a decade, now matched by the citizenship-test policy; the words-vs-record signal is one of consistency, though only partly verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: Nearly a decade later, ACT has got it over the line.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his stated long-running advocacy, so words align with the record on this point.

specificity.statement: Since 2016, I've argued new migrants should understand a simple proposition: in New Zealand, regardless of your gender, sexuality, ethnicity, or religion, you have the same legal rights as everybody else.
specificity.explanation: Names a dated position and a concrete principle (equal legal rights across named characteristics), but no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: Questions will cover basic knowledge of New Zealand law, including the Bill of Rights. That means understanding equal rights regardless of sex or race, free speech, religious freedom, and democratic principles.
specificity.explanation: Concrete description of the test's content areas, though no detail on pass marks, number of questions, or timing.

specificity.statement: This citizenship test says: welcome to New Zealand. Here are the freedoms you inherit, the responsibilities you accept, and the democratic society you are now part of. That is how a confident country welcomes new citizens.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational framing with no concrete detail.

strength.statement: Nearly a decade later, ACT has got it over the line.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for turning a long-held position into an announced government policy; delivery is real but the test is being introduced (announced), not yet fully implemented.

veracity.statement: Questions will cover basic knowledge of New Zealand law, including the Bill of Rights. That means understanding equal rights regardless of sex or race, free speech, religious freedom, and democratic principles.
veracity.explanation: Factual description of the announced test's scope; plausible and consistent with the accompanying minister's announcement.

civility.statement: For too long, politicians have taken these foundations for granted, or worse, apologised for them.
civility.explanation: A rhetorical swipe at unnamed 'politicians' rather than a personal attack, but unsubstantiated and mildly disparaging.

rigor.statement: For too long, politicians have taken these foundations for granted, or worse, apologised for them.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping assertion with no evidence or examples; leans on emotive appeal to shared values.

specificity.statement: Violent crime is coming down, and the values of our community are improving.

charisma.statement: I want to thank Federated Farmers, and many of you here, for the constructive role you've played in helping shape these changes. Your feedback is vital to making sure the final rules are workable, sensible, and fit for purpose.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive and appreciative, crediting the audience's contribution and inviting continued collaboration, though addressed to a friendly sector audience.

veracity.statement: Productivity growth has been flat for nearly two decades, asset price growth, especially in property, is the main way people have gotten ahead.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: NZ labour-productivity growth has been weak and housing has been the dominant wealth-builder over that period.

veracity.statement: Sharesies is the biggest platform in New Zealand with about 550,000 Kiwis on their platform, just above one tenth of the adult population.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with Sharesies' reported user base and NZ adult population share; a checkable, plausibly accurate figure.

veracity.statement: This cost-of-living crisis we're in? It's really a productivity slump. It is not just that inflation has driven up costs. It is that wages have not kept up with inflation. Real economic growth, after inflation, has gone backwards over the last five years.
veracity.explanation: Real per-capita GDP going backwards over recent years is broadly supported; 'last five years' as a blanket claim slightly overstates a mixed record.

veracity.statement: It could be funded out of the roughly $600 million KiwiSaver annual subsidy. There are around 60,000 students in any cohort. $500 each is $30 million. Just five per cent of the annual subsidy could fund a $500 starting investment for every fifth-form student in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The '$600 million KiwiSaver annual subsidy' figure is uncertain given the government contribution was reduced in 2025, so the funding base may be overstated.

civility.statement: Some people think business is easy, so business success isn't earned. They conclude it's more moral just to take it than let you keep unearned wealth. People who have that view suffer from a terrible condition called observer bias.
civility.explanation: Characterises unnamed opponents' views in a caricatured form before rebutting them; a soft strawman.

civility.statement: Many people go their entire lives without encountering them at all, the Green Party's electoral prospects rely on this.
civility.explanation: A gratuitous partisan jab implying the Greens depend on public financial illiteracy; a cheap shot rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Because a freer, more prosperous New Zealand will not be built by telling people to resent success. It will be achieved by having more people who believe in building success.
civility.explanation: Implicitly casts opponents as promoters of resentment, a pointed but not personal characterisation.

specificity.explanation: General direction; the concrete ailments and mechanisms come later, not here.

specificity.statement: The latest New Zealand Health Survey shows that one in four adults said the time taken to get a GP appointment was a barrier to seeing a GP in the previous year. That is more than double the rate recorded in 2021/22, when it was 11.6 per cent.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, gives a precise baseline figure (11.6%) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: New Zealand already has more than a thousand community pharmacies contracted with Health New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives an approximate figure ('more than a thousand') and the contracting body.

specificity.statement: From June 2026, pharmacists can treat six conditions: UTIs, conjunctivitis, head lice, scabies, oral rehydration, and the emergency contraceptive pill. That is a good start, and we can go further.
specificity.explanation: Names all six conditions and a precise start date.

specificity.statement: ACT wants to let pharmacies do three things they can’t do today. First, pharmacies should be able to treat more everyday conditions. Second, pharmacies should be able to help manage long-term medication and order routine blood tests where appropriate. Third, pharmacies should be able to provide skin lesion triage and monitoring.
specificity.explanation: Lays out three concrete, distinct policy proposals, though the 'how' is elaborated further on.

specificity.statement: It will greatly free up overwhelmed GPs and EDs by spreading the load.
specificity.explanation: Predicts relief but with no quantified target.

specificity.explanation: Names the programme, year, number of regions, participant count, and covered conditions.

specificity.statement: Satisfaction with the care they received was broadly similar to a GP visit. Eighty-eight per cent of participants had their needs met through the pharmacy consultation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise 88% figure tied to the pilot.

specificity.statement: In New Zealand, approximately 1.1 million adults are on antihypertensive medication. Around 250,000 New Zealanders have diagnosed type 2 diabetes. Around 600,000 are on statins.
specificity.explanation: Three precise population figures supporting the long-term-medication proposal.

specificity.statement: The UK has tried this, and patients demonstrated approximately a 10 per cent improvement in medication adherence sustained at six months. Australia also reports improved medication adherence and clinical outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified outcome (10%, six months) and named jurisdictions.

specificity.statement: ‘Slip, slop, slap and wrap’ is seared into most of our brains but New Zealand’s Melanoma death rates remain the worst in the world.
specificity.explanation: A stark comparative claim but no figures given.

specificity.statement: The patient would pay a fixed fee, indicatively around $25 to $40. That is intended to be materially cheaper than a standard GP visit. Typical GP visit fees are around $45-$100, so this service would sit at around half that price point, depending on final pricing.
specificity.explanation: Gives indicative price ranges for the service and for GP visits, with the comparison spelled out.

specificity.explanation: Precise performance ranges with benchmarking against GP and specialist performance.

specificity.statement: Wellington has proven over and over again that more bureaucracy does not improve outcomes for patients.
specificity.explanation: Vague slogan-style claim with no example or measure.

veracity.explanation: Inflation and interest rates did fall from 2022-23 peaks, so directionally accurate, but attributing this mainly to government spending discipline overstates the government's role given global drivers and RBNZ monetary policy.

specificity.statement: Currently, 5,000 people die from the harms of tobacco-related illnesses every year. Māori and Pacific whānau are more likely to suffer tobacco harms, with Māori rangatahi being particularly at risk of taking up smoking.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete number and identifies affected populations.

rigor.statement: This National, Act and New Zealand First Government will go down in history as one of the most harmful, anti-evidence governments New Zealand has ever had.
rigor.explanation: Superlative assertion ("most harmful ever") with no comparative evidence; hyperbole.

rigor.statement: Currently, 5,000 people die from the harms of tobacco-related illnesses every year. Māori and Pacific whānau are more likely to suffer tobacco harms, with Māori rangatahi being particularly at risk of taking up smoking.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based claim consistent with health research, supporting the argument against repeal.

rigor.statement: Repealing smoke free legislation means loved ones will die so tobacco companies can continue to profit and the government can cut taxes for the wealthiest few.
rigor.explanation: The health premise has evidential basis, but the causal chain to "tax cuts for the wealthiest" is asserted rather than demonstrated.

veracity.statement: Currently, 5,000 people die from the harms of tobacco-related illnesses every year. Māori and Pacific whānau are more likely to suffer tobacco harms, with Māori rangatahi being particularly at risk of taking up smoking.
veracity.explanation: The ~5,000 annual tobacco deaths figure and higher Māori/Pacific smoking harm are well established in NZ public-health data.

veracity.statement: The plan to reduce the nicotine content of cigarettes and their availability in our communities made Aotearoa a world leader.
veracity.explanation: NZ's 2022 smokefree denicotinisation/retail-reduction law was internationally recognised as world-leading; broadly accurate, with "world leader" being a fair characterisation.

divination.statement: Repealing smoke free legislation means loved ones will die so tobacco companies can continue to profit and the government can cut taxes for the wealthiest few.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased tobacco deaths from the repeal; directionally supported by modelling of the reforms, though the attributed motive is contested.

civility.statement: Climate delay is the new denial. Failure to act now will see the future of communities like South Dunedin swamped in floods
civility.explanation: "Climate delay is the new denial" is a rhetorical jab but aimed at policy stance, not persons.

civility.statement: The Government rejected support for this pilot back in 2024, but as we saw as recently as October, the risks haven’t magically gone away.
civility.explanation: "Haven't magically gone away" is mildly sardonic but the point is substantive about ongoing risk.

specificity.statement: The local community, iwi, researchers and both local councils have all pulled together to create a plan for a future we can all be excited for. All we need is for the Government to back us.
specificity.explanation: References a plan and its authors but gives no detail of its contents.

veracity.statement: The Government rejected support for this pilot back in 2024, but as we saw as recently as October, the risks haven’t magically gone away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2024 government rejection and a recent flood event; plausible and specific, though not independently confirmable from the text.

divination.statement: Climate delay is the new denial. Failure to act now will see the future of communities like South Dunedin swamped in floods
divination.explanation: Predicts increased flooding for low-lying South Dunedin absent adaptation; consistent with sea-level-rise projections, though timeframe is unspecified.

charisma.statement: The local community, iwi, researchers and both local councils have all pulled together to create a plan for a future we can all be excited for. All we need is for the Government to back us.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, coalition-building language emphasising collaboration across community, iwi and councils and inviting the Government in.

charisma.statement: It would also mean creating a workable blueprint for how central government, local government and communities can work together to safeguard our collective future.
charisma.explanation: Frames the proposal as a cooperative model bringing tiers of government and communities together toward a shared goal.

civility.statement: This is a false and harmful tradeoff that should never be on the table when envisioning a future for our youngest learners
civility.explanation: Harsh characterisation of a policy framing but attacks the idea (the quality/affordability tradeoff), not a person.

civility.statement: Instead of investing into our children's critical early years, the Government continues to prop up a profit-driven system that relies on overcharging parents, underpaying kaiako and, as a result, short-changing our tamariki.
civility.explanation: Strong policy criticism attributing bad motives (propping up profit) but framed around system outcomes rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Private profit and greed have no place in the education system.
civility.explanation: Ideological assertion about a sector rather than a personal attack.

rigor.statement: This is a false and harmful tradeoff that should never be on the table when envisioning a future for our youngest learners
rigor.explanation: Asserts the tradeoff is 'false' without evidence; leans on an appeal to values rather than demonstrating the quality/affordability tension is unreal.

rigor.statement: Instead of investing into our children's critical early years, the Government continues to prop up a profit-driven system that relies on overcharging parents, underpaying kaiako and, as a result, short-changing our tamariki.
rigor.explanation: Chain of claims asserted without cited evidence; emotive framing ('short-changing our tamariki').

veracity.statement: Instead of investing into our children's critical early years, the Government continues to prop up a profit-driven system that relies on overcharging parents, underpaying kaiako and, as a result, short-changing our tamariki.
veracity.explanation: ECE underfunding and low kaiako pay are well documented, but 'overcharging parents' and the causal 'short-changing' chain are contestable characterisations.

specificity.statement: In our Green Budget, we've shown the solution is already right in front of us: remove the corporate for-profit sector, and make high-quality ECE free and accessible for all.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete direction (remove for-profit sector, free ECE) tied to a published Green Budget, but no figures, mechanism or timeline given here.

specificity.statement: Private profit and greed have no place in the education system.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like value statement; commits to no measure, figure or mechanism.

strength.statement: In our Green Budget, we've shown the solution is already right in front of us: remove the corporate for-profit sector, and make high-quality ECE free and accessible for all.
strength.explanation: Aspiration from an opposition party with no delivery power; policy proposed, not enacted.

civility.statement: The Government is trying to cut corners on the education of our tamariki, setting them up to fail while setting up businesses for boosted profits
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith ('setting them up to fail') to the Government; more accusation than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: David Seymour and his Ministry of Regulation are laser focussed on how to make ECE more profitable for corporate chains, rather than prioritising what we know works
civility.explanation: Attributes self-interested motive to a named minister rather than engaging the report's stated rationale (access/affordability).

rigor.statement: The Government is trying to cut corners on the education of our tamariki, setting them up to fail while setting up businesses for boosted profits
rigor.explanation: Attributes intent without evidence; rhetorical antithesis ('fail'/'profits') rather than argued causation.

rigor.statement: David Seymour and his Ministry of Regulation are laser focussed on how to make ECE more profitable for corporate chains, rather than prioritising what we know works
rigor.explanation: Assertion of motive presented as fact; false-dichotomy framing (profit vs 'what works').

rigor.statement: Research quite clearly shows that the first 1000 days are foundational to a child's early development.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to research to support the argument, though the body of evidence is only gestured at, not cited.

veracity.statement: The report, released today, recommends what it calls "greater flexibility in workforce qualifications" to support access to ECE.
veracity.explanation: A direct, quoted characterisation of the Ministry for Regulation report's recommendation; presented accurately with the report's own wording.

veracity.statement: Research quite clearly shows that the first 1000 days are foundational to a child's early development.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with established early-childhood development research on the first 1000 days.

civility.statement: The Government has built on its archaic anti-worker legacy by undermining the pay of our ECE teachers
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of policy record ('anti-worker'); charged language but aimed at the Government's actions, not personal insult.

rigor.statement: The working conditions of our teachers are the learning conditions of our tamariki.
rigor.explanation: Plausible causal link asserted as an aphorism; reasonable but unevidenced.

veracity.statement: The Government has built on its archaic anti-worker legacy by undermining the pay of our ECE teachers

veracity.statement: Today's changes announced by the Associate Minister of Education will cut the pay of ECE teachers charged with giving our tamariki the best possible start in life.
veracity.explanation: The changes to pay-parity funding are real; 'cut the pay' overstates a complex funding change and omits context.

veracity.statement: Late last year, community ECE workers took strike action for the first time in their history.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reported 2023 first-ever strike action by community ECE workers; a checkable factual claim.

specificity.statement: The working conditions of our teachers are the learning conditions of our tamariki.
specificity.explanation: Memorable principle but general; no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: The Green Party will continue to fight for pay parity and equity for ECE teachers.
specificity.explanation: General commitment to a cause with no mechanism, figure or timeframe.

strength.statement: The Green Party will continue to fight for pay parity and equity for ECE teachers.
strength.explanation: Statement of intent from opposition; consistent with the party's advocacy but no delivery power to enact it.

divination.statement: Today's changes announced by the Associate Minister of Education will cut the pay of ECE teachers charged with giving our tamariki the best possible start in life.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the announced changes will cut ECE teacher pay; directionally plausible given the pay-parity funding changes, but scale and net effect uncertain.

civility.statement: Whether it's high inflation or a manufactured recession, intentional Government policies see regular New Zealanders pay the price while the rich laugh their way to the bank
civility.explanation: 'Manufactured recession' and 'laugh their way to the bank' are sensational and impute deliberate harm rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Luxon's Government has chosen to double down on trickle down tax cuts which disproportionately benefit the wealthiest by siphoning resources from those who need it
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's fiscal choices with loaded framing ('trickle down', 'siphoning') but targets policy.

rigor.statement: Whether it's high inflation or a manufactured recession, intentional Government policies see regular New Zealanders pay the price while the rich laugh their way to the bank
rigor.explanation: 'Manufactured recession' asserted without support; emotive imagery over evidence.

rigor.statement: That means multi-multi-millionaires are paying a lower effective tax rate than nurses, teachers, firefighters and supermarket checkout operators.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion follows from the cited effective-rate evidence, though the comparison mixes tax-on-income and tax-on-economic-income.

veracity.statement: Whether it's high inflation or a manufactured recession, intentional Government policies see regular New Zealanders pay the price while the rich laugh their way to the bank

veracity.statement: Luxon's Government has chosen to double down on trickle down tax cuts which disproportionately benefit the wealthiest by siphoning resources from those who need it

veracity.statement: A year ago, the IRD told us the wealthiest 311 households hold more wealth than the bottom two and a half million New Zealanders.

veracity.statement: That means multi-multi-millionaires are paying a lower effective tax rate than nurses, teachers, firefighters and supermarket checkout operators.

specificity.statement: The Greens campaigned unapologetically on ensuring the wealthiest pay their fair share. If we did that, we could introduce a tax-free bracket for income below $10,000, fund meaningful climate action, build tens of thousands of public houses, de-carbonise and reduce energy costs for homes, make dental care-free and invest in the infrastructure we all rely on
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete uses (tax-free bracket under $10k, public houses, free dental) but without amounts or timeframes for each.

specificity.statement: A 2.5% Wealth Tax on assets - things like properties or shares - worth more than $4 million (minus mortgages and other debt) for couples and $2 million (minus mortgages and other debt) for individuals.
specificity.explanation: Precise rate (2.5%), thresholds ($4m/$2m), asset base and debt treatment all named.

divination.statement: The Greens campaigned unapologetically on ensuring the wealthiest pay their fair share. If we did that, we could introduce a tax-free bracket for income below $10,000, fund meaningful climate action, build tens of thousands of public houses, de-carbonise and reduce energy costs for homes, make dental care-free and invest in the infrastructure we all rely on
divination.explanation: Conditional forecast that the revenue would fund all these; plausible in direction but the full package's affordability is uncertain and untested.

authenticity.statement: The Greens campaigned unapologetically on ensuring the wealthiest pay their fair share. If we did that, we could introduce a tax-free bracket for income below $10,000, fund meaningful climate action, build tens of thousands of public houses, de-carbonise and reduce energy costs for homes, make dental care-free and invest in the infrastructure we all rely on
authenticity.explanation: Accurately reflects the Greens' actual 2023 campaign platform on wealth taxes and spending; words match the party's stated record.

civility.statement: The advice and evidence is clear: this Government's slash-and-burn economic approach has hurt and will continue to hurt Aotearoa
civility.explanation: Charged label ('slash-and-burn') applied to policy, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Cutting critical public services while funnelling billions of dollars of tax cuts to landlords and hundreds of millions to tobacco companies is no way to run a country.

rigor.statement: The advice and evidence is clear: this Government's slash-and-burn economic approach has hurt and will continue to hurt Aotearoa
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the economists' open letter as authority; 'slash-and-burn' is loaded but a source is invoked.

veracity.statement: Cuts to vital infrastructure spending, such as the irresponsible scaling back of Dunedin Hospital, have long-term effects that go well beyond short-term savings.

veracity.statement: Cutting critical public services while funnelling billions of dollars of tax cuts to landlords and hundreds of millions to tobacco companies is no way to run a country.
veracity.explanation: References real policies (interest deductibility restoration for landlords, smokefree/tobacco excise changes) but 'billions to landlords' and 'hundreds of millions to tobacco companies' are contested framings of the fiscal figures.

specificity.statement: Cuts to vital infrastructure spending, such as the irresponsible scaling back of Dunedin Hospital, have long-term effects that go well beyond short-term savings.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete example (Dunedin Hospital) but the 'long-term effects' remain general.

specificity.statement: Cutting critical public services while funnelling billions of dollars of tax cuts to landlords and hundreds of millions to tobacco companies is no way to run a country.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific beneficiary groups and rough magnitudes, though the figures are characterisations rather than sourced amounts.

divination.statement: The advice and evidence is clear: this Government's slash-and-burn economic approach has hurt and will continue to hurt Aotearoa

divination.statement: If they don't change course, we will all pay the price through a diminished ability to build a resilient economy that strengthens people and planet
divination.explanation: Conditional forecast of broad future harm; too general in mechanism and timeframe to be strongly grounded, though directionally arguable.

civility.statement: We cannot afford to become complacent with Covid, testing is a tool that should remain accessible to all
civility.explanation: Constructive, policy-focused statement without personal attack.

civility.statement: The Government is effectively waving a white flag for this deadly virus to spread more through our communities when the need for protection remains high.

rigor.statement: By withdrawing funding for tests, many will miss out, which could lead to the virus spreading and proliferating under the radar.

rigor.statement: The Government is effectively waving a white flag for this deadly virus to spread more through our communities when the need for protection remains high.

veracity.statement: At up to $11.00 per test it is a cost that many families cannot afford - especially under the current government's regime, which is leaving so many behind.

specificity.statement: We cannot afford to become complacent with Covid, testing is a tool that should remain accessible to all

specificity.statement: At up to $11.00 per test it is a cost that many families cannot afford - especially under the current government's regime, which is leaving so many behind.

divination.statement: By withdrawing funding for tests, many will miss out, which could lead to the virus spreading and proliferating under the radar.

civility.statement: We can have lower household bills, and an energy system that works for our climate and our communities, if only the Government had the guts to require the energy giants to reinvest more of their profit into clean, local energy generation

veracity.statement: Thousands of people have signed a petition that I was proud to table in Parliament this week calling on the government to massively increase support for community renewable energy.

specificity.statement: We can have lower household bills, and an energy system that works for our climate and our communities, if only the Government had the guts to require the energy giants to reinvest more of their profit into clean, local energy generation

specificity.statement: Today, I am calling on the government to break the iron grip of the four big electricity companies, create a fair and transparent electricity market, and invest in community renewable energy.

strength.statement: Thousands of people have signed a petition that I was proud to table in Parliament this week calling on the government to massively increase support for community renewable energy.

civility.statement: Luxon is telling everyone to stock up and prepare to stick out this storm at home. What does that mean for the people he has made homeless?
