civility.statement: We don’t know if a single family has received the $250 she promised last year, so why should Kiwis believe her this this year?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical question attacking the opponent's credibility ('why should Kiwis believe her'), edging toward undermining trustworthiness.

civility.statement: More people are homeless, more children are going hungry and women are going to be paid less. That’s what Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon will be remembered for
civility.explanation: Attaches a damning legacy judgement to named individuals; more character/legacy attack than policy engagement.

civility.statement: After a year of job cuts, now we are on to pay cuts and stealing from our kids’ retirement funds
civility.explanation: Loaded framing ('stealing from our kids') characterising policy as theft; rhetorical and inflammatory.

rigor.statement: We don’t know if a single family has received the $250 she promised last year, so why should Kiwis believe her this this year?
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of information ('we don't know if a single family') used to imply broad failure; weak logical grounding.

divination.statement: Christopher Luxon’s decision to cut the Government KiwiSaver contribution will steal $66,000 from the retirement savings of an 18-year-old entering the scheme today.
divination.explanation: A long-horizon projection of $66,000 lost savings relying on optimistic compounding assumptions; magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: More people are homeless, more children are going hungry and women are going to be paid less. That’s what Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon will be remembered for
divination.explanation: 'women are going to be paid less' forecasts a future outcome from the pay equity changes; directionally arguable but uncertain in magnitude.

specificity.statement: Labour upgraded 98 percent of schools and delivered more than 2200 new classrooms.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (98%, 2200 classrooms).

specificity.statement: Labour was already growing the use off-site manufacturing for classrooms and other government build programmes, driving the uptake of offsite manufacturing by Government agencies by a minimum of 10% year on year.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy approach and a quantified target (10% year on year).

specificity.statement: Just saying “in future budgets” isn’t good enough. Schools deserve certainty and clarity from the Government.
specificity.explanation: General demand for certainty without a specified mechanism.

veracity.statement: Labour upgraded 98 percent of schools and delivered more than 2200 new classrooms.
veracity.explanation: Figures broadly align with Labour's stated school property delivery; presented favourably but plausible.

veracity.statement: Everyone will remember children learning in damp, mouldy classrooms and schools with no space under the last National Government, who were comfortable with kids being taught in gyms and hallways.
veracity.explanation: Overcrowding and property condition issues were reported historically, but 'comfortable with' overstates and personalises intent.

civility.statement: Everyone will remember children learning in damp, mouldy classrooms and schools with no space under the last National Government, who were comfortable with kids being taught in gyms and hallways.
civility.explanation: Imputes attitude ('comfortable with') to opponents and uses vivid negative imagery; more characterisation than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Just saying “in future budgets” isn’t good enough. Schools deserve certainty and clarity from the Government.
civility.explanation: Criticises the vagueness of the Government's commitment; legitimate policy critique.

strength.statement: Labour upgraded 98 percent of schools and delivered more than 2200 new classrooms.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered outputs during Labour's term; specific and largely consistent with the school property programme record.

strength.statement: Labour was already growing the use off-site manufacturing for classrooms and other government build programmes, driving the uptake of offsite manufacturing by Government agencies by a minimum of 10% year on year.
strength.explanation: Claims an in-progress delivery initiative; specific but its follow-through and outcomes are not fully evidenced.

authenticity.statement: Labour upgraded 98 percent of schools and delivered more than 2200 new classrooms.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a delivery record consistent with the party's stated priorities.

specificity.statement: The National-led Government is about to pile unnecessary financial pressure on 1.6 million young New Zealanders. Extra weekly transport costs will put pressure on some of the most in need people nationwide, including working families and students
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific affected population figure and the mechanism (fare rises).

specificity.statement: This backwards step joins a scrapheap of cuts by this Government, which includes scrapping universal free prescriptions, free early-childhood-education for two-year-olds and the electric vehicle exemption from road user charges.
specificity.explanation: Lists several named specific policy changes.

specificity.statement: Whānau are already balancing much on their plates – this Government’s unhealthy obsession with cutting relief for those most in need is completely unacceptable.
specificity.explanation: Emotive general statement without specifics.

veracity.statement: The National-led Government is about to pile unnecessary financial pressure on 1.6 million young New Zealanders. Extra weekly transport costs will put pressure on some of the most in need people nationwide, including working families and students
veracity.explanation: The 1.6 million figure relates to those eligible for the youth/free-fare schemes; broadly plausible though 'about to pile' frames it dramatically.

veracity.statement: The Labour Government made free and half-price fares for young Kiwis permanent to give them one less worry as they went about their daily lives
veracity.explanation: Labour did introduce free/half-price fares for young people; 'permanent' is broadly accurate to their stated policy though later reversed.

veracity.statement: This backwards step joins a scrapheap of cuts by this Government, which includes scrapping universal free prescriptions, free early-childhood-education for two-year-olds and the electric vehicle exemption from road user charges.
veracity.explanation: These specific policy reversals (free prescriptions changes, ECE for two-year-olds, EV RUC exemption ending) are accurate.

civility.statement: Removing this subsidy will only mount further burdens on students, pressured families and working Kiwis, who will all be ultimately paying the price of National’s tax cuts for mega-landlords.
civility.explanation: Charged framing ('mega-landlords') linking fare rises to tax policy; pointed but a policy argument.

civility.statement: This only further proves that any talk of tax cuts are an empty promise with the rising costs that National are placing on New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Policy criticism, charged but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Whānau are already balancing much on their plates – this Government’s unhealthy obsession with cutting relief for those most in need is completely unacceptable.
civility.explanation: Attributes an 'unhealthy obsession' to the Government — characterises motive rather than engaging the policy substance.

strength.statement: The Labour Government made free and half-price fares for young Kiwis permanent to give them one less worry as they went about their daily lives
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered policy during Labour's term, though its 'permanent' status did not survive the change of government.

rigor.statement: Removing this subsidy will only mount further burdens on students, pressured families and working Kiwis, who will all be ultimately paying the price of National’s tax cuts for mega-landlords.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal trade-off between landlord tax policy and transport subsidy cuts without demonstrating the budgetary link.

rigor.statement: This only further proves that any talk of tax cuts are an empty promise with the rising costs that National are placing on New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Claims fare rises 'prove' tax cuts are an empty promise — a non-sequitur; the two are not logically linked.

divination.statement: The National-led Government is about to pile unnecessary financial pressure on 1.6 million young New Zealanders. Extra weekly transport costs will put pressure on some of the most in need people nationwide, including working families and students
divination.explanation: Predicts increased financial pressure on 1.6 million people from scrapping the subsidy; directionally sound but magnitude of impact uncertain.

specificity.statement: Labour sought an extension of time so that all submitters could be heard and their submissions put on the permanent record. Instead, the Justice Select Committee has rammed it through with outrageous haste
specificity.explanation: Names the specific action (seeking an extension) and the committee's response.

specificity.statement: David Seymour told Cabinet that there would be six months of consultation before the select committee, and a Cabinet Minute confirmed that it would be considered until the week of 16 May.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Cabinet Minute), the commitment (six months), and a specific date (week of 16 May).

specificity.statement: This Bill seeks to undermine Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and many of us did not want to have this debate at all.
specificity.explanation: States a position on the Bill's effect but without detailed argument.

veracity.statement: David Seymour told Cabinet that there would be six months of consultation before the select committee, and a Cabinet Minute confirmed that it would be considered until the week of 16 May.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific Cabinet Minute and date; specific and falsifiable, presented as documentary fact though not verifiable here.

veracity.statement: This shows utter contempt for the many New Zealanders who took the time to submit and whose views are now missing from the record.
veracity.explanation: The claim that some submissions were excluded from the record due to early report-back is the factual core; the 'contempt' is interpretation.

civility.statement: Labour sought an extension of time so that all submitters could be heard and their submissions put on the permanent record. Instead, the Justice Select Committee has rammed it through with outrageous haste
civility.explanation: 'Rammed it through with outrageous haste' is charged, but the underlying complaint is about a specific process decision.

civility.statement: Now, with Government members rushing to report the bill back early, the process is exposed for what it really is—a sham.
civility.explanation: 'A sham' is a strong dismissive label, though tied to the specific timeline complaint.

civility.statement: This shows utter contempt for the many New Zealanders who took the time to submit and whose views are now missing from the record.
civility.explanation: Imputes 'utter contempt' to the Government; characterises motive rather than engaging substance.

authenticity.statement: Labour sought an extension of time so that all submitters could be heard and their submissions put on the permanent record. Instead, the Justice Select Committee has rammed it through with outrageous haste
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated opposition to the Bill and its call for full submission hearings.

authenticity.statement: This Bill seeks to undermine Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and many of us did not want to have this debate at all.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated opposition to the Treaty Principles Bill.

rigor.statement: David Seymour told Cabinet that there would be six months of consultation before the select committee, and a Cabinet Minute confirmed that it would be considered until the week of 16 May.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the 'rushed process' claim in a cited Cabinet commitment vs the actual early report-back.

rigor.statement: Now, with Government members rushing to report the bill back early, the process is exposed for what it really is—a sham.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion of 'sham' rests on the earlier evidence of the changed timeline, but the leap to bad faith is asserted.

veracity.statement: This is political posturing of the worst kind. Three strikes did not reduce serious offending, as ACT and National claimed it would.
veracity.explanation: Evaluations of NZ's original three strikes law found little robust evidence it reduced serious offending; broadly supported by review evidence, though causal claims are contested.

veracity.statement: In fact there was almost no evidence to show it deters offending, and instead it resulted in severe distortions in sentencing third strike offenders.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with critiques at repeal that three strikes produced anomalous, disproportionate sentences and lacked deterrent evidence.

veracity.statement: Another saw a person get a sentence of seven years in prison for patting a prison guard’s bottom. That was unjust and can still occur under this new proposal.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a real, widely cited three-strikes case of a disproportionate sentence for a minor indecent assault; broadly accurate though summarised.

veracity.statement: Repeated offending is already an aggravating factor. Judges can already impose sentences of this length, where appropriate.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: previous offending is a recognised aggravating factor and courts retain discretion to impose long sentences.

veracity.statement: This legislation has not even been to Cabinet yet – so it is an announcement about an announcement in an attempt to look tough, when the evidence all shows this doesn’t work.
veracity.explanation: The procedural claim (not yet to Cabinet) is plausibly accurate; 'the evidence all shows this doesn't work' overstates a contested evidence base.

civility.statement: This is political posturing of the worst kind. Three strikes did not reduce serious offending, as ACT and National claimed it would.
civility.explanation: 'Political posturing of the worst kind' is charged and dismissive, but aimed at the policy/motives rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: All this law does is continue the Government’s attack on the judiciary by removing sentencing discretion from the courts.
civility.explanation: 'Attack on the judiciary' is loaded framing, though it targets a policy effect (removing discretion) rather than an individual.

civility.statement: This legislation has not even been to Cabinet yet – so it is an announcement about an announcement in an attempt to look tough, when the evidence all shows this doesn’t work.
civility.explanation: 'Announcement about an announcement... to look tough' mocks motive but engages the policy substance.

rigor.statement: This is political posturing of the worst kind. Three strikes did not reduce serious offending, as ACT and National claimed it would.
rigor.explanation: Asserts an empirical claim about deterrence but gives no citation in this sentence; evidence supplied later.

rigor.statement: In fact there was almost no evidence to show it deters offending, and instead it resulted in severe distortions in sentencing third strike offenders.
rigor.explanation: Claim is followed by concrete examples supporting the 'distortions' point, giving reasonable logical support.

rigor.statement: Repeated offending is already an aggravating factor. Judges can already impose sentences of this length, where appropriate.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based premise leading logically to the conclusion that the new law adds little beyond removing discretion.

rigor.statement: All this law does is continue the Government’s attack on the judiciary by removing sentencing discretion from the courts.
rigor.explanation: The substantive point about removing discretion is sound, but 'attack on the judiciary' is emotive escalation.

specificity.statement: Another saw a person get a sentence of seven years in prison for patting a prison guard’s bottom. That was unjust and can still occur under this new proposal.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete example and sentence length, though without name or year.

veracity.statement: The greyhound racing industry has been on notice for a long time, including three reviews in the last decade into greyhound racing practice.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: greyhound racing was subject to multiple reviews (e.g. Robertson, WHK/Hansen, and later reviews) over roughly a decade.

veracity.statement: There have been thousands of injuries to greyhounds and a number of deaths since the industry was put on notice by the Labour Government in 2021.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with published injury statistics for the sector; 'thousands' is broadly supported by cumulative injury data.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is one of only six countries that still allows greyhound racing.
veracity.explanation: A commonly cited and broadly accurate figure for the small number of jurisdictions with commercial greyhound racing.

veracity.statement: During the election campaign, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon agreed that greyhound racing should be banned.
veracity.explanation: Luxon expressed openness to a ban during the campaign, but 'agreed it should be banned' arguably firms up a more qualified position.

specificity.statement: The greyhound racing industry has been on notice for a long time, including three reviews in the last decade into greyhound racing practice.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count and timeframe but does not name the reviews.

specificity.statement: There have been thousands of injuries to greyhounds and a number of deaths since the industry was put on notice by the Labour Government in 2021.
specificity.explanation: Rough magnitude and start date but no precise figures.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is one of only six countries that still allows greyhound racing.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numeric claim, though countries not named.

specificity.statement: I am calling on the Prime Minister to act urgently and ban greyhound racing, to protect more greyhounds from being injured and killed, and protect the integrity of the wider racing industry which takes animal welfare seriously and contributes significantly to the New Zealand economy.
specificity.explanation: Clear ask (ban greyhound racing) with stated rationale, but no mechanism or timeframe beyond 'urgently'.

strength.statement: I am calling on the Prime Minister to act urgently and ban greyhound racing, to protect more greyhounds from being injured and killed, and protect the integrity of the wider racing industry which takes animal welfare seriously and contributes significantly to the New Zealand economy.
strength.explanation: An opposition call on the Government to act; no delivery power herself, so this is advocacy rather than demonstrated follow-through.

veracity.statement: In the case of Farzana Yaqubi, the Independent Police Conduct Authority found more should have been done to follow lines of enquiry in her case. There’s a chance her death could have been prevented.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects IPCA findings that police handling of the Yaqubi complaints was inadequate; the preventability claim is appropriately hedged.

specificity.statement: The Crimes (Stalking) Amendment Bill would make stalking a separate offence in Part 1 of the Crimes Act 1961 and carry a term of up to five years in prison.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the exact statute and part, the offence created, and the maximum penalty.

specificity.statement: I have worked closely with experts in the sector to develop this bill and I will be engaging with all parties in Parliament to seek their support for a law that just makes sense to enact.
specificity.explanation: States process (expert input, cross-party engagement) but 'makes sense to enact' is somewhat general.

charisma.statement: I have worked closely with experts in the sector to develop this bill and I will be engaging with all parties in Parliament to seek their support for a law that just makes sense to enact.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party, consensus-seeking framing that invites all parties in rather than attacking opponents.

civility.statement: The Prime Minister’s timid view undermines the work of New Zealand governments over decades to support a trading system that offers security for exporters, importers and consumers.
civility.explanation: 'Timid view' is a mild jab at the PM's stance but the criticism engages trade-policy substance.

rigor.statement: The Prime Minister’s timid view undermines the work of New Zealand governments over decades to support a trading system that offers security for exporters, importers and consumers.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable historical premise about a rules-based system, but 'undermines decades of work' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

specificity.statement: Not only will there be a $900 million hit on our exports, we also have to consider how the ripple effect of tariffs on our trading partners such as China will affect prices on goods coming to New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure and names the mechanism, though the ripple effects remain qualitative.

divination.statement: Not only will there be a $900 million hit on our exports, we also have to consider how the ripple effect of tariffs on our trading partners such as China will affect prices on goods coming to New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a $900m export hit and second-order price effects; directionally plausible but magnitude and pass-through are uncertain.

veracity.statement: Labour welcomes the conclusion of a trade deal with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) that was restarted under a Labour government after languishing for many years.
veracity.explanation: NZ–GCC negotiations were long stalled and revived under the previous Labour government; broadly accurate credit claim.

strength.statement: This deal is a reflection and result of the decisions we made in government to explore where we could strengthen our ties and trade relationships to help our economic recovery.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a concluded deal that did originate from work begun under Labour, though it was completed by a successor government.

authenticity.statement: Labour welcomes the conclusion of a trade deal with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) that was restarted under a Labour government after languishing for many years.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit consistent with Labour's actual role in restarting the negotiations.

authenticity.statement: This deal is a reflection and result of the decisions we made in government to explore where we could strengthen our ties and trade relationships to help our economic recovery.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's trade agenda in office, though the deal's conclusion was not solely Labour's doing.

veracity.statement: Just a few months ago, the pilot went haywire with cases of reoffending – and since the truth escaped, the Minister has held a tight grip on information that’s released.
veracity.explanation: There were reported reoffending cases among boot camp pilot participants; 'went haywire' and 'tight grip on information' are more editorial than established fact.

civility.statement: Karen Chhour needs to front up and shed some light on the state of her boot camps experiment.
civility.explanation: 'Front up' is a pointed demand for accountability but not a personal insult; focused on transparency.

civility.statement: Just a few months ago, the pilot went haywire with cases of reoffending – and since the truth escaped, the Minister has held a tight grip on information that’s released.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Minister of suppressing information; charged but centred on conduct in office.

civility.statement: The only plausible conclusion is that the evidence never mattered to begin with. That this was a pointless tick box exercise to look and sound tough, while they force the Bill through regardless of the outcome.

rigor.statement: The only plausible conclusion is that the evidence never mattered to begin with. That this was a pointless tick box exercise to look and sound tough, while they force the Bill through regardless of the outcome.

veracity.statement: We’ve already seen David Seymour butcher the school lunches programme, I’d hate to see the same done to our ECE sector.
veracity.explanation: The revamped school lunches programme drew widely reported problems, but 'butcher' is hyperbolic characterisation.

civility.statement: David Seymour should focus on growing the number of qualified teachers so more children get the support they deserve.
civility.explanation: A substantive policy prescription directed at the Minister without personal insult.

civility.statement: We’ve already seen David Seymour butcher the school lunches programme, I’d hate to see the same done to our ECE sector.
civility.explanation: 'Butcher' is emotive, derogatory framing of the Minister's handling of school lunches.

specificity.statement: David Seymour should focus on growing the number of qualified teachers so more children get the support they deserve.
specificity.explanation: Names a direction (grow qualified teacher numbers) but no target, figure, or mechanism.

charisma.statement: A review into the sector is certainly warranted. It’s important we’re always improving and future-proofing the sector. It’s why we undertook our own review in Government and were clear about what we were modernising.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the merit of reviewing the sector, a measure of common ground before criticising execution.

authenticity.statement: A review into the sector is certainly warranted. It’s important we’re always improving and future-proofing the sector. It’s why we undertook our own review in Government and were clear about what we were modernising.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour having conducted its own ECE review in office; concedes a review is legitimate rather than opposing reflexively.

veracity.statement: But they’ve halved the budget that makes it easier to walk and cycle in our cities, which is disappointing and short-sighted.
veracity.explanation: The 2024 land transport programme did sharply cut walking and cycling funding; 'halved' is a plausible characterisation of the reduction.

veracity.statement: The National Government has cancelled rail-enabled ferries – a vital transport link – and is heaping costs on drivers with increased licencing fees, a driver’s tax of $50 and a planned double-digit fuel excise increase of 12c per litre from 2027.
veracity.explanation: The rail-enabled iRex ferries were cancelled and fuel excise/fee increases were signalled; figures are broadly accurate though 'driver's tax' is a partisan label.

rigor.statement: Taking trucks off our roads is what will permanently fix the pothole problem, not some arbitrary fund that will only result in more patch-up jobs and road cones.
rigor.explanation: Contains a causal claim (freight-to-rail reduces road wear) with real basis, but 'permanently fix' and the dismissal of the fund are asserted, not evidenced.

specificity.statement: But they’ve halved the budget that makes it easier to walk and cycle in our cities, which is disappointing and short-sighted.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the cut ('halved') and the domain, though without exact dollar figures.

specificity.statement: The National Government has cancelled rail-enabled ferries – a vital transport link – and is heaping costs on drivers with increased licencing fees, a driver’s tax of $50 and a planned double-digit fuel excise increase of 12c per litre from 2027.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific measures, a $50 figure, and a 12c/litre excise rise with a 2027 date.

charisma.statement: We too want to build the infrastructure our country needs, and that includes roads – like the vital link replacing the Manawatū Gorge.
charisma.explanation: Concedes common ground on roads and infrastructure, softening the partisan divide before criticising priorities.

divination.statement: Taking trucks off our roads is what will permanently fix the pothole problem, not some arbitrary fund that will only result in more patch-up jobs and road cones.
divination.explanation: Predicts road-maintenance outcomes; directionally reasonable but 'permanently fix the pothole problem' is overstated.

veracity.statement: More te reo Māori in the community is a positive reflection of where we are as a more inclusive society, and reflects te reo Māori’s status as an official language of Aotearoa New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Te reo Māori is indeed an official language of New Zealand (Māori Language Act).

veracity.statement: Recently the National Government has undermined that commitment and taken the revitalisation of te reo Māori backwards by going back to English names for Te Whatu Ora and Waka Kotahi, which are both Crown entities.
veracity.explanation: The Government did direct agencies to prioritise English names; 'taken revitalisation backwards' is an interpretive characterisation of that factual change.

civility.statement: Recently the National Government has undermined that commitment and taken the revitalisation of te reo Māori backwards by going back to English names for Te Whatu Ora and Waka Kotahi, which are both Crown entities.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's policy direction on naming without personal attack.

rigor.statement: This will prevent the need to apply for a special licence to serve alcohol to veterans after Anzac Day services, remove any incentive to stockpile alcohol before Easter, and allow hospitality businesses to operate under normal conditions during some of the busiest and most profitable times of the year.
rigor.explanation: Consequences follow logically from repealing the restrictions, though presented as assertions.

specificity.statement: This will prevent the need to apply for a special licence to serve alcohol to veterans after Anzac Day services, remove any incentive to stockpile alcohol before Easter, and allow hospitality businesses to operate under normal conditions during some of the busiest and most profitable times of the year.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete, specific effects of the bill (special licences, stockpiling, normal trading) tied to named holidays.

charisma.statement: More te reo Māori in the community is a positive reflection of where we are as a more inclusive society, and reflects te reo Māori’s status as an official language of Aotearoa New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, values-based framing, though it appeals mainly to those already sympathetic.

veracity.statement: this court decision means that drivers will be recognised as employees and have the employment rights they have always deserved. This a victory for workers and shows the law works as it should.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the Court of Appeal's ruling that the Uber drivers in question were employees, not contractors.

civility.statement: We now need to turn our attention to Minister for Workplace Relations Brook van Velden, who is currently waging a war on workers’ rights by way of her contractor reform which, because of today’s decision, should be abandoned.
civility.explanation: 'Waging a war on workers' rights' is inflammatory framing of the Minister's policy work.

civility.statement: The minister should reject her ideologically focused attacks on workers’ rights. In light of this decision, her contractor law reform work needs to be ditched.
civility.explanation: 'Ideologically focused attacks' imputes bad motive to the Minister rather than engaging her reform's substance.

rigor.statement: We now need to turn our attention to Minister for Workplace Relations Brook van Velden, who is currently waging a war on workers’ rights by way of her contractor reform which, because of today’s decision, should be abandoned.
rigor.explanation: Links the court ruling to a call to abandon reform, but 'waging a war' is emotive and the logical bridge is asserted.

veracity.statement: Previous rushed overhauls have led to students being the guinea pigs for failed change – like national standards – so we must get this right.
veracity.explanation: National standards were controversial and later scrapped, but 'failed change' and 'guinea pigs' are partisan characterisations.

civility.statement: NCEA is not perfect, which is why we started to implement a fully consulted change process that this Government delayed. Rushing changes through now for political expediency isn’t the answer.

rigor.statement: Previous rushed overhauls have led to students being the guinea pigs for failed change – like national standards – so we must get this right.
rigor.explanation: Uses a historical analogy (national standards) to warn against rushed change; a reasonable but appeal-to-precedent argument.

specificity.statement: Any change must be done with proper sector consultation and be based on evidence that it will lead to better outcomes for all students.

authenticity.statement: NCEA is not perfect, which is why we started to implement a fully consulted change process that this Government delayed. Rushing changes through now for political expediency isn’t the answer.
authenticity.explanation: Concedes NCEA's flaws and points to Labour's own reform process, consistent with the party's earlier change programme.

veracity.statement: Trade Minister Todd McLay told New Zealanders that he didn’t expect New Zealand to be caught in tariffs, but he was proven wrong by today’s announcement.
veracity.explanation: Characterises McClay's earlier optimism as contradicted by the tariff announcement; broadly fair though a compressed account of his statements.

civility.statement: The Government’s strategy of keeping its head down has not given New Zealand any advantage over our competitors.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's negotiating posture ('keeping its head down') without personal attack.

civility.statement: Trade Minister Todd McLay told New Zealanders that he didn’t expect New Zealand to be caught in tariffs, but he was proven wrong by today’s announcement.
civility.explanation: Points to an opponent being 'proven wrong' on a factual prediction rather than a personal insult.

rigor.statement: The Government’s strategy of keeping its head down has not given New Zealand any advantage over our competitors.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the strategy yielded no advantage but offers no comparative evidence at this point.

specificity.statement: There’s going to be $900 million hit on our exports, and there is uncertainty over who will carry the cost of that, whether it will be US consumers or New Zealand exporters.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure and identifies the open question of cost incidence.

divination.statement: There’s going to be $900 million hit on our exports, and there is uncertainty over who will carry the cost of that, whether it will be US consumers or New Zealand exporters.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a $900m export impact while appropriately flagging uncertainty over incidence; plausible but modelling-dependent.

veracity.statement: Unemployment has ticked up to 5.2 percent under Christopher Luxon – clear proof his government is failing New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: The 5.2% figure is plausibly accurate for the period; 'clear proof his government is failing' is the interpretive overlay, but the underlying stat is checkable and roughly right.

veracity.statement: The Government's decision to cancel or delay building projects has contributed to a loss of 18,000 construction jobs since December 2023.
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses in this range are broadly consistent with sector data, though attributing all of it to project cancellations overstates a single cause.

veracity.statement: Kiwis are voting with their feet and leaving in record numbers. That is a clear vote of no confidence in National.
veracity.explanation: Net migration outflows to Australia were high in this period, so 'record numbers' is directionally supportable but likely overstated.

rigor.statement: Unemployment has ticked up to 5.2 percent under Christopher Luxon – clear proof his government is failing New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Treats a single unemployment number as 'clear proof' of government failure — a leap that ignores confounders; correlation asserted as proof.

rigor.statement: The Government's decision to cancel or delay building projects has contributed to a loss of 18,000 construction jobs since December 2023.
rigor.explanation: Plausible causal link but stated as settled; 'contributed to' is appropriately hedged, partially offsetting the causal claim.

rigor.statement: While thousands of people are out of work and struggling to pay the bills, Luxon is looking after property speculators and fossil fuel companies. He has abandoned middle New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Emotive juxtaposition with no evidence linking the two claims; appeal to emotion.

rigor.statement: Kiwis are voting with their feet and leaving in record numbers. That is a clear vote of no confidence in National.
rigor.explanation: Metaphor ('vote of no confidence') substitutes for evidence of causation between departures and government performance.

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon promised that his business experience would make life better for New Zealanders – instead he's making it worse.
civility.explanation: Frames the PM's record as personally making things worse; leans toward character framing rather than engaging specific policy substance.

civility.statement: While thousands of people are out of work and struggling to pay the bills, Luxon is looking after property speculators and fossil fuel companies. He has abandoned middle New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad motive ('looking after speculators', 'abandoned middle New Zealand') rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: He is out of touch and failing to improve the lives of everyday New Zealanders who want to go to work each day and be paid enough to provide for their families.
civility.explanation: 'Out of touch' is a personal characterisation of the PM rather than a policy critique.

specificity.statement: Christopher Luxon promised that his business experience would make life better for New Zealanders – instead he's making it worse.
specificity.explanation: General claim of 'making it worse' with no mechanism, figure, or named policy.

specificity.statement: The Government's decision to cancel or delay building projects has contributed to a loss of 18,000 construction jobs since December 2023.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (18,000), a sector (construction), and a start date (December 2023).

divination.statement: What were once one-in-100-year weather events are now happening every year. And they will keep happening - and they’re going to keep getting worse - unless we act.
divination.explanation: Prediction of worsening extreme weather aligns with climate-science consensus; directionally well-supported, though 'every year' is hyperbolic and the timeframe open-ended.

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis say they “get it” - but they have no idea what life is really like for most New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on opponents' understanding and empathy rather than engaging their policy.

civility.statement: National has had two years to come up with a serious plan to grow the economy and ease the cost of living.
civility.explanation: Criticises the government's performance/timeframe rather than attacking a person.

rigor.statement: Getting the economy growing and balancing the books means we can't say yes to everything - and I make no apology for that.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable acknowledgement of trade-offs, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis say they “get it” - but they have no idea what life is really like for most New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Assertion about opponents' inner awareness with no evidence; ad hominem framing.

specificity.statement: In my first Budget as Finance Minister, I will introduce a simple capital gains tax on profits made from investment and commercial property.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the base (investment and commercial property profits), and a timeframe (first Budget), though no rate.

specificity.statement: The family home is exempt. Farms are exempt. KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, and personal belongings - are all exempt.
specificity.explanation: Detailed enumeration of exemptions, precisely delimiting the tax's scope.

specificity.statement: Every single dollar raised will be ring-fenced to rebuild our health system, including three free doctor's visits a year for every New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Concrete hypothecation (all revenue ring-fenced to health) and a named entitlement (three free GP visits/year).

specificity.statement: I will direct our economy towards solving the biggest challenges we face - like climate change and inequality - through innovation and investment.
specificity.explanation: Broad aspiration naming themes but no mechanisms, amounts, or timeframes.

strength.statement: In my first Budget as Finance Minister, I will introduce a simple capital gains tax on profits made from investment and commercial property.
strength.explanation: A firm commitment but contingent on office and not yet delivered.

authenticity.statement: As a mother of eight - I know what it means to manage responsibly and make every dollar count.
authenticity.explanation: Ties a fiscal-discipline persona to a genuine personal circumstance; consistent self-presentation, though a value claim rather than a record.

authenticity.statement: Getting the economy growing and balancing the books means we can't say yes to everything - and I make no apology for that.
authenticity.explanation: A candid statement of fiscal constraint that resists over-promising; a stated value with no contradicting action visible.

charisma.statement: As a mother of eight - I know what it means to manage responsibly and make every dollar count.
charisma.explanation: Personal, relatable framing to build trust with the audience; appeals to shared experience but does not reach across the aisle.

civility.statement: Now, in Opposition, we spend a lot of time reacting, to the Government, to their policy announcements, to their rhetoric, and to their often-misguided plans for creating a better New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Mild dismissal of government plans as 'misguided' but criticises policy direction, not persons.

specificity.statement: All our kids can grow up proud - Māori, Pasifika, Pākehā, Asian, new migrant, refugee and LGBTQI+ - standing shoulder to shoulder in a country that values every one of them.
specificity.explanation: An aspirational image with no concrete policy or mechanism.

charisma.statement: All our kids can grow up proud - Māori, Pasifika, Pākehā, Asian, new migrant, refugee and LGBTQI+ - standing shoulder to shoulder in a country that values every one of them.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately inclusive, unifying vision that invites a wide range of communities in.

charisma.statement: People who believe that New Zealand can be fairer, kinder, and more united than it is today.
charisma.explanation: Unifying, values-based framing, though it addresses supporters rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: And he holds fast to the belief that politics should be about improving people’s lives, not dividing them.
charisma.explanation: Endorses consensus over division as a governing value; unifying in tone.

charisma.statement: So today, I want us to remember that our job is not just to oppose – it is to aspire and inspire.
charisma.explanation: Calls the movement toward a positive, aspirational posture rather than pure opposition; rhetorically effective but inward-facing to supporters.

veracity.statement: These numbers show the worst February for home consents since 2012
veracity.explanation: Backed by the cited Stats NZ figure (33,595 homes, down 7.4%); the 'worst since 2012' framing is plausible and directionally supported by the consent slowdown, though not shown in full.

veracity.statement: Building consents plummeted after the Government came in, stopped building Kāinga Ora houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public house building and maintenance fund.
veracity.explanation: Names a specific $1.5b figure and asserts causation ('plummeted after'); the funding change is real but the causal link to consents is asserted rather than demonstrated.

veracity.statement: The Government has only funded 1,500 new social housing places from July 2025.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable figure presented as fact; plausible but not independently confirmed in the text.

veracity.statement: The Government has also reintroduced interest deductibility, which removes the incentive for the private sector to invest in new builds. As of yesterday, property investors can claim 100 percent of the interest back on their mortgage due to a $2.9 billion landlord tax break.
veracity.explanation: Interest deductibility was reinstated and phased to 100%, and figures in this range have been cited; accurate on the policy though the '$2.9b landlord tax break' framing is contestable.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has lost more than 13,000 construction workers since this Government took over.
veracity.explanation: Construction employment did fall materially over the period; the figure is plausible and directionally supported.

specificity.statement: These numbers show the worst February for home consents since 2012
specificity.explanation: References a concrete comparison year and a measurable metric, though the claim itself is a headline rather than a mechanism.

specificity.statement: Building consents plummeted after the Government came in, stopped building Kāinga Ora houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public house building and maintenance fund.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure and named programme (Kāinga Ora), giving concrete detail.

specificity.statement: The Government has only funded 1,500 new social housing places from July 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise number and a start date.

specificity.statement: The Government has also reintroduced interest deductibility, which removes the incentive for the private sector to invest in new builds. As of yesterday, property investors can claim 100 percent of the interest back on their mortgage due to a $2.9 billion landlord tax break.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the 100% figure, timing ('as of yesterday'), and a dollar cost.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has lost more than 13,000 construction workers since this Government took over.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number over a defined period.

rigor.statement: Building consents plummeted after the Government came in, stopped building Kāinga Ora houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public house building and maintenance fund.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning ('plummeted after the Government came in') implies causation from sequence without isolating other drivers of the construction downturn.

rigor.statement: The Government has also reintroduced interest deductibility, which removes the incentive for the private sector to invest in new builds. As of yesterday, property investors can claim 100 percent of the interest back on their mortgage due to a $2.9 billion landlord tax break.
rigor.explanation: Claims deductibility 'removes the incentive' to build new, but new-build exemptions cut the other way — a gap between premise and conclusion.

civility.statement: Chris Bishop has talked a great lot of fluff about more homes, but it's a pity he's not great at getting them built
civility.explanation: Dismissive personal jab ('a great lot of fluff', 'not great at getting them built') aimed at the minister's competence rather than engaging the substance.

charisma.statement: Chris Bishop has talked a great lot of fluff about more homes, but it's a pity he's not great at getting them built
charisma.explanation: A combative closing line that rallies rather than persuades or seeks common ground.

veracity.statement: Instead, his office is now saying it's Associate Minister of Police Casey Costello who holds responsibility for delivering 500 police officers in two years.
veracity.explanation: Reports what the minister's office says; the article's own account of the delegation letter partly cuts against the strong 'in charge' reading, so it is only partly supported.

veracity.statement: The heat has come on Mark Mitchell as more and more police officers are speaking out about the insult of the Government's recent pay offer. There are also reports of Christopher Luxon being 'the laughing stock of the station' when he did not know how much a new police officer was paid.
veracity.explanation: Heavily hedged ('there are reports') and relies on anecdote, making the claims hard to verify.

veracity.statement: National campaigned hard and talked tough on restoring law and order. Mark Mitchell even promised that he would resign in a year if New Zealanders did not feel safer, and now he's running for the hills.
veracity.explanation: The 'resign in a year' claim references a real Mitchell comment but its exact terms are paraphrased; 'running for the hills' is characterisation.

specificity.statement: Instead, his office is now saying it's Associate Minister of Police Casey Costello who holds responsibility for delivering 500 police officers in two years.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific commitment (500 officers), the timeframe (two years), and the officials involved.

rigor.statement: Labour has been asking the Police Minister oral and written questions for weeks about how this will be delivered and Mark Mitchell has responded – which is the job of the Minister responsible
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete behaviour (Mitchell answering the questions) as evidence that he is the responsible minister — a reasonable inference, though not conclusive of formal delegation.

civility.statement: In almost unbelievable circumstances, it appears the Minister of Police Mark Mitchell doesn't want to own the commitment of putting more police on the front line
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing ('doesn't want to own') attributes motive, though it targets ministerial responsibility rather than personal character.

civility.statement: The heat has come on Mark Mitchell as more and more police officers are speaking out about the insult of the Government's recent pay offer. There are also reports of Christopher Luxon being 'the laughing stock of the station' when he did not know how much a new police officer was paid.
civility.explanation: Amplifies a mocking 'laughing stock' quote about the Prime Minister — a personal ridicule rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: National campaigned hard and talked tough on restoring law and order. Mark Mitchell even promised that he would resign in a year if New Zealanders did not feel safer, and now he's running for the hills.
civility.explanation: 'Running for the hills' is a derisive characterisation of the minister rather than engagement with the delivery question.

veracity.statement: Labour prioritised mental wellbeing after children and young people said it was the single biggest issue facing their generation. But today we've found out Louise Upston has ignored official advice and scrapped mental wellbeing as priority area.
veracity.explanation: The claim that advice was ignored and the measure dropped is specific and plausible but not independently shown in the text.

veracity.statement: This comes after the Minister previously changed Labour's child poverty reduction targets to make them easier for her Government to achieve.
veracity.explanation: References a real change to targets, but the 'to make them easier' motive is an interpretation presented as fact.

veracity.statement: It is often overlooked that 55% of kids experiencing material hardship are in working households.
veracity.explanation: A specific statistic consistent with commonly cited NZ data on working households and material hardship.

veracity.statement: The Government has stilted minimum wage growth and scrapped universal free prescriptions, all the while rates, rents, power prices are up. Their tax cuts don't even touch the sides for most Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: Minimum wage restraint and the reinstatement of prescription co-payments are accurate; 'don't even touch the sides' is subjective hyperbole.

veracity.statement: So far under Louise Upston's watch, unemployment has risen and beneficiary numbers are soaring – all consequences of her Government's choices
veracity.explanation: Unemployment and benefit numbers did rise over the period; 'all consequences of her Government's choices' overstates attributable causation.

specificity.statement: It is often overlooked that 55% of kids experiencing material hardship are in working households.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise percentage tied to a defined group.

rigor.statement: It's a sad reality when her Government doesn't seem to care that there are struggling families that may go without food because of the Government's choices.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion; asserts families will go without food as a direct consequence without establishing the causal chain.

rigor.statement: The Government has stilted minimum wage growth and scrapped universal free prescriptions, all the while rates, rents, power prices are up. Their tax cuts don't even touch the sides for most Kiwis.
rigor.explanation: Stacks several accurate cost pressures but asserts the overall verdict on tax cuts without quantification.

rigor.statement: So far under Louise Upston's watch, unemployment has risen and beneficiary numbers are soaring – all consequences of her Government's choices
rigor.explanation: Attributes rising unemployment wholly to government choices, ignoring wider macroeconomic drivers.

civility.statement: It's a sad reality when her Government doesn't seem to care that there are struggling families that may go without food because of the Government's choices.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference ('doesn't seem to care') to the government rather than engaging the policy rationale.

authenticity.statement: Labour prioritised mental wellbeing after children and young people said it was the single biggest issue facing their generation. But today we've found out Louise Upston has ignored official advice and scrapped mental wellbeing as priority area.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's own record of having set mental wellbeing as a priority, so the criticism aligns with the speaker's prior actions.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon promised growth. Instead, under his watch the economy has shrunk over the last year - and it hasn't grown at all since he became Prime Minister,
veracity.explanation: Consistent with recorded GDP contraction/stagnation over the relevant period; broadly accurate though 'hasn't grown at all' is a strong summary.

veracity.statement: After two years of Christopher Luxon mismanaging the economy, most Kiwis are worse off. It is harder to pay the bills, groceries cost more, and seeing a doctor is more expensive than ever.
veracity.explanation: Rising grocery and GP costs are broadly accurate; 'most Kiwis are worse off' and 'more expensive than ever' are generalisations.

specificity.statement: Christopher Luxon promised growth. Instead, under his watch the economy has shrunk over the last year - and it hasn't grown at all since he became Prime Minister,
specificity.explanation: Anchors to a timeframe (since he became PM) but cites no figures.

specificity.statement: New Zealanders cannot afford another three years of National. Labour will focus on what matters most to Kiwis: jobs, health, homes, and real action on the cost of living,
specificity.explanation: A list of priority themes with no mechanisms, figures, or timeframes.

civility.statement: After two years of Christopher Luxon mismanaging the economy, most Kiwis are worse off. It is harder to pay the bills, groceries cost more, and seeing a doctor is more expensive than ever.
civility.explanation: 'Mismanaging' is a pointed but policy-directed critique, though it asserts rather than demonstrates.

civility.statement: So, when he stands up and says, 'the economy is turning a corner,' let's be clear about what he really means: the economy is working for a few - not for the rest of New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Reframes the opponent's words to impute a hidden meaning rather than rebutting the claim on evidence.

charisma.statement: So, when he stands up and says, 'the economy is turning a corner,' let's be clear about what he really means: the economy is working for a few - not for the rest of New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: 'A few vs the rest' framing rallies one side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: New Zealanders cannot afford another three years of National. Labour will focus on what matters most to Kiwis: jobs, health, homes, and real action on the cost of living,
charisma.explanation: Confident partisan appeal directed at supporters rather than persuading the undecided.

veracity.statement: National has made it harder to see a doctor and slashed funding to frontline mental health services
veracity.explanation: Directionally reflects rising GP costs and funding pressures, but stated broadly without figures, making it hard to verify.

veracity.statement: This is the work Labour started and National has cut funding for, resulting in providers shutting their doors.
veracity.explanation: Provider closures and funding pressure are plausible but the causal chain is asserted without evidence in the text.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon promised better mental health care, but nearly two years on, things are worse.
veracity.explanation: Cites a real commitment against a claimed deterioration, but 'things are worse' is a broad judgement not quantified here.

specificity.statement: Labour's Medicard will deliver three free doctor's visits – a crucial first step for anyone needing help.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy (Medicard) and a concrete number of free visits, though without cost or timing.

specificity.statement: We back a nationwide, culturally grounded, and youth-focused response with properly funded teams, peer support, and 24/7 access.
specificity.explanation: Lists desired features (peer support, 24/7 access) but no funding levels, timeframe, or delivery mechanism.

civility.statement: National has made it harder to see a doctor and slashed funding to frontline mental health services
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused criticism ('slashed funding') rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon promised better mental health care, but nearly two years on, things are worse.
civility.explanation: Contrasts promise with outcome — pointed but focused on record rather than the person.

authenticity.statement: This is the work Labour started and National has cut funding for, resulting in providers shutting their doors.
authenticity.explanation: Aligns the criticism with Labour's own prior investment record, though the 'started' claim is self-favourable and unverified here.

strength.statement: Labour's Medicard will deliver three free doctor's visits – a crucial first step for anyone needing help.
strength.explanation: An opposition promise ('will deliver') with no delivery record — aspiration, not demonstrated follow-through.

veracity.statement: National has blown the budget on tax cuts for tobacco companies and property speculators, and now they're making Kiwis pay for it.
veracity.explanation: 'Tax cuts for tobacco companies' mischaracterises the smokefree repeal (not a corporate tax cut); the framing is misleading.

veracity.statement: We saw it when National slammed the brakes on construction, and 20,000 tradies lost their jobs.
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses are real but the '20,000' figure is higher than the '13,000 construction workers' cited in Labour's earlier release, suggesting rounding up.

veracity.statement: It doesn't add up that we raise our young people, we teach them, we train them - and then we watch as they board a plane to build their lives somewhere else.
veracity.explanation: Reflects genuine net emigration of young New Zealanders over the period, though stated impressionistically.

specificity.statement: We saw it when National slammed the brakes on construction, and 20,000 tradies lost their jobs.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number tied to a sector.

specificity.statement: A good idea, born in a workshop in Whangārei or a garage in Gisborne, should be able to grow into a great company right here, and stay here. The next Trade Me. The next Xero. The next Rocket Lab.
specificity.explanation: Evocative examples but no policy mechanism to make it happen.

rigor.statement: And it is the idea that if you hand tax breaks to those at the very top - to the landlords, the tobacco companies, the tech giants and the fossil fuel companies - the benefits will somehow trickle down to the rest of us.
rigor.explanation: Sets up trickle-down as the opponent's premise to knock down — leans toward strawman, and the critique is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It doesn't add up that we raise our young people, we teach them, we train them - and then we watch as they board a plane to build their lives somewhere else.
rigor.explanation: Primarily an emotional appeal about a felt problem rather than an evidenced argument.

civility.statement: National has blown the budget on tax cuts for tobacco companies and property speculators, and now they're making Kiwis pay for it.
civility.explanation: Loaded framing tying opponents to tobacco and speculators, though aimed at policy choices.

charisma.statement: And it is the idea that if you hand tax breaks to those at the very top - to the landlords, the tobacco companies, the tech giants and the fossil fuel companies - the benefits will somehow trickle down to the rest of us.
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-'those at the very top' contrast that energises supporters more than it persuades.

charisma.statement: A good idea, born in a workshop in Whangārei or a garage in Gisborne, should be able to grow into a great company right here, and stay here. The next Trade Me. The next Xero. The next Rocket Lab.
charisma.explanation: Vivid, aspirational and place-based imagery that invites a broad audience to identify with the vision.

civility.statement: We've got a Prime Minister so out of touch he lobbied for rates relief on his holiday home - while pushing up costs for everyone else.
civility.explanation: Personal attack framing the PM as 'out of touch' and self-serving rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: A Prime Minister who blames young people for an economic mess they didn't create, then tells them to move to where the work is.
civility.explanation: Characterises the PM as blaming young people; an accusatory paraphrase rather than substantive policy critique.

civility.statement: And it has failed on the two things it promised: grow the economy and fix the cost of living.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused criticism of the Government's record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: So, when Nicola Willis told people who lost their jobs not to "take it personally," I was disgusted.
civility.explanation: Quotes an opponent's actual words to criticise them; the reaction is emotive but tethered to a real statement rather than a fabricated attack.

civility.statement: Where Christopher Luxon wants to sell us out to foreign investors, Labour will back our own people and ideas.
civility.explanation: 'Sell us out' is a loaded personal characterisation of the PM's motives, near-strawman.

veracity.statement: We've got a Prime Minister so out of touch he lobbied for rates relief on his holiday home - while pushing up costs for everyone else.
veracity.explanation: References a real reported episode about Luxon and property costs, but compresses it into a loaded framing that omits context.

veracity.statement: In just twelve months, a record 73,000 Kiwis have left to look for work that should be available here.
veracity.explanation: Net/gross departures of NZ citizens have hit record highs around this figure per Stats NZ migration data; broadly accurate though 'to look for work' is an inference.

veracity.statement: Today - as they did yesterday, and as they will again tomorrow - nearly 200 New Zealanders will make the decision to leave the country.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with the ~73,000/year figure (≈200/day); a reasonable arithmetic restatement.

veracity.statement: Nine out of 10 New Zealanders won't pay a cent, but everyone will benefit from a stronger economy.
veracity.explanation: The 90% claim is a projection about a proposed capital gains tax's incidence; plausible for the family-home-exempt design but unverified and forward-looking.

veracity.statement: Right now, our emergency departments are overcrowded because far too many people can't afford to see a doctor.
veracity.explanation: ED overcrowding is real, but attributing it primarily to GP unaffordability oversimplifies multiple causes.

veracity.statement: No country has ever created more well-paid jobs or boosted productivity by locking up its wealth in property.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported by economic literature but the universal 'no country ever' is hyperbolic.

rigor.statement: A Prime Minister who blames young people for an economic mess they didn't create, then tells them to move to where the work is.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a paraphrase of the opponent's position (near-strawman) rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: And it has failed on the two things it promised: grow the economy and fix the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping conclusory judgement asserted without supporting data in the statement.

rigor.statement: Right now, our emergency departments are overcrowded because far too many people can't afford to see a doctor.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause explanation asserted for a complex problem without evidence in the statement.

rigor.statement: Where Christopher Luxon wants to sell us out to foreign investors, Labour will back our own people and ideas.
rigor.explanation: False-dichotomy framing (foreign investors vs 'our own people') with no evidence.

rigor.statement: No country has ever created more well-paid jobs or boosted productivity by locking up its wealth in property.
rigor.explanation: A defensible economic argument that property speculation doesn't drive productivity, but stated as sweeping absolute without citation.

specificity.statement: In just twelve months, a record 73,000 Kiwis have left to look for work that should be available here.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and timeframe given.

specificity.statement: We will grow the economy and lift living standards for everyone - not just a privileged few.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Every promise that I put my name to at the next election will be a promise I know we can deliver on.
specificity.explanation: General assurance about future promises with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: And as part of our plan to build a better economy for Kiwi families, the family home will always be exempt.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy design feature (family-home exemption) though lacking the fuller tax detail.

specificity.statement: Nine out of 10 New Zealanders won't pay a cent, but everyone will benefit from a stronger economy.
specificity.explanation: Gives a proportion but not the rate, threshold, or coverage detail.

specificity.statement: Every dollar - every single dollar - raised will be ring-fenced to fix our health system - including three free doctor's visits a year for every New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (ring-fencing) plus a named, quantified policy (three free visits/year).

specificity.statement: Over the past few months, we've worked with experts on a plan to free up 4.5 million appointments a year through smarter digital tools and more efficient systems.
specificity.explanation: Quantified target (4.5m appointments) and stated mechanism, though the 'how' of the tools is thin.

specificity.statement: The Family Doctor Loan Scheme will provide doctors with low-interest loans to help them get started.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete scheme and instrument (low-interest loans) but no amounts or eligibility figures.

divination.statement: Today - as they did yesterday, and as they will again tomorrow - nearly 200 New Zealanders will make the decision to leave the country.
divination.explanation: Prediction that departures continue at this rate; plausible given current migration trends but assumes continuity.

divination.statement: Over the past few months, we've worked with experts on a plan to free up 4.5 million appointments a year through smarter digital tools and more efficient systems.
divination.explanation: Forecast of appointment savings from digital efficiency; optimistic and unverified magnitude.

charisma.statement: We will grow the economy and lift living standards for everyone - not just a privileged few.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'everyone' framing but rallies own side with 'privileged few' contrast.

authenticity.statement: Every promise that I put my name to at the next election will be a promise I know we can deliver on.
authenticity.explanation: A commitment to consistency between words and deeds; defensible but unverifiable from the text and stated by a leader whose past government faced delivery criticism.

strength.statement: Every dollar - every single dollar - raised will be ring-fenced to fix our health system - including three free doctor's visits a year for every New Zealander.
strength.explanation: A specific opposition commitment not yet enacted; delivery unproven as Labour is not in government.

veracity.statement: Growing from reparation and Treaty settlements to an asset base worth over 126 billion dollars and contributing 32 billion to New Zealand's gross domestic product.
veracity.explanation: Figures for the Māori economy asset base and GDP contribution are close to published estimates in recent reports.

specificity.statement: We will not merely possess seats and be the party FOR Māori, we will be the Party that walks and thrives WITH Māori.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational positioning with no concrete policy or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Growing from reparation and Treaty settlements to an asset base worth over 126 billion dollars and contributing 32 billion to New Zealand's gross domestic product.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures cited.

specificity.statement: That's why we invested so heavily in Te Matatini and recognised Matariki as a kaupapa of national significance and introduced the Matariki public holiday, embraced by all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete achievements (Matariki holiday, Te Matatini investment).

specificity.statement: That made unprecedented investment in Māori housing and created direct funding relationships with iwi and hapu, trusting our knowledge of our communities.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy area and approach but no figures or programme detail.

charisma.statement: We will not merely possess seats and be the party FOR Māori, we will be the Party that walks and thrives WITH Māori.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, partnership-framed rhetoric that invites Māori in, though appeals mainly to its own base.

authenticity.statement: That's why we invested so heavily in Te Matatini and recognised Matariki as a kaupapa of national significance and introduced the Matariki public holiday, embraced by all New Zealanders.
authenticity.explanation: Claim is consistent with Labour's actual record in office.

strength.statement: That's why we invested so heavily in Te Matatini and recognised Matariki as a kaupapa of national significance and introduced the Matariki public holiday, embraced by all New Zealanders.
strength.explanation: The Matariki public holiday and increased Te Matatini funding were actually delivered by the previous Labour government — words backed by delivery.

strength.statement: That made unprecedented investment in Māori housing and created direct funding relationships with iwi and hapu, trusting our knowledge of our communities.
strength.explanation: Labour did expand Māori housing funding and direct iwi relationships in office; 'unprecedented' is somewhat rhetorical but grounded in real programmes.

civility.statement: You have carried the vision of Tā Mason Durie and Dame Tariana Turia, building a model that has transformed Māori health and wellbeing,
civility.explanation: Respectful, honouring language acknowledging workers and founders; constructive tone.

civility.statement: This decision does not reflect on your mahi—it is a political attack on the very existence of Māori-led solutions.
civility.explanation: Frames the Government's decision as a deliberate 'political attack', an accusatory characterisation of motive.

civility.statement: This isn't just about job losses. This is about whānau who depend on these services—who will now be left without the support they need,
civility.explanation: Focuses on human impact of a policy rather than personal attack.
