specificity.statement: I’m calling on all political parties to support my bill to remove GST from kai,
specificity.explanation: Concrete named policy (remove GST from all food) tied to his member's bill.

rigor.statement: We know that GST hits lower income whānau the hardest.
rigor.explanation: A sound economic premise stated to support the bill, though asserted without citation.

veracity.statement: We know that GST hits lower income whānau the hardest.
veracity.explanation: GST is regressive as a share of income for lower-income households, broadly supported by tax-incidence evidence.

divination.statement: It is a change that can be made over night that will have an immediate impact,
divination.explanation: Predicts immediate impact from removing GST on food; plausible on prices but pass-through to consumers is uncertain.

charisma.statement: It shouldn’t matter where you sit on the political spectrum. Removing GST from kai should be a no brainer for any party who is serious about supporting whānau during a cost of living crisis.
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-spectrum appeal inviting all parties in, though the 'no brainer' framing mildly pressures rather than fully persuades.

charisma.statement: On some kaupapa, parties must put the rubbish politicking aside and come to a mutual agreement for the wellbeing of our mokopuna.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking call for cross-party mutual agreement, inclusive in intent.

specificity.statement: We have placed sixteen Fast-Track applicants on notice that Te Pāti Māori will hold them retrospectively liable and immediately revoke their consents when we form the next Government,
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure (sixteen applicants) and concrete actions (retrospective liability, revoke consents).

divination.statement: We have placed sixteen Fast-Track applicants on notice that Te Pāti Māori will hold them retrospectively liable and immediately revoke their consents when we form the next Government,
divination.explanation: Implies a future TPM government able to act retrospectively; electorally and legally uncertain.

strength.statement: We have placed sixteen Fast-Track applicants on notice that Te Pāti Māori will hold them retrospectively liable and immediately revoke their consents when we form the next Government,
strength.explanation: Bold future commitment contingent on forming a government TPM does not lead; aspirational with no present delivery mechanism.

civility.statement: This is what the erosion of Te Tiriti looks like. It is why they stole our Foreshore and Seabed in 2004: so they could sell it off to these companies who care about nothing but profit.
civility.explanation: Attacks a policy and 'these companies' rather than an individual, but 'stole' and 'care about nothing but profit' are inflammatory.

rigor.statement: Iwi have won every court case against TTR, and have proven beyond doubt that this company cannot meet the environmental threshold.
rigor.explanation: Uses the litigation record as evidence, but overgeneralises from procedural wins to a definitive impossibility.

rigor.statement: This is what the erosion of Te Tiriti looks like. It is why they stole our Foreshore and Seabed in 2004: so they could sell it off to these companies who care about nothing but profit.
rigor.explanation: Imputes a single profit-driven motive to a 2004 policy and links it causally to present mining; asserts intent without evidence.

veracity.statement: Iwi have won every court case against TTR, and have proven beyond doubt that this company cannot meet the environmental threshold.
veracity.explanation: TTR's consents were indeed struck down through the courts (including the Supreme Court); 'proven beyond doubt they cannot meet the threshold' overstates what the litigation settled.

veracity.statement: This is what the erosion of Te Tiriti looks like. It is why they stole our Foreshore and Seabed in 2004: so they could sell it off to these companies who care about nothing but profit.
veracity.explanation: The 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act vested title in the Crown but the 'stole to sell off to companies' framing is a contested, motive-laden characterisation.

divination.statement: If TTR fails to meet the EPA’s environmental threshold again, which we are certain they will, there is nothing stopping this government from fast tracking their consent anyway.
divination.explanation: Predicts both a renewed failure and possible government fast-tracking; directionally plausible given history but speculative on intent.

charisma.statement: Te Pāti Māori will not rest until seabed mining is banned in Aotearoa once and for all. We will fight this company, and the government backing them, every step of the way
charisma.explanation: Rallying and combative ('fight every step of the way'); energises supporters but purely us-vs-them.

strength.statement: Te Pāti Māori will not rest until seabed mining is banned in Aotearoa once and for all. We will fight this company, and the government backing them, every step of the way
strength.explanation: Signals sustained commitment consistent with a 12-year opposition record, though it is resolve rather than delivered outcome.

civility.statement: Only 2% of politicians are under the age of 30. We risk losing a whole generation, particularly with this government who is consistently attacking our being, from engaging in politics,
civility.explanation: 'Attacking our being' is a charged claim about the government, though the core point is about youth participation.

specificity.statement: For me, this is about holding space for future wahine Māori, and Māori rangatahi and hopefully inspiring them to use their Māori magic and aspire to achieve.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational and inspirational language with no concrete mechanism or measure.

veracity.statement: Only 2% of politicians are under the age of 30. We risk losing a whole generation, particularly with this government who is consistently attacking our being, from engaging in politics,
veracity.explanation: The under-30 share statistic is plausible but unsourced; 'consistently attacking our being' is a subjective characterisation stated as fact.

divination.statement: Only 2% of politicians are under the age of 30. We risk losing a whole generation, particularly with this government who is consistently attacking our being, from engaging in politics,
divination.explanation: Predicts 'losing a whole generation' from politics; directionally arguable but vague and hard to falsify.

specificity.statement: Budget 2024 will provide an additional $1.1 billion over five years to address demand and cost pressures on the support services funded by the Ministry of Disabled People – Whaikaha.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure ($1.1b), timeframe (five years), named ministry and purpose.

specificity.statement: This includes an $80 million pre-Budget commitment to see the Ministry through to the end of the 2023/24 financial year, and $322 million for 2024/25.
specificity.explanation: Breaks the funding into precise amounts ($80m, $322m) tied to specific financial years.

specificity.statement: The coalition Government wants the best outcomes for the disability community, which is why we are prioritising the essential frontline services they rely on,
specificity.explanation: General statement of intent with no mechanism or figure (the specifics come in following sentences).

specificity.statement: An independent review that is now underway into the disability support system will also help the Government improve the long-term financial sustainability of these services and ensure taxpayers are getting value.
specificity.explanation: References a concrete, in-progress independent review, but its scope and outcomes are described only in general terms.

veracity.statement: Budget 2024 will provide an additional $1.1 billion over five years to address demand and cost pressures on the support services funded by the Ministry of Disabled People – Whaikaha.
veracity.explanation: A concrete stated Budget appropriation; consistent with an official Budget announcement and verifiable.

veracity.statement: This includes an $80 million pre-Budget commitment to see the Ministry through to the end of the 2023/24 financial year, and $322 million for 2024/25.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable appropriation figures presented as official Budget detail.

strength.statement: Budget 2024 will provide an additional $1.1 billion over five years to address demand and cost pressures on the support services funded by the Ministry of Disabled People – Whaikaha.
strength.explanation: As the responsible minister announcing a funded Budget line, this is a committed and delivered allocation rather than mere aspiration.

strength.statement: An independent review that is now underway into the disability support system will also help the Government improve the long-term financial sustainability of these services and ensure taxpayers are getting value.
strength.explanation: A review is underway (in-progress action) but its delivery of sustainability improvements is not yet realised.

specificity.statement: The investment includes extra funding for new classrooms, additional teacher support and early childhood education
specificity.explanation: Names concrete areas (classrooms, teacher support, ECE) but no figures or timeframes attached to this sentence itself.

specificity.statement: Education has the power to change lives. We want every child to have the opportunity to gain the skills and qualifications they need to achieve their potential.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational platitude with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We're determined to improve achievement for all children by establishing a knowledge-rich curriculum, improving reading and maths outcomes, implementing consistent ways of monitoring student progress, improving teacher training, providing better support to students with additional needs and making greater use of data.
specificity.explanation: Lists several named directions (curriculum, monitoring, teacher training) but without measures, targets or dates for any of them.

specificity.statement: Together with the other investments we are making in education, these investments demonstrate the Government’s commitment to lifting student achievement.
specificity.explanation: Generic claim of commitment with no concrete detail beyond referencing the investments already listed.

veracity.statement: The investment includes extra funding for new classrooms, additional teacher support and early childhood education
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the itemised Budget figures listed in the release; broadly accurate description of the allocations.

charisma.statement: Education has the power to change lives. We want every child to have the opportunity to gain the skills and qualifications they need to achieve their potential.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, uplifting 'every child' framing that most sides would share, but a generic sentiment rather than a bridge-building appeal.

strength.statement: We're determined to improve achievement for all children by establishing a knowledge-rich curriculum, improving reading and maths outcomes, implementing consistent ways of monitoring student progress, improving teacher training, providing better support to students with additional needs and making greater use of data.
strength.explanation: Stated intent across a broad reform agenda; mostly in-progress or announced rather than demonstrably delivered at time of statement.

specificity.statement: Transport is a critical enabler for economic growth and productivity, and with over 20,000 vehicles travelling this motorway every day, the new higher speed will help ensure people and freight can get to where they need to go, quickly and safely
specificity.explanation: Includes a concrete traffic figure (20,000 vehicles/day) but the growth/productivity rationale stays general.

specificity.statement: More than 7,900 submissions were received across Northland and Auckland. Responses were overwhelmingly positive, with 94% in support of the increasing the speed limit and 91% strongly in favour.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for submission count and support percentages.

specificity.statement: Since opening in 2023, no one has died in a crash.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, precise claim with a clear timeframe.

specificity.statement: Kiwis have had their say and NZTA has completed all required technical assessments, with the motorway being assessed as safe to increase the speed limit to 110km/h. Now, we’re getting on and delivering it.
specificity.explanation: Names the process (consultation, technical assessments) and the concrete outcome, though this sentence omits the exact date given elsewhere.

specificity.statement: The Pūhoi to Warkworth motorway has vastly improved the safety, connectivity, and resilience of the network between Auckland and Northland, and has opened access to popular destinations between the two regions.
specificity.explanation: General benefits language without measures for the improvements claimed.

veracity.statement: Transport is a critical enabler for economic growth and productivity, and with over 20,000 vehicles travelling this motorway every day, the new higher speed will help ensure people and freight can get to where they need to go, quickly and safely
veracity.explanation: The ~20,000 vehicles/day figure is consistent with NZTA data for this route; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: More than 7,900 submissions were received across Northland and Auckland. Responses were overwhelmingly positive, with 94% in support of the increasing the speed limit and 91% strongly in favour.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific consultation results; presented as verifiable NZTA data with no obvious overstatement.

veracity.statement: Since opening in 2023, no one has died in a crash.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable safety claim about the motorway's record since 2023; presented as fact.

veracity.statement: The Pūhoi to Warkworth motorway has vastly improved the safety, connectivity, and resilience of the network between Auckland and Northland, and has opened access to popular destinations between the two regions.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported (a new motorway improves connectivity) but 'vastly improved' is an unquantified booster claim.

strength.statement: Kiwis have had their say and NZTA has completed all required technical assessments, with the motorway being assessed as safe to increase the speed limit to 110km/h. Now, we’re getting on and delivering it.
strength.explanation: A concrete change (110km/h limit from 1 July) being actually implemented, not merely announced as aspiration.

rigor.statement: Transport is a critical enabler for economic growth and productivity, and with over 20,000 vehicles travelling this motorway every day, the new higher speed will help ensure people and freight can get to where they need to go, quickly and safely
rigor.explanation: Links speed increase to economic benefit plausibly but leans on general assertion rather than evidence of the productivity gain.

rigor.statement: More than 7,900 submissions were received across Northland and Auckland. Responses were overwhelmingly positive, with 94% in support of the increasing the speed limit and 91% strongly in favour.
rigor.explanation: Uses actual consultation data to support the claim of public support, though a self-selected submission pool has limits.

specificity.statement: Cabinet has directed Invest NZ to provide the certainty international investors need and accelerate international investment into New Zealand to turbo charge growth, and create jobs
specificity.explanation: Names the body and its purpose but no targets, funding, or timeframe for the investment increase.

specificity.statement: Invest NZ will be a one stop shop and a problem solver. If it’s good for New Zealand, and good for New Zealander’s, we will be saying yes to investment.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like ('one stop shop', 'saying yes') with no concrete mechanism or criteria.

specificity.statement: We will shortly commence the process to recruit a highly skilled investment specialist with international experience as the Chief Executive, and are working toward the establishment of an executive board.
specificity.explanation: Concrete next steps (CE recruitment, board) but 'shortly' and 'working toward' leave timing vague.

specificity.statement: By attracting global companies we can grow the economy, provide more opportunities and create more jobs
specificity.explanation: Vague causal claim with no numbers or named investments.

strength.statement: Cabinet has directed Invest NZ to provide the certainty international investors need and accelerate international investment into New Zealand to turbo charge growth, and create jobs
strength.explanation: A Cabinet direction to set up an agency — an early establishment step rather than demonstrated delivery of investment or jobs.

strength.statement: We will shortly commence the process to recruit a highly skilled investment specialist with international experience as the Chief Executive, and are working toward the establishment of an executive board.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to begin recruitment; setup in progress rather than delivered.

divination.statement: By attracting global companies we can grow the economy, provide more opportunities and create more jobs
divination.explanation: Predicts economic and jobs growth from FDI — plausible in direction but unquantified and contingent on the agency succeeding.

specificity.statement: In today’s world, security is the foundation of prosperity - and India is a key partner of New Zealand in the Indo-Pacific
specificity.explanation: A framing statement about the relationship; no concrete detail beyond naming India as a partner.

specificity.statement: This arrangement will open up new areas of collaboration between our defence forces and facilitate closer defence ties.
specificity.explanation: Refers to a concrete arrangement but the 'new areas of collaboration' remain undefined.

specificity.statement: My meetings today have allowed us to unlock new opportunities and potential partnerships that will serve the people of New Zealand and India.
specificity.explanation: Generic diplomatic language ('unlock new opportunities', 'potential partnerships') with no concrete outcomes named.

charisma.statement: In today’s world, security is the foundation of prosperity - and India is a key partner of New Zealand in the Indo-Pacific
charisma.explanation: Warm, partnership-oriented language appropriate to bilateral diplomacy, but a broad statement rather than persuasion of a divided audience.

divination.statement: This arrangement will open up new areas of collaboration between our defence forces and facilitate closer defence ties.
divination.explanation: Predicts closer defence collaboration following the arrangement — plausible given the signed cooperation arrangement, but outcomes unspecified.

specificity.statement: The big story is that international expenditure grew almost 60 per cent in the year ending March 2024
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete percentage and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Tourism now contributes 7.5 per cent of GDP according to this data – and continues to be our second highest export. I want to see it back at number 1.
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure and a clear goal (back to number 1) but no plan or timeframe for reaching it.

veracity.statement: The big story is that international expenditure grew almost 60 per cent in the year ending March 2024
veracity.explanation: Matches the Stats NZ figure of 59.9 per cent growth cited in the release; accurate.

veracity.statement: This encouraging news reflects a healthy recovery following the end of border restrictions in June 2022 and shows that many people all over the world couldn’t wait to visit New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Border restrictions did end in 2022 and a rebound followed; the causal attribution is plausible but simplified.

veracity.statement: Tourism now contributes 7.5 per cent of GDP according to this data – and continues to be our second highest export. I want to see it back at number 1.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the 7.5% GDP and second-export claims to the released data; consistent with the Tourism Satellite Account framing.

strength.statement: Tourism now contributes 7.5 per cent of GDP according to this data – and continues to be our second highest export. I want to see it back at number 1.
strength.explanation: States an aspiration to restore tourism as top export with no concrete mechanism attached here.

rigor.statement: This encouraging news reflects a healthy recovery following the end of border restrictions in June 2022 and shows that many people all over the world couldn’t wait to visit New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The border-reopening explanation is reasonable, but 'couldn't wait to visit' is an emotive gloss beyond what the data shows.

authenticity.statement: We do also recognise a drop in domestic tourism spend reported today.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges an unfavourable figure in the same data rather than only citing the positive, a consistency-positive signal.

forthrightness.statement: We do also recognise a drop in domestic tourism spend reported today.
forthrightness.explanation: Volunteers the negative domestic result openly, though quickly pivots to the growth argument.

specificity.statement: The public feel safer when Police are visible and when they know Police are close at hand and accessible.
specificity.explanation: General assertion about public sentiment with no data or detail.

specificity.statement: In the last year, victimisations are down 17 per cent, robbery has dropped 25 per cent, and theft is down by 21 per cent.
specificity.explanation: Three precise figures for named crime categories over a stated period.

specificity.statement: Public safety is at the core of this Government’s law and order agenda and is what drives our police officers
specificity.explanation: Mission-statement language with no concrete policy or measure.

specificity.statement: The base will be home to Auckland’s 51 inner city beat officers, who provide 24/7 policing coverage, and who continue to make a real difference in our largest city.
specificity.explanation: Gives the officer count (51) and 24/7 coverage, though 'make a real difference' is unquantified.

specificity.statement: The community have been asking for a central police station for some time, and I am very pleased that Police have been able to deliver on this.
specificity.explanation: Refers to a delivered station but 'for some time' keeps the detail loose.

veracity.statement: In the last year, victimisations are down 17 per cent, robbery has dropped 25 per cent, and theft is down by 21 per cent.
veracity.explanation: Specific crime-reduction figures presented as fact; plausible for the beat area but selectively presented without the baseline or scope caveats.

veracity.statement: The base will be home to Auckland’s 51 inner city beat officers, who provide 24/7 policing coverage, and who continue to make a real difference in our largest city.
veracity.explanation: The staffing and coverage details are concrete and presented as verifiable facts.

strength.statement: The community have been asking for a central police station for some time, and I am very pleased that Police have been able to deliver on this.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete facility (the new central station) actually opened and delivered, matching a stated community demand.

rigor.statement: The public feel safer when Police are visible and when they know Police are close at hand and accessible.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable premise but an unevidenced generalisation about how the public feels.

rigor.statement: In the last year, victimisations are down 17 per cent, robbery has dropped 25 per cent, and theft is down by 21 per cent.
rigor.explanation: Cites figures to support the beat team's value but implies causation from a localized correlation without controlling for other factors.

specificity.statement: It’s the fourth consecutive quarter inflation has remained within the target range – a stark contrast to under the previous government, where inflation raged on unchecked, reaching 7.3 per cent in 2022
specificity.explanation: Cites the streak of quarters and a precise past figure (7.3%).

specificity.statement: New Zealanders can be assured it now has a Government that is paying attention to forces that affect their cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Reassurance line with no concrete policy or measure.

specificity.statement: It’s pleasing to see non-tradeables inflation – which paints a picture of domestic demand and supply conditions – continues to fall.
specificity.explanation: References a specific technical measure (non-tradeables inflation) and its direction, but no figures.

specificity.statement: That’s why this Government has also been clear in its call to councils to focus on the basics and keep rates under control. We look forward to councils taking heed of this and playing their role as stewards of ratepayers’ money better in the future.
specificity.explanation: Directional call to councils ('focus on the basics') without any concrete lever or requirement.

specificity.statement: That’s why this Government is focused on economic growth, because that is New Zealand’s pathway to more jobs, higher incomes and the money to pay for schools, hospitals and safer communities.
specificity.explanation: States growth as the priority but names no mechanism, target, or timeframe.

veracity.statement: It’s the fourth consecutive quarter inflation has remained within the target range – a stark contrast to under the previous government, where inflation raged on unchecked, reaching 7.3 per cent in 2022
veracity.explanation: The 7.3% 2022 peak is accurate, but 'raged on unchecked' overstates and ignores that rate hikes were underway; partly misleading framing.

veracity.statement: It’s pleasing to see non-tradeables inflation – which paints a picture of domestic demand and supply conditions – continues to fall.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the trend in the CPI data cited; a defensible characterisation of domestic inflation easing.

charisma.statement: New Zealanders can be assured it now has a Government that is paying attention to forces that affect their cost of living.
charisma.explanation: Confident, reassuring tone but appeals to its own base and implicitly contrasts with opponents rather than uniting.

rigor.statement: That’s why this Government is focused on economic growth, because that is New Zealand’s pathway to more jobs, higher incomes and the money to pay for schools, hospitals and safer communities.
rigor.explanation: The growth-funds-services chain is a reasonable general argument but asserted rather than evidenced.

civility.statement: It’s the fourth consecutive quarter inflation has remained within the target range – a stark contrast to under the previous government, where inflation raged on unchecked, reaching 7.3 per cent in 2022
civility.explanation: Legitimate contrast with the prior record but the loaded 'raged on unchecked' is a partisan swipe rather than pure policy critique.

civility.statement: That’s why this Government has also been clear in its call to councils to focus on the basics and keep rates under control. We look forward to councils taking heed of this and playing their role as stewards of ratepayers’ money better in the future.
civility.explanation: Critical of councils' spending but directed at conduct/policy rather than personal, though 'better in the future' is a pointed rebuke.

civility.statement: It is unconscionable that Aotearoa New Zealand demands Palestinians prove their 'governance' and 'democracy' while remaining silent on Israel's ongoing genocidal apartheid regime, breaches of international law, and the mass killing of civilians
civility.explanation: Joint co-leader statement. Attacks the Government's stance with charged, absolutist language ('genocidal apartheid regime') rather than engaging its stated reasoning.

civility.statement: We acknowledge the $10 million of additional humanitarian aid, but money does not absolve complicity in silence. True solidarity requires political courage to call Israel's actions what they are: war crimes, apartheid, and attempted genocide.
civility.explanation: Joint statement; acknowledges the aid but accuses the Government of 'complicity' and cowardice, framing rather than engaging its position.

veracity.statement: It is unconscionable that Aotearoa New Zealand demands Palestinians prove their 'governance' and 'democracy' while remaining silent on Israel's ongoing genocidal apartheid regime, breaches of international law, and the mass killing of civilians
veracity.explanation: Mass killing of civilians is documented, but 'genocidal apartheid regime' is a heavily contested legal characterisation asserted as settled fact.

specificity.statement: It is unconscionable that Aotearoa New Zealand demands Palestinians prove their 'governance' and 'democracy' while remaining silent on Israel's ongoing genocidal apartheid regime, breaches of international law, and the mass killing of civilians
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete double standard (governance/democracy conditions vs silence) but no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: We acknowledge the $10 million of additional humanitarian aid, but money does not absolve complicity in silence. True solidarity requires political courage to call Israel's actions what they are: war crimes, apartheid, and attempted genocide.
specificity.explanation: Cites the $10m figure but the core demand ('call it what it is') is rhetorical rather than a concrete action.

specificity.statement: Te Pāti Māori will continue to stand unequivocally with the people of Palestine.
specificity.explanation: A statement of solidarity with no mechanism, measure, or action.

authenticity.statement: Te Pāti Māori will continue to stand unequivocally with the people of Palestine.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the party's repeated pro-Palestine statements across 2023-2025 in this same set of releases; words match a sustained position.

civility.statement: The conveners are meant to be independent. For a Minister so loudly pro-seabed mining to admit publicly he is trying to gain access is political bullying and corporate cronyism at its worst.
civility.explanation: Labels a named Minister's conduct 'political bullying and corporate cronyism', an accusation of corruption rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: For Shane Jones to use his Ministerial office to tilt the table in favour of TTR is corrupt politics, plain and simple
civility.explanation: Direct accusation of corruption against a named Minister.

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court has already rejected this destructive project.
veracity.explanation: The Supreme Court did rule against TTR's seabed mining consent (Trans-Tasman Resources v Taranaki-Whanganui, 2021); accurate, though 'destructive' is her characterisation.

specificity.statement: When we are in government, Te Pāti Māori will repeal all legislation that allows seabed mining and restore integrity to decision-making in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (repeal seabed mining legislation) but no detail on which statutes or timeframe.

authenticity.statement: When we are in government, Te Pāti Māori will repeal all legislation that allows seabed mining and restore integrity to decision-making in Aotearoa.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Ngarewa-Packer's long-standing, prominent opposition to seabed mining.

rigor.statement: The conveners are meant to be independent. For a Minister so loudly pro-seabed mining to admit publicly he is trying to gain access is political bullying and corporate cronyism at its worst.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the claim to Jones's own quoted admission (real evidence) but leaps to 'cronyism at its worst' beyond what the quote establishes.

strength.statement: When we are in government, Te Pāti Māori will repeal all legislation that allows seabed mining and restore integrity to decision-making in Aotearoa.
strength.explanation: Conditional on being in government, which they are not; aspiration without delivery capacity.

civility.statement: This Government's attack on vocational training is short-sighted and regressive. Job cuts don't just mean fewer roles, they mean the loss of experienced and passionate kaimahi who genuinely care for their students.
civility.explanation: 'Attack' is charged but the criticism engages the policy's consequences rather than attacking individuals.

specificity.statement: We won't sit back while this Government shuts the door on Māori futures. Our commitment is clear—we would invest more in regional tertiary education, not less.
specificity.explanation: 'Invest more' with no figures or named programmes; direction only.

charisma.statement: We won't sit back while this Government shuts the door on Māori futures. Our commitment is clear—we would invest more in regional tertiary education, not less.
charisma.explanation: Rallies its own base with us-vs-Government framing rather than reaching across.

civility.statement: This decision not only undermines basic legal practices but also perpetuates the ongoing tyranny of the majority against Māori representation,
civility.explanation: Strong 'tyranny of the majority' framing of the committee, but aimed at process/institution rather than a person.

civility.statement: Parliament continues to dismiss tikanga and justice, and this Committee is no different. They have already decided our fate. This is not a fair hearing. It is s a display of power designed to silence us.
civility.explanation: Accuses the committee of a predetermined outcome; adversarial but directed at process.

civility.statement: No just legal system would tolerate such a blatant denial of rights,
civility.explanation: Sweeping but directed at the process's fairness rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: How can we defend tikanga when their decisions are predetermined? The Committee's actions are yet another example of how Māori voices are systematically marginalised, entrenching discrimination within the halls of power.
civility.explanation: Asserts the committee prejudged them; rhetorical but process-focused.

rigor.statement: This decision not only undermines basic legal practices but also perpetuates the ongoing tyranny of the majority against Māori representation,
rigor.explanation: Asserts systemic prejudice without laying out the specific denials of rights in this statement.

rigor.statement: How can we defend tikanga when their decisions are predetermined? The Committee's actions are yet another example of how Māori voices are systematically marginalised, entrenching discrimination within the halls of power.
rigor.explanation: Assumes the conclusion (decisions predetermined) as a premise; assertion rather than evidenced.

civility.statement: Reinstating Three Strikes will empower a systematically racist system and exacerbate the overrepresentation of Māori in prisons.
civility.explanation: Critiques the system and policy rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: If the government's goal is to put more Māori, Pacific Islanders, and poor people in prison, this bill will succeed. It is not a bill that will reduce crime in this country,
civility.explanation: Imputes an intent to imprison Māori and the poor to the government, a strawman of its stated aim.

veracity.statement: Despite being only 20% of the total population, we are half of the prison population.
veracity.explanation: Māori are roughly half the prison population (accurate), but ~16-17% of the total population, so '20%' is somewhat overstated.

specificity.statement: The Government is focused on growing the economy, creating jobs, lifting wages and help Kiwis with the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Generic list of aspirations with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: While NCEA was designed to be flexible, for many students that flexibility has encouraged a focus on simply attaining the qualification. This has come at the cost of developing the critical skills and knowledge they need for clear pathways into future study, training or employment,
specificity.explanation: Diagnoses a specific mechanism but with no figures on how many students are affected.

specificity.statement: Every student is already taught at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths, we've banned cell phones in classrooms, we've introduced a world-leading Maths and English curriculum, mandated structured literacy and maths programmes, equipped teachers and students with high-quality resources, made huge investments into learning support and stopped building open-plan classrooms,

specificity.statement: This is about making sure our national qualification opens doors for every young person, whether they're heading into a trade, university, or straight into work. Parents can be assured their kids will get the best possible opportunity to thrive,

rigor.statement: The evidence shows NCEA is not consistent and can be hard to navigate. It doesn't always deliver what students and employers need.

rigor.statement: While NCEA was designed to be flexible, for many students that flexibility has encouraged a focus on simply attaining the qualification. This has come at the cost of developing the critical skills and knowledge they need for clear pathways into future study, training or employment,
rigor.explanation: Coherent cause-effect argument (flexibility → credit-chasing → skill gaps); plausible but asserted rather than evidenced with data.

strength.statement: We're backing Kiwi kids with a new internationally benchmarked national qualification designed to do exactly that,
strength.explanation: A proposal to replace NCEA, announced not delivered.

strength.statement: Every student is already taught at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths, we've banned cell phones in classrooms, we've introduced a world-leading Maths and English curriculum, mandated structured literacy and maths programmes, equipped teachers and students with high-quality resources, made huge investments into learning support and stopped building open-plan classrooms,
strength.explanation: Lists concrete education measures actually enacted (cell phone ban, structured literacy mandate, hour-a-day requirement) — demonstrated delivery, though 'world-leading' is self-assessment.

charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing spanning trades, university and work; reassuring but appeals to a broad audience.

veracity.explanation: Shrinking section sizes and rising cost of living are broadly accurate trends; the shed characterisation is a fair description of the old setback rule.

veracity.statement: Frustration with the building consent system is one of the top issues flagged to the Red Tape Tipline.
veracity.explanation: A claim about tipline submissions that is plausible but not independently verifiable from the text.

specificity.statement: We've heard the frustration about this regulation through the Red Tape Tipline. Section sizes are shrinking, and the cost of living rising. Forcing people to put sheds in the middle of their lawn or pay for a consent to store tools doesn't make sense.

specificity.statement: There is no justification for such generous setback distances on private property.

specificity.statement: Frustration with the building consent system is one of the top issues flagged to the Red Tape Tipline.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the issue and its source but with no counts or ranking detail.

specificity.statement: This Government is relentlessly focused on making it easier and more affordable to build,
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like framing with no mechanism or measure in this sentence.

rigor.statement: There is no justification for such generous setback distances on private property.

divination.statement: By the end of the year, homeowners will be able to put up a small shed or garage closer to their boundary or another building without needing a consent.
divination.explanation: Predicts the rule change will be in force by year-end; well-supported since Cabinet has already agreed it.

strength.statement: By the end of the year, homeowners will be able to put up a small shed or garage closer to their boundary or another building without needing a consent.
strength.explanation: Cabinet has agreed the change; delivery of the regulatory change is in progress with a stated deadline of late 2025.

veracity.statement: Lower Hutt is currently the only metropolitan area in New Zealand without a daytime urgent care service. That's why the Government identified it as a priority location under the urgent care expansion announced in May.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual claim about Lower Hutt's service gap; plausible but not independently verifiable from the text.

specificity.statement: Lower Hutt is currently the only metropolitan area in New Zealand without a daytime urgent care service. That's why the Government identified it as a priority location under the urgent care expansion announced in May.
specificity.explanation: Concrete claim tied to a named policy and timing (urgent care expansion announced in May).

specificity.statement: With seven consulting rooms, two triage rooms, a plaster and phlebotomy room, a carer's room, and a much larger waiting area, this centre is purpose-built to meet the needs of a growing community.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates exact facilities (seven consulting rooms, two triage rooms, etc.).

specificity.statement: This new location enables the staged rollout of a dedicated daytime urgent care service, starting from December 2025.
specificity.explanation: Concrete service and a start date (December 2025).

divination.statement: This new location enables the staged rollout of a dedicated daytime urgent care service, starting from December 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a daytime service starting December 2025; plausible given the facility is already open, but a future rollout.

strength.statement: This new location enables the staged rollout of a dedicated daytime urgent care service, starting from December 2025.
strength.explanation: Facility opened and lease taken over (delivered), with the daytime service a staged future step.

strength.statement: It's a clear example of the Government delivering on its promise to improve health services right across the country,
strength.explanation: Backed by an actually opened facility, but the daytime service is not yet operational.

authenticity.statement: It's a clear example of the Government delivering on its promise to improve health services right across the country,
authenticity.explanation: Ties a concrete opened facility to a stated promise; the opening supports the claim, though 'right across the country' generalises from one site.

veracity.statement: The abolition of petrol tax, and the move towards all vehicles (whether they be petrol, diesel, electric or hybrid) paying for roads based on distance and weight, is the biggest change to how we fund our roading network in 50 years,
veracity.explanation: Shifting all vehicles to distance/weight charging is a major structural change; 'biggest in 50 years' is a plausible but unquantified superlative.

veracity.statement: Right now, New Zealanders pay Fuel Excise Duty (FED, or petrol tax) of about 70c per litre of petrol every time they fill up at the pump with a petrol car.
veracity.explanation: FED of roughly 70c/litre is accurate for the period.

veracity.statement: We are also seeing a fast uptake of fuel-efficient petrol hybrid vehicles. In 2015, there were 12,000 on our roads, while today there are over 350,000.
veracity.explanation: The scale of hybrid growth is directionally accurate; the precise 12,000-to-350,000 figures are asserted without a cited source.

specificity.statement: The abolition of petrol tax, and the move towards all vehicles (whether they be petrol, diesel, electric or hybrid) paying for roads based on distance and weight, is the biggest change to how we fund our roading network in 50 years,
specificity.explanation: Describes the policy mechanism (distance and weight, all fuel types) clearly.

specificity.statement: Right now, New Zealanders pay Fuel Excise Duty (FED, or petrol tax) of about 70c per litre of petrol every time they fill up at the pump with a petrol car.
specificity.explanation: Gives the concrete rate (~70c per litre).

specificity.statement: We are also seeing a fast uptake of fuel-efficient petrol hybrid vehicles. In 2015, there were 12,000 on our roads, while today there are over 350,000.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete data points with years illustrating the trend.

specificity.statement: I expect to pass legislation in 2026, followed by an updated Code of Practice for RUC providers. We will also engage with the market in 2026 to assess technological solutions and delivery timelines.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete steps and a year (legislation in 2026, updated Code of Practice, market engagement).

specificity.statement: By 2027, the RUC system will be 'open for business', with third-party providers able to offer innovative payment services and a consistent approval process in place.
specificity.explanation: Gives a target year (2027) and the intended end-state (third-party providers, consistent approval).

specificity.statement: At this stage, no date has been set for the full transition of the light vehicle fleet. That's a deliberate choice, as we're focused on getting the system right rather than rushing its rollout.
specificity.explanation: Honest but necessarily vague on the key date, since none has been set.

specificity.statement: Eventually, paying for RUC should be like paying a power bill online, or a Netflix subscription. Simple and easy.
specificity.explanation: Vivid but non-committal comparison with no mechanism or measure.

rigor.statement: We are also seeing a fast uptake of fuel-efficient petrol hybrid vehicles. In 2015, there were 12,000 on our roads, while today there are over 350,000.
rigor.explanation: Uses fleet data to support the argument that petrol tax is a decaying proxy for road use; evidence backs the conclusion.

rigor.statement: It isn't fair to have Kiwis who drive less and who can't afford a fuel-efficient car paying more than people who can afford one and drive more often.
rigor.explanation: A coherent equity argument that follows from the earlier point about FED's declining accuracy; leans partly on a fairness appeal.

rigor.statement: Eventually, paying for RUC should be like paying a power bill online, or a Netflix subscription. Simple and easy.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to analogy (power bill/Netflix) to promise simplicity rather than evidence the system will be that easy.

divination.statement: I expect to pass legislation in 2026, followed by an updated Code of Practice for RUC providers. We will also engage with the market in 2026 to assess technological solutions and delivery timelines.
divination.explanation: Forecasts passing legislation in 2026; plausible for a government with a majority but dependent on the parliamentary timetable.

divination.statement: By 2027, the RUC system will be 'open for business', with third-party providers able to offer innovative payment services and a consistent approval process in place.
divination.explanation: Predicts a working third-party RUC system by 2027; plausible but dependent on 2026 legislation and market delivery, so uncertain.

strength.statement: I expect to pass legislation in 2026, followed by an updated Code of Practice for RUC providers. We will also engage with the market in 2026 to assess technological solutions and delivery timelines.
strength.explanation: A staged plan with Cabinet decisions taken, but the legislation is future and unpassed at the time of speaking.

charisma.statement: It isn't fair to have Kiwis who drive less and who can't afford a fuel-efficient car paying more than people who can afford one and drive more often.
charisma.explanation: Frames the reform around fairness to lower-income drivers, an inclusive appeal beyond one constituency.

forthrightness.statement: At this stage, no date has been set for the full transition of the light vehicle fleet. That's a deliberate choice, as we're focused on getting the system right rather than rushing its rollout.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes there is no set date for the full transition and explains why, rather than deflecting the open question of timing.

veracity.statement: Despite being in the top 10% of high-income countries for infrastructure spend over the last 20 or so years, we are in the bottom 10% for what we get for our spending.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the Infrastructure Commission's benchmarking findings that NZ spends heavily but ranks poorly on value/efficiency; broadly supported though the precise deciles are a simplification.

veracity.statement: In 1965, we built the longest submarine cable of its kind – the Cook Strait cable between Benmore and Lower Hutt, which is 610km long.
veracity.explanation: Conflates the whole HVDC inter-island link (~610km, mostly overhead line) with the submarine cable section, which is only around 40km; describing a 610km 'submarine cable' is misleading.

veracity.statement: The NIP is not this government's Plan, it's New Zealand's Plan. Each political party in Parliament was offered a briefing on the NIP. I'm really pleased that most parties accepted the offer and have had one or more meetings with the Commission.
veracity.explanation: Claim that the NIP was developed independently by the Commission and offered to all parties is plausible and consistent with the process; specifics unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: What I oppose is the $30 billion light-rail-metro-monstrosity that New Zealanders couldn’t afford.
veracity.explanation: The '$30 billion' figure sits at the high end of/above official Auckland light rail estimates (commonly cited around $14.6bn), and 'monstrosity' is loaded exaggeration.

veracity.statement: The Pipeline includes over 8,000 initiatives underway and in planning from 114 contributing organisations. It represents over $200 billion in investment value – with over $110 billion of the Pipeline having a funding source confirmed.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Infrastructure Commission's published pipeline data; figures plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: We are seeing a fast uptake of fuel-efficient petrol hybrid vehicles. In 2015, there were 12,000 on our roads, while today there are over 350,000.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate — hybrid numbers have grown very substantially over the decade; exact figures plausible though unverified here.

veracity.statement: An independent analysis by Castalia estimated the new system could reduce compliance and administrative costs by $14.8 billion – potentially removing about 10 Transmission Gullys worth of red tape from the economy.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports a commissioned estimate, but such savings figures are speculative projections, not realised outcomes.

veracity.statement: A draft decision has been released for the Port of Auckland expansion signalling it will be approved shortly. I’m told what could have taken five years took instead just five months.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track draft decision is real, but the 'five years vs five months' contrast is hedged ('I'm told') and a favourable, unverified comparison.

veracity.statement: This was notable with the NZ Upgrade projects, for which funding was approved in early 2020 – and some of these projects are only just beginning construction now (with large cost overruns).
veracity.explanation: NZ Upgrade Programme (2020) projects did face significant delays and cost escalation; broadly accurate, presented to make a point about funding-to-delivery lag.

rigor.statement: Despite being in the top 10% of high-income countries for infrastructure spend over the last 20 or so years, we are in the bottom 10% for what we get for our spending.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative international data to support the conclusion that more money alone won't fix the system; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Now we find it difficult to consent a solar farm. Not even build it, just getting permission to build it.
rigor.explanation: An anecdotal illustration of over-regulation rather than an evidenced claim.

rigor.statement: One option is we grow slowly – or not at all - muddle along, take years to make tough decisions, react to things as they come up, and just largely be OK with the status quo. I call this managed mediocrity. At worst, it is managed decline.
rigor.explanation: Frames the situation as two stark choices (managed decline vs bold reform) — a false-dichotomy rhetorical device rather than reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: But the current system is regressive. Lower income Kiwis don’t necessarily have the option to buy a new, efficient hybrid vehicle. Wealthier folk like me who can afford newer, more efficient cars pay relatively less.
rigor.explanation: Logical argument: fuel-economy-based charging shifts road-funding burden toward those unable to afford efficient cars; conclusion follows, includes self as example.

rigor.statement: An independent analysis by Castalia estimated the new system could reduce compliance and administrative costs by $14.8 billion – potentially removing about 10 Transmission Gullys worth of red tape from the economy.
rigor.explanation: Cites an external analysis (appeal to authority) but the figure is a modelled 'could' estimate presented favourably.

rigor.statement: Regulated utilities and local government are legislatively required to do these things – I don’t see why central government thinks it should hold others to a higher standard than it does itself.
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument: if utilities and councils must publish asset management plans, central government should meet the same standard; the premise supports the conclusion.

rigor.statement: As I’ve said before, we need to start saying ‘yes’ a lot more, and ‘no’ a lot less – this is especially true for infrastructure. But simply throwing money at the problem won’t fix things because our current system is too inefficient.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable claim that spending alone won't fix an inefficient system, linked to the efficiency evidence he cites.

specificity.statement: Despite being in the top 10% of high-income countries for infrastructure spend over the last 20 or so years, we are in the bottom 10% for what we get for our spending.
specificity.explanation: Concrete comparative metric (top 10% spend vs bottom 10% return), though the source and exact measure are not named.

specificity.statement: Now we find it difficult to consent a solar farm. Not even build it, just getting permission to build it.
specificity.explanation: Illustrative point about consenting difficulty but no figures, timeframes, or named case.

specificity.statement: The Pipeline includes over 8,000 initiatives underway and in planning from 114 contributing organisations. It represents over $200 billion in investment value – with over $110 billion of the Pipeline having a funding source confirmed.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts and dollar figures for initiatives, organisations and funded value.

specificity.statement: We are seeing a fast uptake of fuel-efficient petrol hybrid vehicles. In 2015, there were 12,000 on our roads, while today there are over 350,000.
specificity.explanation: Concrete before/after counts with years.

specificity.statement: Essentially, the government will be abolishing petrol tax. People will pay for the roads based on how much they use them.
specificity.explanation: Clear goal (abolish FED, distance-based charging) but the 'how much/by when' for the full fleet is deliberately left open.

specificity.statement: The full transition of the light vehicle fleet will come later – once the market is ready. I am not going to put a date on that today, intentionally – we are choosing to get this right, not to do it fast.
specificity.explanation: Explicitly commits to no timeframe for the full transition.

specificity.statement: We expect to legislate for these changes in 2026, amend the regulations, and introduce an updated Code of Practice for RUC retailers and customer service providers.
specificity.explanation: Names the instruments and a year.

specificity.statement: An independent analysis by Castalia estimated the new system could reduce compliance and administrative costs by $14.8 billion – potentially removing about 10 Transmission Gullys worth of red tape from the economy.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific commissioned estimate and dollar figure with a concrete comparison.

specificity.statement: In the meantime, our second RMA Amendment Bill will pass into law next week.
specificity.explanation: Specific bill and timeframe ('next week').

specificity.statement: A few weeks ago, the Minister for Economic Growth and I released an update showing that over $6 billion of government-funded infrastructure is due to start construction between now and Christmas. Workers will start construction on $3.9 billion of roading projects – like Melling and Ōtaki to north of Levin, $800 million of school property projects, and a range of health projects and other government buildings.
specificity.explanation: Named projects, dollar breakdowns and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: As I’ve said before, we need to start saying ‘yes’ a lot more, and ‘no’ a lot less – this is especially true for infrastructure. But simply throwing money at the problem won’t fix things because our current system is too inefficient.
specificity.explanation: Directional slogan-like framing ('say yes more') with the substantive detail supplied elsewhere in the speech.

charisma.statement: One option is we grow slowly – or not at all - muddle along, take years to make tough decisions, react to things as they come up, and just largely be OK with the status quo. I call this managed mediocrity. At worst, it is managed decline.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective framing but rallies around the speaker's own reform agenda rather than building cross-party bridges.

charisma.statement: The NIP is not this government's Plan, it's New Zealand's Plan. Each political party in Parliament was offered a briefing on the NIP. I'm really pleased that most parties accepted the offer and have had one or more meetings with the Commission.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly inclusive and consensus-seeking, framing the plan as cross-partisan and welcoming other parties in.

charisma.statement: We need to move away from the rhetoric of needing a bipartisan pipeline and instead build bipartisan consensus on the idea that governments of all flavours should use best-practice to plan, select, fund and finance, deliver, and look after infrastructure.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground across 'governments of all flavours' and reframes debate toward shared process rather than partisan conflict.

charisma.statement: The rhetoric in New Zealand politics that “the left hate roads and cars, and the right hate cycleways and light-rail”, has distracted from this important question. I will also say that the polarity is overstated.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to depolarise a partisan divide and acknowledges the caricature on both sides, inviting a shared frame.

charisma.statement: I am not opposed to light rail. Like most New Zealanders, I love visiting cities like Melbourne and Sydney and zipping around on their trams.
charisma.explanation: Warm, relatable and inclusive ('like most New Zealanders'), softening a partisan wedge issue.

civility.statement: We need to move away from the rhetoric of needing a bipartisan pipeline and instead build bipartisan consensus on the idea that governments of all flavours should use best-practice to plan, select, fund and finance, deliver, and look after infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Focuses on ideas and process, no personal attacks.

civility.statement: What I oppose is the $30 billion light-rail-metro-monstrosity that New Zealanders couldn’t afford.
civility.explanation: Attacks a project/policy rather than a person, but 'monstrosity' is disparaging hyperbole.

civility.statement: Regulated utilities and local government are legislatively required to do these things – I don’t see why central government thinks it should hold others to a higher standard than it does itself.
civility.explanation: Critiques the system/central government's own double standard without personal attack.

civility.statement: This was notable with the NZ Upgrade projects, for which funding was approved in early 2020 – and some of these projects are only just beginning construction now (with large cost overruns).
civility.explanation: Points to a systemic delivery failure with a concrete example rather than attacking individuals.

authenticity.statement: I am not opposed to light rail. Like most New Zealanders, I love visiting cities like Melbourne and Sydney and zipping around on their trams.
authenticity.explanation: Stated openness to light rail from a minister whose government cancelled Auckland light rail; a defensible distinction (mode vs cost) but the pro/anti signal is mixed.

authenticity.statement: But the current system is regressive. Lower income Kiwis don’t necessarily have the option to buy a new, efficient hybrid vehicle. Wealthier folk like me who can afford newer, more efficient cars pay relatively less.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly acknowledges he personally benefits from the status quo he is proposing to change, which aligns words with the direction of the reform.

strength.statement: Essentially, the government will be abolishing petrol tax. People will pay for the roads based on how much they use them.
strength.explanation: A major announced intention with no full-transition date; described as the biggest change in 50 years but delivery is early-stage, so this is commitment rather than delivery.

strength.statement: We are on track to replace the RMA with new legislation next year. Our new system will be effects-based, embrace standardised zoning, and be far more permissive and enabling – while also protecting the environment.
strength.explanation: RMA replacement is a flagship commitment in progress with bills drafted, but not yet enacted at the time of speaking.

strength.statement: A few weeks ago, the Minister for Economic Growth and I released an update showing that over $6 billion of government-funded infrastructure is due to start construction between now and Christmas. Workers will start construction on $3.9 billion of roading projects – like Melling and Ōtaki to north of Levin, $800 million of school property projects, and a range of health projects and other government buildings.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete funded projects reaching construction, though 'due to start' is forthcoming rather than delivered.

forthrightness.statement: The full transition of the light vehicle fleet will come later – once the market is ready. I am not going to put a date on that today, intentionally – we are choosing to get this right, not to do it fast.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly declines to give a completion date and explains why, which is candid, but the core 'when' remains unanswered.

divination.statement: We expect to legislate for these changes in 2026, amend the regulations, and introduce an updated Code of Practice for RUC retailers and customer service providers.
divination.explanation: Forecasts 2026 legislation; plausible for a government with a majority but subject to legislative-programme slippage.

divination.statement: In 2027, the RUC system will be open for business, with innovative tech and a range of retail offerings able to operate and compete in the market.
divination.explanation: A dated prediction of a functioning competitive E-RUC market by 2027; achievable but dependent on legislation, market response and NZTA system readiness.

divination.statement: We are on track to replace the RMA with new legislation next year. Our new system will be effects-based, embrace standardised zoning, and be far more permissive and enabling – while also protecting the environment.
divination.explanation: Predicts new RMA-replacement legislation next year; credible given majority and drafting underway, but large reforms often slip.

divination.statement: In the meantime, our second RMA Amendment Bill will pass into law next week.
divination.explanation: Near-term, near-certain prediction for a bill at final stages with a government majority.

divination.statement: A draft decision has been released for the Port of Auckland expansion signalling it will be approved shortly. I’m told what could have taken five years took instead just five months.
divination.explanation: Predicts imminent approval based on a released draft decision — reasonably well-supported.

divination.statement: A few weeks ago, the Minister for Economic Growth and I released an update showing that over $6 billion of government-funded infrastructure is due to start construction between now and Christmas. Workers will start construction on $3.9 billion of roading projects – like Melling and Ōtaki to north of Levin, $800 million of school property projects, and a range of health projects and other government buildings.
divination.explanation: Forecasts $6bn of construction starts before Christmas; specific and evidenced but construction start dates commonly slip.

veracity.statement: It’s of note, however, that today’s data confirms 8000 fewer unemployed people than Treasury forecast would be the case in its pre-election update.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reported 5.2% actual vs 5.4% forecast; the 8000 figure is a plausible derivation but selectively favourable framing.

veracity.statement: Rising unemployment is tough on every New Zealander impacted and is the unfortunate after-effect of a historic period of out-of-control inflation, rapidly rising interest rates and stagnant growth.
veracity.explanation: Inflation and rate rises did precede the labour-market softening, but 'out-of-control' and 'historic' are hyperbolic characterisations.

veracity.statement: Treasury, in its pre-election fiscal update, made clear that unemployment would peak in the middle of this year.
veracity.explanation: Broadly reflects Treasury forecasting of a mid-cycle unemployment peak, though presenting a forecast as settled fact overstates its certainty.

veracity.statement: A recovery is now underway with inflation back under control, interest rates falling and healthy rates of growth in the first three months of the year.
veracity.explanation: Inflation had eased and rates were falling, but 'recovery underway' and 'healthy growth' are optimistic characterisations set against still-rising unemployment.

veracity.statement: We also note that average hourly earnings rose 4.5 per cent in the past year driven by wages in the private sector. This is well ahead of inflation at 2.7 per cent.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable wage-growth and inflation figures presented as a real-wage comparison; consistent with the period's data.

rigor.statement: Rising unemployment is tough on every New Zealander impacted and is the unfortunate after-effect of a historic period of out-of-control inflation, rapidly rising interest rates and stagnant growth.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation from prior inflation/rates to current unemployment without evidence, leaning on emotive language ('out-of-control').

specificity.statement: It’s of note, however, that today’s data confirms 8000 fewer unemployed people than Treasury forecast would be the case in its pre-election update.
specificity.explanation: Concrete number tied to a named forecast.

specificity.statement: A recovery is now underway with inflation back under control, interest rates falling and healthy rates of growth in the first three months of the year.
specificity.explanation: Several directional claims but few precise figures in this sentence.

specificity.statement: We also note that average hourly earnings rose 4.5 per cent in the past year driven by wages in the private sector. This is well ahead of inflation at 2.7 per cent.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages for earnings growth and inflation.

specificity.statement: Despite global volatility and factors outside our control, we remain confident in New Zealand’s economic prospects and are working hard to create the conditions for future job creation with $6 billion of government-funded construction work kicking off before Christmas, fast-track projects beginning, exports growing and the Investment Boost tax policy giving businesses a reason to invest and grow.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete levers ($6bn construction, fast-track, Investment Boost) though outcomes are aspirational.

authenticity.statement: Rising unemployment is tough on every New Zealander impacted and is the unfortunate after-effect of a historic period of out-of-control inflation, rapidly rising interest rates and stagnant growth.
authenticity.explanation: Attributes rising unemployment to inherited conditions; a defensible framing but one that deflects from the current government's own period in office.

strength.statement: Despite global volatility and factors outside our control, we remain confident in New Zealand’s economic prospects and are working hard to create the conditions for future job creation with $6 billion of government-funded construction work kicking off before Christmas, fast-track projects beginning, exports growing and the Investment Boost tax policy giving businesses a reason to invest and grow.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted/announced measures (Investment Boost, funded construction) but frames job creation as a forthcoming condition rather than a delivered result.

charisma.statement: In today's uncertain world, one certainty is that the Australia-New Zealand relationship is the bedrock as we look out into the world.

specificity.statement: This is tough legislation. That is the point. Gang members make up less than one quarter of one per cent of the New Zealand adult population, yet are linked to about 18 per cent of serious violent crime. We make no apologies for getting tough on law and order.

strength.statement: Our tough gangs laws which came into effect a year ago, as committed to in the National, Act and NZ First coalition agreements, have contributed to that reduction and restoration of law and order.

veracity.statement: Of course, now Labour is back with a capital gains tax because they can’t help themselves, but go after everything you own – your bach, your rental, or your small business.
veracity.explanation: Misleading exaggeration of a capital gains proposal's scope.

veracity.statement: Between 2017 and 2023, violent crime rose 30 per cent, gang membership increased by 50 per cent, retail crime doubled, and ram raids quadrupled.
veracity.explanation: Ram-raid and gang-list increases are broadly supported; the 30% violent crime figure relies on victimisation survey framing and is selectively presented.

veracity.explanation: Plausible for a large mortgage at lower rates, but depends heavily on loan size and fixed term chosen for the illustration.
