specificity.statement: The FTA that you have been told about, has unprecedented immigration settings including uncapped student numbers with working rights and 5000 visa holders entering New Zealand able to bring in families with them - which increases that number to 20,000+ at any one time.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete numbers (5000 visas, 20,000+ with families) and named settings.

specificity.statement: New Zealand was once the greatest country on earth and it can be again – that’s worth fighting for.
specificity.explanation: An aspirational slogan with no mechanism, measure, or timeframe.

veracity.statement: The project represents just over $77 million in the region, with a $20 million loan from the RIF and $57 million in co-funding from Hawkes Bay Racing, and NZ Thoroughbred Racing.
veracity.explanation: Detailed funding-breakdown claim about a real Regional Infrastructure Fund project; specific and plausible, unverified in full here.

veracity.statement: The last three years of the Labour government oversaw a deteriorating economy, deteriorating education and health systems, worsening law and order on our streets, ramraids everywhere, massively increased debt, record immigration, crumbling infrastructure, a cost-of-living crisis, and a hugely divided society.
veracity.explanation: A sweeping list mixing some defensible points (rising debt, cost-of-living pressure) with hyperbole ('ramraids everywhere'); presented without qualification.

veracity.statement: They sent out a press release and confused $500 million, with $500 billion.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual claim about a Green Party error; plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Then they decided in their wisdom to put out their own budget. Then had to recall it and issue a correction because their calculations were out by $400 million. Then, not long after that, they had to recall that as well, and issue another correction because they found out they were actually out by $800 million.
veracity.explanation: Detailed sequence of specific errors attributed to opponents; unverifiable here and framed for maximum embarrassment.

veracity.statement: They are a bunch of radical racists who wear cowboy hats and half the South Island’s pounamu around their necks.
veracity.explanation: The 'radical racists' characterisation is an unevidenced pejorative, not a supportable factual claim.

veracity.statement: They are currently polling at 1.5%. They claim that 17% of New Zealand population are Māori, so that means that not even ten percent of Māori even vote for them. Who do they represent exactly?
veracity.explanation: The ~17% Māori population figure is roughly accurate; the derived 'less than ten percent of Māori' conclusion is misleading.

veracity.statement: A third of their MPs have had enough and left the party already.
veracity.explanation: A specific claim about departures from Te Pāti Māori; plausible given known turnover but unverified and stated in the harshest framing.

veracity.statement: By the way this was a full month before National decided to steal our KiwiSaver policy and claim it as their own.
veracity.explanation: A claim of chronological priority that is plausible but unverified and framed to imply bad faith.

veracity.statement: A few weeks ago the Prime Minister said that National will be doing its best to honour the Paris obligations. If that’s true, up to $22 billion of our hard-earned taxpayers’ money is going offshore.
veracity.explanation: The $22 billion 'going offshore' figure is a contested worst-case estimate presented as a near-certain outflow.

veracity.statement: Around sixty percent of the worlds CO2 emissions come from four countries – China, United States, Russia, and India. New Zealand’s emissions amount to only around 0.17%.
veracity.explanation: Both figures are broadly accurate — those four nations account for well over half of global CO2, and NZ's share is a small fraction of a percent.

veracity.statement: China built more than 50 large coal powered power plants just last year – that’s one a week.
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with reports of large Chinese coal build-out, though the precise count depends on how 'plants' vs units are defined.

veracity.statement: The FTA that you have been told about, has unprecedented immigration settings including uncapped student numbers with working rights and 5000 visa holders entering New Zealand able to bring in families with them - which increases that number to 20,000+ at any one time.
veracity.explanation: The '20,000+' figure derives from a multiplier assumption about dependants; a contestable extrapolation presented as fact.

veracity.statement: this deal of which the Prime Minister has made so much, alongside obsequious business leaders, is expected to lift our GDP by the staggering amount of 0.1%, or a tenth of one percent - by 2050.
veracity.explanation: Small modelled GDP gains from such FTAs are plausible, but citing a single low figure without the wider modelling context may understate the estimate.

veracity.statement: under this deal New Zealand can export apples to India for two months in a year – the two months that this country doesn’t even produce apples.
veracity.explanation: A specific claim about seasonal apple access; plausible as a criticism of quota timing but unverified and likely simplified.

veracity.statement: That clause is directly contrary to the coalition agreement between National and New Zealand First, which specifically disowns any UNDRIP adherence or recognition.
veracity.explanation: The coalition agreement does contain anti-UNDRIP language; whether the FTA clause 'directly' contradicts it is a contested interpretation.

strength.statement: The project represents just over $77 million in the region, with a $20 million loan from the RIF and $57 million in co-funding from Hawkes Bay Racing, and NZ Thoroughbred Racing.
strength.explanation: As a governing coalition partner overseeing the RIF, describes a funded, in-progress project rather than mere aspiration — partial delivery.

strength.statement: We have announced policies to break up the power companies, split the supermarket duopoly, re-establish a competitive state owned bank, return mining royalties created in the regions back to the regions, we announced our KiwiSaver policy of making it compulsory with automatic sign-up at birth $1000 kickstart.
strength.explanation: These are announced policies, not delivered — announcement alone is not follow-through.

strength.statement: New Zealand First is saying we need to get out of the Paris Accord altogether – and we will campaign on this issue in this election.
strength.explanation: A firm campaign commitment, but as an intent to campaign it is not yet delivered.

divination.statement: The project will create more than 400 fulltime construction jobs during its construction phase, and once completed, the racecourse will sustain around 270 jobs across the local racing industry.
divination.explanation: Forecasts specific job numbers from the project; plausible order of magnitude but construction job estimates are commonly optimistic and unverifiable now.

divination.statement: We will turn these current media polls into confetti.
divination.explanation: Predicts NZ First will greatly outperform current polling; optimistic and metaphorical, hard to falsify precisely.

rigor.statement: “Free” actually means taxpayers pay for it - because whether Labour understands it or not, money doesn’t grow on trees. And guess what. People who get the free stuff are the same taxpayers and workers who are going to pay for it.
rigor.explanation: A valid basic point that public services are tax-funded, but delivered as rhetorical assertion rather than costed analysis.

rigor.statement: They are currently polling at 1.5%. They claim that 17% of New Zealand population are Māori, so that means that not even ten percent of Māori even vote for them. Who do they represent exactly?
rigor.explanation: The inference wrongly assumes only Māori would party-vote a Māori party and treats a single poll as fixed; the arithmetic is a rhetorical simplification.

rigor.statement: A few weeks ago the Prime Minister said that National will be doing its best to honour the Paris obligations. If that’s true, up to $22 billion of our hard-earned taxpayers’ money is going offshore.
rigor.explanation: Conditional framing is fair, but the headline number is asserted at its maximum without supporting derivation.

rigor.statement: Around sixty percent of the worlds CO2 emissions come from four countries – China, United States, Russia, and India. New Zealand’s emissions amount to only around 0.17%.
rigor.explanation: Accurate data, but used to imply NZ action is pointless — a relevance argument that ignores per-capita emissions and collective-action logic.

rigor.statement: under this deal New Zealand can export apples to India for two months in a year – the two months that this country doesn’t even produce apples.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete example to argue the deal is lopsided, though presented as a rhetorical 'gotcha' rather than full analysis.

civility.statement: “Free” actually means taxpayers pay for it - because whether Labour understands it or not, money doesn’t grow on trees. And guess what. People who get the free stuff are the same taxpayers and workers who are going to pay for it.
civility.explanation: Mocking tone ('whether Labour understands it or not') but the criticism is aimed at a policy, not a person.

civility.statement: The last three years of the Labour government oversaw a deteriorating economy, deteriorating education and health systems, worsening law and order on our streets, ramraids everywhere, massively increased debt, record immigration, crumbling infrastructure, a cost-of-living crisis, and a hugely divided society.
civility.explanation: Harsh but largely policy/record-focused critique of a government, though heavily exaggerated.

civility.statement: As for the Greens – they are nuttier than squirrel scat and have the political IQ of mung beans.
civility.explanation: Pure insult attacking the intelligence of opponents; no policy substance.

civility.statement: They have proven themselves to be the most hypocritical, shallow, vacuous bunch of Marxists.
civility.explanation: String of pejoratives and a labelling attack on character rather than argued critique.

civility.statement: Then they decided in their wisdom to put out their own budget. Then had to recall it and issue a correction because their calculations were out by $400 million. Then, not long after that, they had to recall that as well, and issue another correction because they found out they were actually out by $800 million.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic ('in their wisdom') but centred on an alleged competence failing rather than pure abuse.

civility.statement: They are economic morons.
civility.explanation: Direct insult to opponents' intelligence.

civility.statement: They are a bunch of radical racists who wear cowboy hats and half the South Island’s pounamu around their necks.
civility.explanation: Personal, derisive attack including a 'racist' slur and mockery of appearance.

civility.statement: They are currently polling at 1.5%. They claim that 17% of New Zealand population are Māori, so that means that not even ten percent of Māori even vote for them. Who do they represent exactly?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical dismissal of a party's legitimacy, framed as a question.

civility.statement: By the way this was a full month before National decided to steal our KiwiSaver policy and claim it as their own.
civility.explanation: 'Steal' is a loaded charge against a coalition partner, though it concerns policy provenance rather than personal character.

civility.statement: this deal of which the Prime Minister has made so much, alongside obsequious business leaders, is expected to lift our GDP by the staggering amount of 0.1%, or a tenth of one percent - by 2050.
civility.explanation: 'Obsequious business leaders' is a swipe, though the core is a sarcastic critique of the deal's benefits.

civility.statement: What’s most important, is that we are the only party that can counter-balance the present spectrum of extremists in parliament.
civility.explanation: Labels other parliamentary parties 'extremists' while positioning NZ First as the sole reasonable option.

charisma.statement: As for the Greens – they are nuttier than squirrel scat and have the political IQ of mung beans.
charisma.explanation: Divisive ridicule that rallies his own side and alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: What’s most important, is that we are the only party that can counter-balance the present spectrum of extremists in parliament.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to his own base by casting rivals as extremes rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: New Zealand was once the greatest country on earth and it can be again – that’s worth fighting for.
charisma.explanation: Emotive and rallying, but appeals to national pride for his own side rather than building cross-party consensus.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First will not be going with Labour.
authenticity.explanation: A clear commitment, but sits in tension with NZ First's own record of forming a coalition with Labour in 2017; a defensible but notable reversal of past willingness.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First is saying we need to get out of the Paris Accord altogether – and we will campaign on this issue in this election.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-standing scepticism of climate commitments; a position held reasonably consistently.

authenticity.statement: That clause is directly contrary to the coalition agreement between National and New Zealand First, which specifically disowns any UNDRIP adherence or recognition.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's stated coalition position opposing UNDRIP/co-governance; words align with the party's negotiated agreement.

forthrightness.statement: New Zealand First will not be going with Labour.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the repeatedly-asked coalition question ('gripper questions') with a plain no.

authenticity.statement: We demanded in our coalition agreement that super won't be touched - this will never change while New Zealand First has a say.
authenticity.explanation: NZ First did secure a commitment protecting superannuation in the current coalition agreement, so the claim is consistent with the party's record and long-standing position.

authenticity.statement: No government with New Zealand First will touch our seniors' superannuation – no means testing, no eligibility age increase, no indexing.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's decades-long defence of universal superannuation.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has been the only party that has consistently protected super for our seniors.
authenticity.explanation: NZ First has genuinely championed superannuation over decades; the 'only party' claim inflates an otherwise consistent record.

authenticity.statement: In 2017 when we became part of the Government, immigration was dramatically cut back.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-stated anti-high-immigration position, though the delivery claim is questionable.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand demanded in our coalition agreement that we do not recognise UNDRIP as having any legal standing – so why has National and Act, as part of the Government, signed up to this?
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's stated position on UNDRIP; the party did secure related provisions in the coalition agreement.

authenticity.statement: By the way, you would have seen reported in the last few days that work is underway right now to remove the references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi in legislation. New Zealand First were the ones who demanded that be included in the coalition agreement.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-standing position; the coalition agreement does contain such a commitment.

authenticity.statement: We set out in the 2023 election to do one thing – ensure the left were kept out. And we did that.
authenticity.explanation: Matches the party's actual 2023 campaign stance and outcome.

strength.statement: We demanded in our coalition agreement that super won't be touched - this will never change while New Zealand First has a say.
strength.explanation: A concrete commitment backed by an actual coalition-agreement provision that has held during this term.

strength.statement: In 2017 when we became part of the Government, immigration was dramatically cut back.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on an immigration reduction that the record does not clearly show occurred.

strength.statement: New Zealand demanded in our coalition agreement that we do not recognise UNDRIP as having any legal standing – so why has National and Act, as part of the Government, signed up to this?
strength.explanation: Points to a secured coalition commitment, though the FTA clause suggests incomplete follow-through.

strength.statement: By the way, you would have seen reported in the last few days that work is underway right now to remove the references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi in legislation. New Zealand First were the ones who demanded that be included in the coalition agreement.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for in-progress delivery of a coalition commitment to remove Treaty principles references; work is underway but not complete.

strength.statement: We set out in the 2023 election to do one thing – ensure the left were kept out. And we did that.
strength.explanation: NZ First did return to Parliament and form a coalition that excluded Labour/Greens; the stated goal was achieved.

strength.statement: New Zealand First is going to make KiwiSaver enrolment compulsory at birth and there will be an automatic immediate Crown contribution of $1000 for New Zealand citizens only.
strength.explanation: A campaign policy announcement with no delivery; contingent on winning office.

strength.statement: This new policy will work in conjunction with our existing campaign policy of compulsory KiwiSaver enrolment for the wider workforce and increasing employee and employer contributions to 8% initially and eventually to 10%.
strength.explanation: Aspirational campaign policy, not enacted.

strength.statement: New Zealand First will be proposing a buy-back of the Bank of New Zealand from National Australia Bank. It will be merged with Kiwibank to form the "National Bank of New Zealand (NBNZ)" – a fully Crown owned, commercially run, systemically significant domestic bank with the scale to genuinely compete with ANZ, ASB and Westpac.
strength.explanation: A proposal only, dependent on election and a large uncosted acquisition.

specificity.statement: We demanded in our coalition agreement that super won't be touched - this will never change while New Zealand First has a say.
specificity.explanation: Names the coalition-agreement mechanism but gives no detail beyond 'won't be touched'.

specificity.statement: No government with New Zealand First will touch our seniors' superannuation – no means testing, no eligibility age increase, no indexing.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates three concrete lines it will not cross (means testing, age, indexing).

specificity.statement: We need immigration to New Zealand. It has been an essential part of our history. But this should be smart, controlled immigration policy – bringing in immigrants who we need, not who need us.
specificity.explanation: States a direction ('smart, controlled') but no mechanism, cap, or criteria.

specificity.statement: That's a total of $55 billion going overseas and not being invested in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete total dollar figure, though its derivation is dubious.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is going to make KiwiSaver enrolment compulsory at birth and there will be an automatic immediate Crown contribution of $1000 for New Zealand citizens only.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (compulsory birth enrolment), dollar figure ($1000) and eligibility (citizens only).

specificity.statement: This new policy will work in conjunction with our existing campaign policy of compulsory KiwiSaver enrolment for the wider workforce and increasing employee and employer contributions to 8% initially and eventually to 10%.
specificity.explanation: States concrete contribution-rate targets (8% then 10%) and a compulsory-enrolment mechanism.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First will be proposing a buy-back of the Bank of New Zealand from National Australia Bank. It will be merged with Kiwibank to form the "National Bank of New Zealand (NBNZ)" – a fully Crown owned, commercially run, systemically significant domestic bank with the scale to genuinely compete with ANZ, ASB and Westpac.
specificity.explanation: Names the target (BNZ from NAB), the vehicle (merger with Kiwibank), the entity name and its structure.

specificity.statement: the Kiwi dream should not be reserved for the few, it should be delivered for everybody who calls New Zealand home.
specificity.explanation: A values statement with no concrete mechanism or measure.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First has been the only party that has consistently protected super for our seniors.
veracity.explanation: Directionally true about NZ First's stance but 'only party' is an overstatement given other parties have also defended the current settings at times.

veracity.statement: Super currently sits at around 5% of New Zealand's GDP, which is far below the OECD average of other pension schemes.
veracity.explanation: NZ Super costs roughly 5% of GDP and this is below the OECD average public pension spend; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Stunning isn't it, that in all three articles, they make out that there is an affordability problem even though the cost against GDP is around 5%, but here's the rub, the Cullen Fund that is over two decades old, and now over $86 billion, which was designed to smooth out the predicted time of high costs of our national super, is not even mentioned.
veracity.explanation: The NZ Super (Cullen) Fund is over two decades old and roughly $80b+, established to pre-fund future super costs; the figures are close to accurate.

veracity.statement: In 2021, when we were no longer part of the Government, the Government's feet came totally off the brakes, and Labour governing with the Greens began approving 213,000 residencies in just 18 months.
veracity.explanation: The 2021 one-off residence pathway did grant residence to roughly 200,000 people; the figure is close, though '18 months' and framing compress the timeline.

veracity.statement: In 2017 when we became part of the Government, immigration was dramatically cut back.
veracity.explanation: Net migration remained high through 2017–2019; there was no dramatic cut, so the claim is largely unsupported.

veracity.statement: Around sixty percent of the worlds CO2 emissions come from four countries – China, United States, Russia, and India. New Zealand's emissions amount to only around 0.17%.
veracity.explanation: China, US, India and Russia together account for roughly 55–60% of CO2 emissions, and NZ's share is a fraction of a percent; the figures are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: In trying to honour our Paris commitments, $22 billion plus, of our hard-earned taxpayers' money will be siphoned offshore in a total self-defeating economic and climatic shambles.
veracity.explanation: Estimates of offshore carbon purchases exist but the $22b figure and 'siphoned' framing overstate the settled evidence.

veracity.statement: That's a total of $55 billion going overseas and not being invested in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Combines a contested $22b Paris figure with a $33b India 'promotion of investment' figure; conflating a target to promote investment with money 'going overseas' is misleading.

veracity.statement: under this deal, not only will there be five thousand work visas issued at any one time, but under current law those visa holders can bring in their families – that five thousand now turns into twenty or twenty-five thousand.
veracity.explanation: The multiplier assumption is asserted rather than substantiated and is contested by other parties.

veracity.statement: Four Australian owned banks control around 85 percent of the system.
veracity.explanation: ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac (all Australian-owned) do hold roughly 85–90% of the NZ banking market; accurate.

veracity.statement: Kiwibank, the only domestically owned bank of any scale, currently holds just under 8 percent of the mortgage market.
veracity.explanation: Kiwibank's home-loan share is in the high single digits; the figure is close to accurate.

veracity.statement: After all, when National sold BNZ to NAB in November 1992, it then had six of every ten New Zealand banking customers.
veracity.explanation: BNZ was indeed sold to NAB in 1992, but the '60% of customers' claim is likely overstated and hard to verify.

veracity.statement: The buy-back is self-financing in expectation. The fiscal impact is a one-off balance-sheet expansion, not an ongoing cost.
veracity.explanation: The 'self-financing' and 'no ongoing cost' claims are assertions unsupported by any costing in the text.

veracity.statement: Kiwibank was created in 2002 precisely to provide a domestic challenger. But after two decades it remains a marginal player. Successive governments have starved it of the capital it would need to be a genuine system-shaping competitor.
veracity.explanation: Kiwibank was launched in 2002 as a domestic challenger and has remained comparatively small, partly due to capital constraints; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Crown-owned commercial banks operating at scale are not radical. They are normal in serious economies – Singapore, Norway, Germany, Canada, France, all have large-scale state-owned banks that have serious stakes in the market.
veracity.explanation: Several named countries do have significant state-linked banks, though 'Canada' and the uniformity of the list overstate the point.

veracity.statement: The fact is half of all New Zealand Citizens who have moved to Australia were not born in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Presented as an authoritative statistic but the 'half' figure is dubious and not clearly supported by migration data.

veracity.statement: Chris Hipkins has said that Labour is willing to means test superannuation that would affect hundreds of thousands of Kiwi seniors - just like Labour did in the 1980s, and National did in the 1990's.
veracity.explanation: Characterises Hipkins as 'willing to means test' super, which overstates Labour's more tentative position on the debate; the 1980s/1990s historical references are broadly accurate.

rigor.statement: Super currently sits at around 5% of New Zealand's GDP, which is far below the OECD average of other pension schemes.
rigor.explanation: Uses relevant comparative data to rebut the affordability claim; conclusion follows reasonably.

rigor.statement: Stunning isn't it, that in all three articles, they make out that there is an affordability problem even though the cost against GDP is around 5%, but here's the rub, the Cullen Fund that is over two decades old, and now over $86 billion, which was designed to smooth out the predicted time of high costs of our national super, is not even mentioned.
rigor.explanation: Points to a genuinely relevant omitted fact (the pre-funding vehicle) to challenge the affordability framing; reasonable though rhetorically loaded.

rigor.statement: Why are we making a rod for our own backs, punishing our farmers and our taxpayers and our economy, when China or the US could sneeze and produce more CO2 overnight than we do in a year?
rigor.explanation: A 'drop in the bucket' / relative-size appeal that does not follow logically to inaction; ignores per-capita and collective-action reasoning.

rigor.statement: Those out of touch, bureaucratic, left elitists would all rather live in crap than let the world see them use a shovel.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem with no evidence or argument.

rigor.statement: Over the past decade or more, New Zealand has seen our country swing to the far woke left, being influenced by the woke, communist, cultural Marxists who would sooner see our country go broke for the sake of political correctness and ideology, than stand up for what were once proud traditional Kiwi values.
rigor.explanation: Loaded terms and imputed motives with no evidence; appeal to emotion.

rigor.statement: Their cultural Marxism has spread like a cancer throughout our society, in our political system, education system, our schools, government departments, and has been let to seep into our everyday world.
rigor.explanation: Unsupported sweeping assertion relying on a loaded metaphor rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Politicians like Hipkins perversely say "diversity is a strength" to shut you down, but it is not - unity is a strength, not diversity.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy between unity and diversity; asserted, not argued.

rigor.statement: No one has the right to not be offended, nor do they have the right to be protected from having hurt feelings. In fact it is precisely the right to be able to offend which is the foundation of freedom of speech in our country.
rigor.explanation: A coherent, principled free-speech argument, though stated as assertion without citing law.

rigor.statement: If we start to accept this kind of overreach by police to curtail individual freedom of speech, our democracy will fall into the type of totalitarian oblivion that will destroy our country.
rigor.explanation: Slippery-slope reasoning with no intermediate justification.

rigor.statement: If we sell our state assets to foreign owned corporations, the security of our country and our future generations will be over.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic appeal to fear with no supporting mechanism or evidence.

rigor.statement: Kiwibank was created in 2002 precisely to provide a domestic challenger. But after two decades it remains a marginal player. Successive governments have starved it of the capital it would need to be a genuine system-shaping competitor.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal argument linking under-capitalisation to Kiwibank's limited market impact.

rigor.statement: Crown-owned commercial banks operating at scale are not radical. They are normal in serious economies – Singapore, Norway, Germany, Canada, France, all have large-scale state-owned banks that have serious stakes in the market.
rigor.explanation: Comparative evidence used, but leans on an appeal to precedent without addressing differences between the examples.

charisma.explanation: An inclusive, unifying appeal to a shared democratic principle across viewpoints.

charisma.statement: the Kiwi dream should not be reserved for the few, it should be delivered for everybody who calls New Zealand home.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, aspirational framing inviting a broad group in (as quoted by Peters).

divination.statement: In trying to honour our Paris commitments, $22 billion plus, of our hard-earned taxpayers' money will be siphoned offshore in a total self-defeating economic and climatic shambles.
divination.explanation: A forecast of ~$22b in offshore carbon costs; figures for offshore mitigation have been debated and the exact amount is uncertain and contested.

divination.statement: under this deal, not only will there be five thousand work visas issued at any one time, but under current law those visa holders can bring in their families – that five thousand now turns into twenty or twenty-five thousand.
divination.explanation: Projects a 4–5x multiplier from family visas; a speculative extrapolation the other parties dispute, with no cited basis for the multiplier.

divination.statement: If we start to accept this kind of overreach by police to curtail individual freedom of speech, our democracy will fall into the type of totalitarian oblivion that will destroy our country.
divination.explanation: Predicts national collapse into totalitarianism from one police visit; an implausible magnitude escalation.

divination.statement: If we sell our state assets to foreign owned corporations, the security of our country and our future generations will be over.
divination.explanation: Predicts that asset sales would end national security 'over'; a sweeping, implausible absolute outcome.

divination.statement: The buy-back is self-financing in expectation. The fiscal impact is a one-off balance-sheet expansion, not an ongoing cost.
divination.explanation: Predicts the acquisition will pay for itself; optimistic and unproven for a multi-billion-dollar bank purchase.

specificity.statement: We have worked hard over the past three years to fight for the changes we promised, and that our country needed, to keep the left out, build a new foundation for the future, and prepare for 2026.
specificity.explanation: Broad framing ('worked hard', 'changes we promised') with no specific policy, figure, or timeframe named here.

specificity.statement: This year New Zealand First began our election meetings in March, first with a packed hall in Tauranga with over 1000 people attending, and we have been travelling around the country filing halls every week and will be continuing to do so through until the election.
specificity.explanation: Names month (March), location (Tauranga), and a crowd figure (over 1000).

specificity.statement: That is simply because New Zealand First is resonating with ordinary, hard-working kiwis, who want a voice in parliament that represents them.
specificity.explanation: Platitude about 'ordinary, hard-working kiwis' with no measurable content.

specificity.statement: The last time we stood here in Warkworth, just four years ago, New Zealand First was out of parliament, ignored, marginalised by the media, and polling at 1%. Well, we aren’t any more.
specificity.explanation: Names place, rough timeframe, and a polling figure, but the comparison is broad.

specificity.statement: We have announced policies to break up the power companies so we stop power companies owning the market and ripping consumers off.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy direction (breaking up power companies) but no mechanism, figures, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We also announced our KiwiSaver policy of making it compulsory with automatic sign-up at birth $1000 kickstart.
specificity.explanation: Concrete elements: compulsory, auto sign-up at birth, and a $1000 kickstart figure.

specificity.statement: We are nationalists and we need to look after our own country first – not hand over anywhere up to $22 billion overseas when we create just 0.17% of the entire world’s CO2 emissions.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure ($22 billion) and an emissions share (0.17%).

specificity.statement: Think about it, four countries, US, China, Russian, and India, combined are responsible for just under 60% of the world’s CO2 emissions. We are responsible for just 0.17%.
specificity.explanation: Names specific countries and precise percentage figures.

specificity.statement: Ratepayers now pay millions of dollars annually to support IMSB operations, including $3.5 million last year alone, despite having no ability to elect or remove its members.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, an annual cost figure ($3.5 million), and the accountability mechanism at issue.

specificity.statement: The removal of the IMSB will ensure that those who influence public spending and public decision making are directly accountable to the public.
specificity.explanation: Clear policy intent tied to a named body, but the mechanism of 'accountability' is left general.

specificity.statement: We are announcing today that New Zealand First will change the law that only citizens can vote in local and general elections.
specificity.explanation: Concrete policy: restrict voting to citizens; direction is clear though enactment detail is limited.

specificity.statement: But in the Electoral Act, anyone on a visa without an expiry date counts as a permanent resident. That means, in certain circumstances, someone can be eligible to vote in our country’s general election if they are living in our country on an indefinite visa after just one year.
specificity.explanation: Explains a precise legal distinction between Electoral Act and immigration definitions of 'permanent resident'.

specificity.statement: Voting in our country should be a privilege of those who have sworn allegiance to New Zealand and who have made the commitment to make New Zealand their home and their future.
specificity.explanation: States a value/principle about who should vote without policy mechanics.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First has introduced a bill to parliament that will define what a woman and man is in law.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill and its purpose.

specificity.statement: There was a Curia poll conducted not so long ago which showed 51% of kiwis supported the bill, and just 29% were against it.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named pollster (Curia) and precise figures (51% / 29%).

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is the only party that campaigned on keeping men out of women’s sports, keeping men out of women's and girl's changing rooms, and we have received two petitions to protect the term ‘woman’ in legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names specific campaign planks and a concrete detail (two petitions received).

specificity.statement: Strident idealistic promises you have heard before. They are worthless without commitment, resolve and determination to make such dreams a reality.
specificity.explanation: General rhetoric about promises and commitment with no concrete content.

authenticity.statement: We have worked hard over the past three years to fight for the changes we promised, and that our country needed, to keep the left out, build a new foundation for the future, and prepare for 2026.
authenticity.explanation: Claims consistency between prior promises and action; NZ First did enter government in 2023 and pursue some pledges, but the sweeping claim is only partly verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First is the only party that campaigned on keeping men out of women’s sports, keeping men out of women's and girl's changing rooms, and we have received two petitions to protect the term ‘woman’ in legislation.
authenticity.explanation: Presents consistency between what NZ First campaigned on and its current legislative action; largely aligns with the party's stated record.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First set out in the election to get rid of the ‘Relationship, and Sexual Education’ guidelines in our schools – we have done that.
authenticity.explanation: Words match action — a campaigned position followed by a matching government move.

authenticity.statement: We campaigned on ensuring we have fairness in women’s sports – that men cannot compete against women and girls – we have done that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the party's campaign stance, but the claim of completion runs ahead of concrete legislative delivery.

authenticity.statement: Strident idealistic promises you have heard before. They are worthless without commitment, resolve and determination to make such dreams a reality.
authenticity.explanation: Positions NZ First as delivering rather than merely promising; a values statement whose backing depends on the party's actual delivery record.

civility.statement: if we don’t win in 2026 the opportunity will be lost to make the real changes we need in this country, and the values of our enemies will destroy the chance we have to make this country great again.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents as 'enemies' whose values will 'destroy' the country — us-vs-them character framing rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: It is to the detriment of democracy that other parties just are not holding any real public meetings.
civility.explanation: Criticises rival parties' conduct rather than attacking individuals, but broadly dismissive.

civility.statement: All of the other parties are either self-confessed globalists, socialists, Marxists, separatists - or all of the above.
civility.explanation: Labels all rival parties with pejorative terms; strawmanning and name-calling rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: No one cares what Vance thinks. She might think they do in her little Wellington Bluesky bubble full of lanyard-wearing woke lefty losers, but there’s a reason New Zealand First support is growing out in the real world.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on journalist Andrea Vance and 'lanyard-wearing woke lefty losers' — insults, no substance.

civility.statement: We are the enemy of what she stands for and the enemy of the woke mind virus that has infected so much of our mainstream media that they can’t even figure out why no one trusts their industry anymore.
civility.explanation: 'Woke mind virus' and 'enemy' framing; sensationalist attack on the media as a class.

civility.statement: By the way this was a full month before National decided to steal our KiwiSaver policy and claim it as their own.
civility.explanation: Accuses coalition partner National of 'stealing' a policy — pointed jab but about policy provenance, not personal character.

civility.statement: If New Zealand sunk into the South Pacific tomorrow, taking all of our emissions with it, we would have zero effect on the world’s climate.
civility.explanation: Provocative but aimed at the policy argument, not a person.

civility.statement: Voting in our country should be a privilege of those who have sworn allegiance to New Zealand and who have made the commitment to make New Zealand their home and their future.
civility.explanation: Argues a principled position on citizenship and voting without attacking individuals.

civility.statement: But it seems now, when the representatives of Rural Women NZ leave the farm, the suffer from the same wokeness that is afflicting Wellington bureaucrats and the purple-haired Green Party weirdos.
civility.explanation: Mockery ('purple-haired Green Party weirdos') and derision of a group and MPs — personal insult, not policy critique.

civility.statement: And that sort of behaviour from the mainstream media is just outright cheating.
civility.explanation: Accusatory characterisation ('cheating') of the media generally rather than a substantiated point.

civility.statement: Our message to the bureaucracy and any other political party pursuing such policies is simple. Do you want to be part of the solution or do you want to remain part of the problem?
civility.explanation: Confrontational ultimatum but directed at policy positions rather than individuals.

civility.statement: In New Zealand’s history there have been politicians of different persuasions who deserve our respect. For the improvements they delivered to ordinary people. Richard Seddon, Peter Fraser, Holyoake and others.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges respected figures across political persuasions — rare cross-party generosity in this speech.

charisma.statement: if we don’t win in 2026 the opportunity will be lost to make the real changes we need in this country, and the values of our enemies will destroy the chance we have to make this country great again.
charisma.explanation: Rallies supporters via existential fear of 'enemies'; alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: No one cares what Vance thinks. She might think they do in her little Wellington Bluesky bubble full of lanyard-wearing woke lefty losers, but there’s a reason New Zealand First support is growing out in the real world.
charisma.explanation: Purely divisive mockery of opponents; alienating.

charisma.statement: In New Zealand’s history there have been politicians of different persuasions who deserve our respect. For the improvements they delivered to ordinary people. Richard Seddon, Peter Fraser, Holyoake and others.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared national history and figures across the aisle, mildly unifying.

divination.statement: if we don’t win in 2026 the opportunity will be lost to make the real changes we need in this country, and the values of our enemies will destroy the chance we have to make this country great again.
divination.explanation: Predicts loss of opportunity and destruction of values if NZ First loses in November 2026 — vague, alarmist, and hard to falsify.

divination.statement: They aren’t asking if we will get back in, they are all asking how many more seats we will have in November, and just how strong we will be in the next government.
divination.explanation: Implicitly predicts NZ First returns and grows its seats in the November 2026 election — plausible for an incumbent minor party but not assured.

veracity.statement: This year New Zealand First began our election meetings in March, first with a packed hall in Tauranga with over 1000 people attending, and we have been travelling around the country filing halls every week and will be continuing to do so through until the election.
veracity.explanation: Attendance and meeting claims are plausible but unverifiable from the text; specific enough to be checkable in principle.

veracity.statement: It is to the detriment of democracy that other parties just are not holding any real public meetings.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping claim that no other party holds 'real' public meetings; overstated — other parties do hold public events, though NZ First disputes their format.

veracity.statement: All of the other parties are either self-confessed globalists, socialists, Marxists, separatists - or all of the above.
veracity.explanation: Demonstrably overstated — no NZ party self-identifies as 'Marxist'; misleading characterisation.

veracity.statement: The last time we stood here in Warkworth, just four years ago, New Zealand First was out of parliament, ignored, marginalised by the media, and polling at 1%. Well, we aren’t any more.
veracity.explanation: NZ First was indeed out of Parliament after 2020 and polling very low; the 1% figure is roughly accurate for parts of that period, though 'four years ago' is loose.

veracity.statement: We are the enemy of what she stands for and the enemy of the woke mind virus that has infected so much of our mainstream media that they can’t even figure out why no one trusts their industry anymore.
veracity.explanation: Declining media trust is real, but attributing it wholly to a 'woke mind virus' is an unsupported, misleading causal claim.

veracity.statement: By the way this was a full month before National decided to steal our KiwiSaver policy and claim it as their own.
veracity.explanation: Timing claim ('a full month before') is a checkable assertion but 'steal' is a loaded, unverifiable characterisation of policy overlap.

veracity.statement: We are nationalists and we need to look after our own country first – not hand over anywhere up to $22 billion overseas when we create just 0.17% of the entire world’s CO2 emissions.
veracity.explanation: NZ's share of global CO2 is roughly 0.17%, but the '$22 billion overseas' figure is a contested worst-case Paris cost estimate presented as certain.

veracity.statement: Think about it, four countries, US, China, Russian, and India, combined are responsible for just under 60% of the world’s CO2 emissions. We are responsible for just 0.17%.
veracity.explanation: The four named countries do account for roughly 55–60% of global CO2 emissions and NZ ~0.17%; broadly accurate figures.

veracity.statement: China built more than 50 large coal powered power plants just last year – that’s one a week. And what did the Labour Party do? Ban coal. Close down Marsden Point.
veracity.explanation: China did approve/begin large volumes of coal capacity, but Marsden Point was an oil refinery (owner Refining NZ), not a coal plant closed by 'banning coal' — conflates distinct facts.

veracity.statement: Just two weeks ago, the former longest serving Labour Party PM in the UK, Tony Blair, made a similar statement to New Zealand First’s about what the world needs to do on the Paris Accord.
veracity.explanation: Blair did make comments critical of current climate policy approaches around that time, but 'similar statement to NZ First's' overstates the alignment.

veracity.statement: Ratepayers now pay millions of dollars annually to support IMSB operations, including $3.5 million last year alone, despite having no ability to elect or remove its members.
veracity.explanation: The IMSB is indeed an appointed (unelected) body funded by Auckland ratepayers; the $3.5m figure is a specific, checkable claim presented plausibly.

veracity.statement: But in the Electoral Act, anyone on a visa without an expiry date counts as a permanent resident. That means, in certain circumstances, someone can be eligible to vote in our country’s general election if they are living in our country on an indefinite visa after just one year.
veracity.explanation: NZ's Electoral Act does grant voting rights to permanent residents after one year's residence, with a broader definition than immigration status — substantially accurate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First has introduced a bill to parliament that will define what a woman and man is in law.
veracity.explanation: NZ First has advanced such a member's-bill/legislative push; the claim of introduction is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: There was a Curia poll conducted not so long ago which showed 51% of kiwis supported the bill, and just 29% were against it.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable poll claim; plausible but unverified here and 'not so long ago' is vague on timing/wording.

veracity.statement: We campaigned on ensuring English is an official language, that our country’s name remains New Zealand, that English names are used as a primary name on all departments – we have done that.
veracity.explanation: English is not formally an 'official language' of NZ in law; the blanket 'we have done that' overstates completion of that specific item.

rigor.statement: That is simply because New Zealand First is resonating with ordinary, hard-working kiwis, who want a voice in parliament that represents them.
rigor.explanation: Attributes crowd sizes to 'resonating' — appeal to popularity, no evidence beyond anecdote.

rigor.statement: All of the other parties are either self-confessed globalists, socialists, Marxists, separatists - or all of the above.
rigor.explanation: False-dichotomy/name-calling with no evidence; caricatures opponents' positions.

rigor.statement: No one cares what Vance thinks. She might think they do in her little Wellington Bluesky bubble full of lanyard-wearing woke lefty losers, but there’s a reason New Zealand First support is growing out in the real world.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem against Vance; asserts growing support without evidence.

rigor.statement: We are nationalists and we need to look after our own country first – not hand over anywhere up to $22 billion overseas when we create just 0.17% of the entire world’s CO2 emissions.
rigor.explanation: Uses real-sounding figures but leans on a 'we're too small to matter' framing that ignores per-capita emissions.

rigor.statement: If New Zealand sunk into the South Pacific tomorrow, taking all of our emissions with it, we would have zero effect on the world’s climate.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic thought experiment; 'zero effect' overstates and dismisses cumulative/marginal contribution — rhetorical, not rigorous.

rigor.statement: China built more than 50 large coal powered power plants just last year – that’s one a week. And what did the Labour Party do? Ban coal. Close down Marsden Point.
rigor.explanation: Whataboutism contrasting China's coal with NZ actions; the Marsden Point example is misapplied.

rigor.statement: Just two weeks ago, the former longest serving Labour Party PM in the UK, Tony Blair, made a similar statement to New Zealand First’s about what the world needs to do on the Paris Accord.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority (Blair) to validate the position; the cited comparison is loose.

rigor.statement: The removal of the IMSB will ensure that those who influence public spending and public decision making are directly accountable to the public.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable accountability argument (unelected body influences spending), though it assumes removal necessarily improves accountability.

rigor.statement: But in the Electoral Act, anyone on a visa without an expiry date counts as a permanent resident. That means, in certain circumstances, someone can be eligible to vote in our country’s general election if they are living in our country on an indefinite visa after just one year.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based reasoning about a genuine statutory gap, though framed to maximise concern.

rigor.statement: But it seems now, when the representatives of Rural Women NZ leave the farm, the suffer from the same wokeness that is afflicting Wellington bureaucrats and the purple-haired Green Party weirdos.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem/name-calling in place of engaging the opposing argument.

rigor.statement: And that sort of behaviour from the mainstream media is just outright cheating.
rigor.explanation: Infers deliberate 'cheating' from one poll not being reported — assumes motive without evidence.

rigor.statement: Our message to the bureaucracy and any other political party pursuing such policies is simple. Do you want to be part of the solution or do you want to remain part of the problem?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — 'solution or problem' with no middle ground.

strength.statement: We have announced policies to break up the power companies so we stop power companies owning the market and ripping consumers off.
strength.explanation: An announced policy, not delivered — announcement alone is not follow-through.

strength.statement: We also announced our KiwiSaver policy of making it compulsory with automatic sign-up at birth $1000 kickstart.
strength.explanation: Announced policy only; no delivery given it is a campaign proposal.

strength.statement: We are announcing today that New Zealand First will change the law that only citizens can vote in local and general elections.
strength.explanation: A campaign announcement, not a delivered change.

strength.statement: New Zealand First has introduced a bill to parliament that will define what a woman and man is in law.
strength.explanation: A concrete legislative step (bill introduced) beyond mere announcement, though not yet enacted.

strength.statement: New Zealand First set out in the election to get rid of the ‘Relationship, and Sexual Education’ guidelines in our schools – we have done that.
strength.explanation: Claims a campaign commitment delivered; the government did move to scrap the RSE guidelines, so this reflects follow-through, though 'done' may run ahead of full implementation.

strength.statement: We campaigned on ensuring English is an official language, that our country’s name remains New Zealand, that English names are used as a primary name on all departments – we have done that.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on coalition commitments (English naming of departments), some of which have been actioned, though 'English as an official language' has not been legislated — mixed delivery.

strength.statement: We campaigned on ensuring we have fairness in women’s sports – that men cannot compete against women and girls – we have done that.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered outcome, but there is no binding national law banning this; largely guidance/policy signalling, so 'done' overstates follow-through.

veracity.statement: Mining isn't some outdated industry of the past, it is one of our most productive sectors today.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about mining's productivity. Mining is a real contributor but is a small share of NZ GDP (~1-2%); 'one of our most productive sectors' overstates its relative scale.

veracity.statement: It contributes billions to our economy, supports thousands of jobs, and has the ability to drive growth, real growth, without fuelling inflation.
veracity.explanation: 'Billions' and 'thousands of jobs' are broadly in line with mining's contribution; the 'growth without fuelling inflation' part is an unquantified assertion.

veracity.statement: New Zealand's last comprehensive geological survey dates back decades.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — NZ's comprehensive regional geological mapping is indeed old — though 'comprehensive' is imprecise and periodic surveys have occurred.

veracity.statement: In some cases we've seen it take two years for a permit, while the workers and the project sit idle.
veracity.explanation: Plausible for some cases and consistent with known consenting delays, but 'in some cases' cherry-picks and the claim is unverified.

veracity.statement: Have a look at OceanaGold's Globe Progress Mine in Reefton – they have delivered a world-class rehabilitation programme, beautiful landscapes, cycling and walking tracks – and I'm told that it's even been acknowledged by the Department of Conservation that it is world-class.
veracity.explanation: The Globe Progress rehabilitation is a real and well-regarded programme; the specific DOC 'world-class' acknowledgement is second-hand and unverified.

veracity.statement: Mining communities like the West Coast have carried this country on their back, and they must see the rewards for that.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic — mining regions have contributed, but 'carried this country on their back' vastly overstates their share of the national economy.

specificity.statement: Mining isn't some outdated industry of the past, it is one of our most productive sectors today.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a status ('most productive') with no figures or mechanism to back it.

specificity.statement: It contributes billions to our economy, supports thousands of jobs, and has the ability to drive growth, real growth, without fuelling inflation.
specificity.explanation: Gives rough magnitudes ('billions', 'thousands') but no precise figures, sources, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: If mining happens in a region, a 50% share of the royalties will stay in that region, so local communities directly benefit from the resources around them – not Wellington.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (50%) and mechanism (regional retention of royalties), though no dollar amounts or start date.

specificity.statement: Under our policy, we will invest in a modern, world-class geological survey - AI-ready, open-access, and available to investors and businesses who want to back New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deliverable (geological survey) with attributes (AI-ready, open-access) but no cost, scope, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: So we will rebuild the pipeline by reopening the School of Mines (last in Thames) and investing in trades and training across the resources sector.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete, identifiable policy (reopening the School of Mines) but omits location, funding, and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Have a look at OceanaGold's Globe Progress Mine in Reefton – they have delivered a world-class rehabilitation programme, beautiful landscapes, cycling and walking tracks – and I'm told that it's even been acknowledged by the Department of Conservation that it is world-class.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific mine, operator, location, and concrete features (tracks, rehabilitation).

specificity.statement: Mining communities like the West Coast have carried this country on their back, and they must see the rewards for that.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical slogan with no measure, figure, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Yes, communities deserve a voice. But consultation should not become an endless process that prevents decisions from ever being made. We will restore discipline to that process, so engagement happens, but outcomes are delivered in a timely fashion.
specificity.explanation: 'Restore discipline' and 'timely fashion' state a direction but no concrete timeframes or rules.

strength.statement: If mining happens in a region, a 50% share of the royalties will stay in that region, so local communities directly benefit from the resources around them – not Wellington.
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment for a future term, not delivered; announcement rather than demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: Under our policy, we will invest in a modern, world-class geological survey - AI-ready, open-access, and available to investors and businesses who want to back New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Aspirational commitment to 'invest'; no mechanism or delivery, contingent on winning office.

strength.statement: So we will rebuild the pipeline by reopening the School of Mines (last in Thames) and investing in trades and training across the resources sector.
strength.explanation: A promise conditional on the election; announcement, not delivery.

strength.statement: We will make sure that the role of government agencies,like the Department of Conservation, who have been left to run roughshod over local and regional prosperity, will be brought back into line.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to rein in agencies, but no concrete mechanism and contingent on office.

strength.statement: This builds on what we said we'd do and what we've already done under Fast-track.
strength.explanation: Points to something actually enacted (Fast-track) as delivered follow-through, lending some credibility beyond mere aspiration.

civility.statement: In a future world where extraction industries will be critical. You have got luddite politicians in New Zealand who want to shut the industry down.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents 'luddite' — a personal disparagement rather than engagement with their arguments.

civility.statement: The mining and extracting industries have been the victim of some of the shallowest, narrowest, most illogical, and most inane comment. In fact it's a new form of insanity.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist and dismissive ('insanity', 'inane') rather than engaging the substance of critics' positions.

civility.statement: We will make sure that the role of government agencies,like the Department of Conservation, who have been left to run roughshod over local and regional prosperity, will be brought back into line.
civility.explanation: Charges DOC with running 'roughshod' — accusatory framing of an agency rather than substantive critique of specific decisions.

rigor.statement: In a future world where extraction industries will be critical. You have got luddite politicians in New Zealand who want to shut the industry down.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem plus a strawman (that opponents simply 'want to shut the industry down'); no evidence.

rigor.statement: The mining and extracting industries have been the victim of some of the shallowest, narrowest, most illogical, and most inane comment. In fact it's a new form of insanity.
rigor.explanation: Pure invective with no evidence or argument; appeal to ridicule.

rigor.statement: It is an absurd and myopic argument to say it's either protecting the environment or creating jobs and dollars for our regions and our country. You can have both – and this region has shown exactly how it can be done.
rigor.explanation: Correctly rejects a false dichotomy and points to a real-world example, though the 'absurd/myopic' framing asserts more than it demonstrates.

rigor.statement: Have a look at OceanaGold's Globe Progress Mine in Reefton – they have delivered a world-class rehabilitation programme, beautiful landscapes, cycling and walking tracks – and I'm told that it's even been acknowledged by the Department of Conservation that it is world-class.
rigor.explanation: Backs the 'you can have both' claim with a concrete, checkable example rather than assertion, though the DOC endorsement is hedged ('I'm told').

charisma.statement: In a future world where extraction industries will be critical. You have got luddite politicians in New Zealand who want to shut the industry down.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that demonises opponents rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: It is an absurd and myopic argument to say it's either protecting the environment or creating jobs and dollars for our regions and our country. You can have both – and this region has shown exactly how it can be done.
charisma.explanation: Seeks a both/and resolution rather than pure conflict, but still frames the opposing view as 'absurd'.

charisma.statement: Yes, communities deserve a voice. But consultation should not become an endless process that prevents decisions from ever being made. We will restore discipline to that process, so engagement happens, but outcomes are delivered in a timely fashion.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges that communities 'deserve a voice' before arguing for limits — a mild attempt at balance, but appeals mainly to its own side.

divination.statement: In a future world where extraction industries will be critical. You have got luddite politicians in New Zealand who want to shut the industry down.
divination.explanation: Prediction that extraction industries will be 'critical' in future; directionally plausible given critical-minerals demand, but vague on timeframe and magnitude.

divination.statement: Importantly, it will help the industry to continue to grow, providing more New Zealanders with a prosperous future.
divination.explanation: Predicts industry growth and broader prosperity from the policy; optimistic and unquantified with no timeframe.

authenticity.statement: This builds on what we said we'd do and what we've already done under Fast-track.

civility.statement: The only thing most of them seem to be experienced at is being a bunch of Communists – they openly admit it.
civility.explanation: Personal smear on named opponents' character and competence.

civility.statement: The last three years of the Labour government oversaw a deteriorating economy, deteriorating education and health systems, worsening law and order on our streets, massively increased debt, record immigration, crumbling infrastructure, a cost-of-living crisis, and a hugely divided society.
civility.explanation: Harsh but aimed at the government's record and policy outcomes rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: We can tell you right here and now what Labour’s campaign policies will be: tax you more, borrow more, spend more – and begger the consequences.
civility.explanation: Mocking mischaracterisation of opponents' platform.

civility.statement: Let’s be clear - we will not apologise for defending our country from you wokesters and cultural Marxists.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents 'wokesters and cultural Marxists' — insult in place of substance.

civility.statement: It’s not wrong to push back against weak-kneed do-gooders who want to take our country down a path of separatism and division.
civility.explanation: 'Weak-kneed do-gooders' is a personal put-down attached to a strawman of opponents' aims.

civility.statement: We won’t have a bunch of people who have been here for five minutes trying to tell us all what our country should be.
civility.explanation: Dismissive jibe at newer arrivals rather than engagement with any position.

charisma.statement: We are not talking about the lanyard wearing, soft handed, gluten free, soy boy, virtue signallers that walk around in comfortable shoes.
charisma.explanation: Alienating caricature of opponents' supporters; rallies one side by demeaning another, the opposite of consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Let’s be clear - we will not apologise for defending our country from you wokesters and cultural Marxists.
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them framing that rallies supporters by casting opponents as enemies.

charisma.statement: For all those conservative, old school, egalitarian, common sense Labour voters out there who feel abandoned, you’ve only got one place to come, there is only one real party for the workers, and you’re looking at it.
charisma.explanation: Reaches out to disaffected Labour voters to bring them in — a persuasive appeal, but defined against others rather than genuinely cross-party.

charisma.statement: It’s not wrong to push back against weak-kneed do-gooders who want to take our country down a path of separatism and division.
charisma.explanation: Divisive framing that casts opponents as a threat rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: We won’t have a bunch of people who have been here for five minutes trying to tell us all what our country should be.
charisma.explanation: Exclusionary insider/outsider framing that alienates rather than unifies.

rigor.statement: We are not talking about the lanyard wearing, soft handed, gluten free, soy boy, virtue signallers that walk around in comfortable shoes.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem stereotyping with no evidence or argument.

rigor.statement: The Greens constantly cry martyrdom about the poor and vulnerable, but the irony is their party now only exists because of the votes from inner-city wealth.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation from three won electorates to the party's entire existence; no evidence for the 'only exists' claim.

rigor.statement: The only thing most of them seem to be experienced at is being a bunch of Communists – they openly admit it.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem with a fabricated premise ('they openly admit it') and no evidence.

rigor.statement: We can tell you right here and now what Labour’s campaign policies will be: tax you more, borrow more, spend more – and begger the consequences.
rigor.explanation: Strawman of an opponent's position with no evidence, especially as he notes Labour has released no policy.

rigor.statement: When the leaders of these unions are Labour Party candidates, sitting on Labour Party policy committees, run third party campaigns for the Labour Party in elections, and affiliated unions get a vote for the Labour Party leader, New Zealanders need to be asking who do the Unions truly work for – the workers, or Labour.
rigor.explanation: Points to real structural union–Labour links but leaps to a loaded rhetorical conclusion rather than establishing it.

rigor.statement: It’s not wrong to push back against weak-kneed do-gooders who want to take our country down a path of separatism and division.
rigor.explanation: Combines ad hominem with a strawman ('want to take our country down a path of separatism') and no evidence.

veracity.statement: Look at the Greens – they hold three seats, Auckland Central, Rongatai, and Wellington Central – all three seats are the heart of the Green Party Vote and the heart of the ‘Remuera-swiller’ types.
veracity.explanation: Factually correct that the Greens won those three electorates (Auckland Central, Wellington Central, Rongotai) in 2023; the 'Remuera-swiller' framing is rhetorical colour.

veracity.statement: The Greens constantly cry martyrdom about the poor and vulnerable, but the irony is their party now only exists because of the votes from inner-city wealth.
veracity.explanation: Misleading: the Greens polled around 11-12% nationwide, so 'only exists because of inner-city wealth' overstates the electorate-seat point into a false generalisation.

veracity.statement: The spiritual home of the Labour Party is here in the West Coast – the site of the miners’ strike in 1908, which gave birth to the party that used to represent the workers of New Zealand
veracity.explanation: The 1908 Blackball miners' strike is real and seminal to NZ's labour movement, but 'gave birth to the party' is loose — the Labour Party was founded in 1916.

veracity.statement: The only thing most of them seem to be experienced at is being a bunch of Communists – they openly admit it.
veracity.explanation: Demonstrably false — Labour front-benchers do not openly identify as Communists; a smear presented as fact.

veracity.statement: The last three years of the Labour government oversaw a deteriorating economy, deteriorating education and health systems, worsening law and order on our streets, massively increased debt, record immigration, crumbling infrastructure, a cost-of-living crisis, and a hugely divided society.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: increased government debt, a cost-of-living crisis and record net migration are broadly accurate, but the sweeping list is one-sided and several items (education/health/'divided society') are contestable and lack context.

veracity.statement: So you remember when Helen Clark was Prime Minister? She proposed to shut the West Coast down. By stopping their traditional industries.
veracity.explanation: Clark's government ended native-timber logging on West Coast public land in 2002, but 'proposed to shut the West Coast down' is a hyperbolic mischaracterisation.

veracity.statement: And here you are with about 85 percent of your land owned by the state.
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate — a large majority of the West Coast region is public conservation/Crown land, in the ~80s percent range.

veracity.statement: Back then before she did that you were the only province, from the only country exporting wood to Scandinavia.
veracity.explanation: An oddly precise 'only province from the only country' claim that is implausible and effectively unverifiable as stated.

veracity.statement: When the leaders of these unions are Labour Party candidates, sitting on Labour Party policy committees, run third party campaigns for the Labour Party in elections, and affiliated unions get a vote for the Labour Party leader, New Zealanders need to be asking who do the Unions truly work for – the workers, or Labour.
veracity.explanation: Partly grounded: affiliated unions do have a formal role in electing the Labour leader and some union figures are Labour-aligned, but the sweeping framing generalises beyond what's shown.

veracity.statement: Chris Hipkins even said at his State of the Nation speech that they will not be announcing any policy until around July.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable attribution of a timing statement to Hipkins; plausible and consistent with a delayed-policy strategy, though not independently confirmed in the text.

specificity.statement: Look at the Greens – they hold three seats, Auckland Central, Rongatai, and Wellington Central – all three seats are the heart of the Green Party Vote and the heart of the ‘Remuera-swiller’ types.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact three electorate seats — concrete and checkable.

specificity.statement: The spiritual home of the Labour Party is here in the West Coast – the site of the miners’ strike in 1908, which gave birth to the party that used to represent the workers of New Zealand
specificity.explanation: Anchors the claim to a specific event, date (1908) and place (West Coast/Blackball).

specificity.statement: The last three years of the Labour government oversaw a deteriorating economy, deteriorating education and health systems, worsening law and order on our streets, massively increased debt, record immigration, crumbling infrastructure, a cost-of-living crisis, and a hugely divided society.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates many domains but supplies no figures, dates or magnitudes.

specificity.statement: And here you are with about 85 percent of your land owned by the state.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete quantified figure.

specificity.statement: When the leaders of these unions are Labour Party candidates, sitting on Labour Party policy committees, run third party campaigns for the Labour Party in elections, and affiliated unions get a vote for the Labour Party leader, New Zealanders need to be asking who do the Unions truly work for – the workers, or Labour.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete mechanisms (candidates, policy committees, leadership vote) though without naming instances.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First has always fought and achieved changes for workers across multiple governments
specificity.explanation: No named policy, figure or timeframe — a general boast about the party's record.

specificity.statement: For all those conservative, old school, egalitarian, common sense Labour voters out there who feel abandoned, you’ve only got one place to come, there is only one real party for the workers, and you’re looking at it.
specificity.explanation: An emotional appeal ('one real party for the workers') with no concrete offer.

specificity.statement: It’s not wrong to want to take our country to a place of hard work, responsibility, and virtue.
specificity.explanation: Abstract values platitude with no policy, mechanism or measure.

divination.statement: We can tell you right here and now what Labour’s campaign policies will be: tax you more, borrow more, spend more – and begger the consequences.
divination.explanation: A prediction about a rival's yet-unannounced election policies; a partisan caricature unlikely to match the eventual detail.

strength.statement: New Zealand First has always fought and achieved changes for workers across multiple governments
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivering 'changes for workers' but names no specific enacted policy, so follow-through is asserted rather than demonstrated.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has always fought and achieved changes for workers across multiple governments
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's record of participating in multiple governments, but the 'always fought for workers' claim is vague and unverified from the text.
